articles.title: DOE eyes P5.6-B 2027 budget as conventional energy, EV programs get big boost
articles.summary: The largest percentage increase is for the Electric Vehicle Industry Development Program, whose funding rises more than sevenfold to P228.92 million from P32.46 million in 2026

blocks.text: COMMITTEE HEARING. Energy Secretary Sharon Garin at the Senate PROTECT committee hearing on Monday, April 3, 2026.
Voltaire F Domingo/Senate OSEC-SMU
The largest percentage increase is for the Electric Vehicle Industry Development Program, whose funding rises more than sevenfold to P228.92 million from P32.46 million in 2026

items: The Department of Energy (DOE) is proposing a budget of P5.58 billion for 2027, a 26% increase from 2026, with significant allocations for conventional energy development, the electric power industry, and a sevenfold increase in funding for the electric vehicle program.

Most of the DOE's funding will come from automatic appropriations, particularly a Special Account in the General Fund, which has increased significantly from previous years, while new congressional appropriations are set to decrease by 31.6%.

The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) is proposed to receive P944 million in 2027, with a slight increase from the previous year, focusing on consumer education and protection within its regulatory programs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Energy (DOE) is seeking a spending program of P5.58 billion in 2027 with the biggest allocations going to conventional energy development, the electric power industry, and energy efficiency, while funding for its electric vehicle program is set to jump more than sevenfold.

The DOE’s proposed 2027 budget is up from P4.43 billion in 2026, a 26% increase. But the amount Congress is being asked to approve as new appropriations actually falls 31.6% to P2.03 billion from P2.96 billion this year.
Instead, P3.55 billion will come from automatic appropriations, meaning funds already authorized under existing laws and not dependent on a new annual appropriation from Congress.

Almost all of DOE’s automatic appropriations come from a P3.46-billion Special Account in the General Fund, up from P1.40 billion in 2026. The account consists of government revenues already earmarked by law for energy-related purposes and kept separately within the National Treasury.

The fund traces its roots to Presidential Decree No. 910, issued in 1976 by the late dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos Sr., which created a special fund from fees, revenues, royalties, and government shares from energy resource exploration and development. The 1992 law creating the DOE later allowed up to 20% of the fund’s outstanding balance to be used for expenses necessary for the department to perform its functions.
The account includes government revenues from energy projects such as Malampaya, although not all money in the account necessarily comes from Malampaya.

Maintenance and other operating expenses account for the largest share of DOE’s full spending program at P3.26 billion. Capital outlays get P1.25 billion, while personnel services receive P1.07 billion.

The spending plan comes after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. made energy security and lower electricity costs an important theme of his 2026 State of the Nation Address, including bringing additional generation capacity online and pushing reforms meant to reduce electricity charges.

blocks.caption: [READOUT] The race to deliver cheaper power

blocks.text: Most of the DOE’s operating programs draw the bulk of their funding from the aforementioned automatic appropriations under its Special Account in the General Fund, rather than from new congressional appropriations. For 2027, DOE’s full program funding is proposed at:

items: Conventional Energy Development Program: P1.46 billion, up 88% from P775.86 million in 2026. It covers the promotion, supervision, and regulation of the exploration and production of conventional energy resources.
Electric Power Industry Development Program: P720.92 million, up 7.4% from P671.14 million
Energy Efficiency and Conservation Program: P421.08 million, down 20% from P526.03 million
Downstream Energy Development Program: P236.13 million, nearly unchanged
Electric Vehicle Industry Development Program: P228.92 million, more than seven times the P32.46 million programmed for 2026
Alternative Fuels and Energy Technologies Program: P222.03 million, down 51.5% from P457.83 million
Renewable Energy Development Program: P165.12 million, down 14.5% from P193.03 million
National and Regional Energy Planning Program: P84.82 million, down 14.8% from P99.58 million

blocks.text: The sharpest increase is for the Electric Vehicle Industry Development Program, whose funding jumps more than sevenfold to P228.92 million from P32.46 million in 2026. The program covers the regulation, promotion, research, and development of electric vehicles and charging infrastructure, with the 2027 targets showing a greater emphasis on regulating the growing charging network.

The DOE plans to process the accreditation of charging station providers and registration of charging stations within prescribed timelines and conduct eight enforcement, monitoring, inspection, and verification activities. The NEP, however, does not identify a single new project or specific allocation, such as government-funded charging stations, that accounts for the large increase.

blocks.caption: [READOUT] The Philippines’ path to EVs runs through hybrids

blocks.text: The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), meanwhile, is proposed to receive P944.07 million in 2027, up just 1.4% from P931.25 million this year.
Of this, P915.85 million consists of new appropriations, while P28.21 million comes from automatic appropriations for retirement and life insurance premiums.
Its operating budget actually falls to P341.76 million from P363.69 million.

Within its P326.15-million Electric Power Industry Regulatory Program, the largest allocation is P119.76 million for consumer education and protection. Screening and registration gets P108.27 million, monitoring of regulated entities P65.68 million, and enforcement of rules and regulations P32.44 million.
The House appropriations committee will deliberate on the DOE’s 2027 budget on Wednesday, September 2. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sandiganbayan drops plunder, graft cases vs Manuel Bonoan
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman moves to junk the cases against Bonoan as part of its bid to make him a state witness in the multi-billion flood control scandal

blocks.text: BONOAN. Former Public Works secretary arrives at the Sandiganbayan graft court in Quezon City on June 2, 2026, for the arraignment of his graft case.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
The Office of the Ombudsman moves to junk the cases against Bonoan as part of its bid to make him a state witness in the multi-billion flood control scandal

items: The Sandiganbayan 5th Division has dropped plunder and graft cases against former DPWH secretary Manuel Bonoan, although he still faces charges in the 2nd Division.
Bonoan is being considered as a state witness in a multi-billion flood control scandal, but his immunity is uncertain due to ongoing cases against him.
The Ombudsman believes Bonoan's testimony could implicate former Speaker Martin Romualdez in illegal budget insertions related to the DPWH.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Sandiganbayan 5th Division dropped the plunder and graft cases against former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) secretary Manuel Bonoan, Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Geraldine Faith Econg confirmed to Rappler on Wednesday, September 2.
“Yes, he’s been dropped [from the cases],” Econg told Rappler in a mix of Filipino and English.

Bonoan is the Office of the Ombudsman’s latest prospect to be a state witness in the multi-billion flood control scandal. He, however, is still not off the hook yet because the 2nd Division junked the Ombudsman’s bid to drop the graft case against him in August 3.

blocks.caption: Sandiganbayan denies Ombudsman’s bid to exclude Bonoan from flood control case

blocks.text: The former DPWH chief is facing two sets of cases before the Sandiganbayan, where Senator Jinggoy Estrada is accused as well: one count of graft at the 2nd Division; then a count of plunder and graft at the 5th Division.
They were charged in May after the Ombudsman found an “intricate mechanism” involving allegedly illegal budget insertions and project allocations at the DPWH in 2025.
Meanwhile, Bonoan will be released from detention since the 5th Division dropped the cases against him, while he’s on bail at the 2nd Division.

“I intend to avail myself of all remedies provided under our laws. This development does not end my legal recourse, and I will continue to place my trust in due process and the rule of law,” Estrada said.

However, Bonoan’s bid to become a state witness is still uncertain given the 2nd Division’s ruling. If he is given immunity, he will become the fifth state witness in the list that includes ex-DPWH officials like former undersecretary Roberto Bernardo and former district engineer Henry Alcantara.

blocks.caption: LIST: State witnesses in flood control corruption and what they know

blocks.text: To give immunity to state witnesses in the flood control mess, the Ombudsman and the Department of Justice’s method is to drop the witnesses as respondents from the complaints. In this way, they will not be included in the charges or cases that will be filed with the Sandiganbayan.
This was what happened to Bernardo, Alcantara, and the other witnesses.
Bonoan’s case, however, is unique because the Ombudsman moved to make him a witness only after he was arrested and charged.

In June, the Ombudsman first announced its intention to put the former DPWH chief in the list of state witnesses. The investigative body believes that Bonoan’s testimony can pin former speaker Martin Romualdez and shed light on how lawmakers allegedly inserted allocations in the national budget through the DPWH.

“The case against former Speaker Martin Romualdez is getting stronger by the day, and the reason why we accepted former DPWH Sec. Manny Bonoan as a state witness is precisely because his intention to cooperate with us is for that case specifically,” Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said in June. – With a report from Sundy Locus/Rappler.com

articles.title: Antipolo bishop: Gov’t officials must account for flood-control failures
articles.summary: LUCENA CITY — Amid the devastating floods that have hit various parts of the country in recent days, Bishop Ruperto Cruz Santos of the Diocese of Antipolo called on government officials to account…

blocks.text: LUCENA CITY — Amid the devastating floods that have hit various parts of the country in recent days, Bishop Ruperto Cruz Santos of the Diocese of Antipolo called on government officials to account for their actions and responsibilities.

“As your shepherd, I call upon those in positions of authority: Ask yourselves. Are you truly serving the people? Are you honest? Do you truly care about our nation?” Santos said in a scathing message written in Filipino titled “Hanggang Kailan” (Until When?) and posted on the diocese’s official Facebook page on Tuesday.
“You are there to protect, serve, and safeguard us. You have the power, time, and ability to address the problems of this country. But why do these recurring tragedies remain unresolved?”
“Why did funds intended for the welfare of the people fail to reach where they were supposed to go? Why have so many enriched themselves while the nation is sinking?” he asked.
Santos said the country has once again been plunged into deep suffering by seemingly endless flooding caused by the southwest monsoon, or “habagat.”
The weather disturbances have triggered widespread flooding, destroyed livelihoods and crops, and damaged infrastructure that should have helped protect communities from disasters.
“Many families have been forced to evacuate, many areas have become impassable, and once again, many Filipinos are asking: How long?” Santos said.
The bishop acknowledged that the rains have been heavy and that a lack of discipline, including improper waste disposal, has contributed to flooding.

“But these are not the only reasons. There is a deeper wound that we must acknowledge: projects that were supposed to prevent flooding, but were never started, never built, or never fulfilled their intended purpose,” he said.

“Funds intended to protect our communities were not properly used. What should have been our defense against disasters became ghosts — ghost projects that were never seen, never felt, and never helped the people,” he lamented.
Santos stressed, however, that corruption and ghost projects are not the fault of ordinary Filipinos.
“All these are the result of the evil, greed, and negligence of those in power,” he said.
The bishop said Filipinos also have a responsibility to help rid the government of corrupt officials through their choices at the ballot box.

“In the coming elections, be discerning. Do not be swayed by temporary favors or handouts. The price of accepting a few thousand pesos in exchange for your vote is years of suffering, destroyed livelihoods, and lost hope. Have compassion for our country. Have compassion for ourselves. Have compassion for the generations to come,” Santos said.
Despite the situation, Santos appealed to Filipinos not to lose hope and to continue putting their faith in God.

“In the midst of the storm, let us hold hands. In the midst of the floods, let us help one another. In the midst of corruption, let us stand firm. In the midst of darkness, let us be the light,” the bishop said.

Meanwhile, Sen. Vicente Sotto III has filed Proposed Senate Resolution No. 631 seeking a Senate investigation into the root causes and devastating effects of typhoons and monsoon rains, with the aim of strengthening disaster mitigation efforts.

Sotto said the probe should assess the country’s disaster mitigation measures and the resilience of public infrastructure, particularly flood-control projects intended to protect communities from flooding. /dp

articles.title: Oriental Mindoro health office issues advisory on haze, air quality
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Provincial Health Office (PHO) of Oriental Mindoro urged residents to take precautionary measures against the possible health effects of haze and air pollution,…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Provincial Health Office (PHO) of Oriental Mindoro urged residents to take precautionary measures against the possible health effects of haze and air pollution, with Provincial Health Officer Dr. Cielo Ante leading the call for vigilance.

“Our health and safety are our topmost priority. By taking preventive steps together, we can protect ourselves, our families, and our entire community,” Dr. Ante said in a public health advisory released on Tuesday (September 1).
The health warning comes amid concerns over haze — a mixture of fine particulate matter that can irritate the eyes, nose, throat, and lungs — and its potential health impacts.

According to the PHO, extended exposure to haze may lead to “itching, redness, or watering of the eyes, irritation or pain in the nose and throat, coughing and hoarseness, headaches and dizziness, a difficulty of breathing or shortness of breath, the worsening of asthma and other respiratory and heart conditions.”

Dr. Ante urged all residents to follow these guidelines by reducing outdoor activities and to avoid strenuous physical exertion outdoors, stay indoors with windows and doors closed whenever air quality is poor, consume plenty of water, and to wear protective N95 masks or use the equivalent respirator when going outside becomes necessary. /jpv

articles.title: DOH monitoring possible rise in hospital cases linked to haze
articles.summary: The Department of Health (DOH) is monitoring the possible increase in hospitalizations and medical consultations linked to the haze affecting parts of Luzon and the Visayas from the wildfires in…

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 9:09am

The Department of Health (DOH) is monitoring the possible increase in hospitalizations and medical consultations linked to the haze affecting parts of Luzon and the Visayas from the wildfires in Indonesia.
On Wednesday, DOH Environmental and Occupational Health Division chief Dr. Gabriel Borlongan said there has been no reported increase in hospital admissions or consultations due to the haze so far.

“Sa ngayon po, nagmo-monitor pa rin po tayo pero wala pa pong nare-report po na naitatala na mas marami ang na-ospital, nagpapakonsulta, inuubo, o kaya lumalala ang hika,” he told GMA News’ Unang Balita in an interview.
(Right now, we are still monitoring but there are no reports yet of more people being hospitalized, seeking consultations, coughing, or worsening asthma.)
“Pero aantabayanan po namin yan dito sa DOH kasi gusto po natin mapaigting ang ating surveillance para tunay po nating makita kung ano po ba yung kalagayan ng ating mga mamamayan,” he added.
(But we will keep an eye on that here at the DOH because we want to intensify our surveillance so that we can truly see what the situation of our citizens is.)
The haze contains fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, which can enter the respiratory system and potentially reach the bloodstream, according to Borlongan.
Exposure may cause coughing, nose and throat irritation, difficulty breathing, and the worsening of asthma and other lung conditions, he said.

Children, older adults, pregnant women, and people with existing respiratory or cardiovascular diseases such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), heart disease, and a history of stroke are considered more vulnerable.
Borlongan advised people to reduce their exposure when air quality is poor.
Those who need to go outside are advised to use an N95 respirator or a similar mask. Double masking may also be considered if an N95 is not available.

The DOH is in with the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) as the agency is preparing an advisory for the public, employers, and institutions on measures to reduce exposure to the haze.

Borlongan said that as of the 6 a.m. monitoring by the DENR, air quality had generally improved in Metro Manila. But, some areas in Las Piñas, Makati, Malabon, and Parañaque remained unhealthy for sensitive groups, he added. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Pangasinan buri bags headed for New York Filipino Fashion Week
articles.summary: CALASIAO, Pangasinan – Bags woven from buri, a common palm, and other indigenous materials from Pangasinan have found their way to the international market and are set to take center stage in New…

blocks.text: CALASIAO, Pangasinan – Bags woven from buri, a common palm, and other indigenous materials from Pangasinan have found their way to the international market and are set to take center stage in New York City during FashionPhilippines New York 2026 on September 16-18.

The Olly+Fely brand is owned and managed by Kawayan Nature EcoFriendly Product Trading, a Bolinao-based enterprise that produces fashionable yet sustainably made bags from buri, a material abundant on Santiago Island in Bolinao town and the nearby island town of Anda.

“We are proud and honored to share that Olly+Fely officially joins the roster of emerging Filipino brands for FashionPhilippines New York 2026,” said Precious Cayaon, who, together with her husband Jeff, owns and manages the community-based enterprise.
Their business works with local residents who weave indigenous materials into bags and other fashion pieces, turning a traditional craft into products that now reach markets beyond the Philippines.
“For Olly+Fely, this marks another meaningful step in bringing proudly Filipino craftsmanship and woven artistry to the global fashion stage,” Cayaon said.
When the couple entered the industry, many island weavers were on the verge of giving up their craft because traditional designs fetched low prices.
The couple started their business modestly, producing simple bags, purses and mats.

Over the years, however, the buri-weaving industry has experienced a revival. Islanders—mostly women—are now engaged in stripping, dyeing and weaving buri fibers into elegant and sustainable fashion pieces that appeal to environmentally conscious consumers around the world.

The bags, Cayaon said, have also “leveled up,” now incorporating premium-grain leather, quality hardware and carefully selected accessories. Yet at the heart of every piece remain the skilled women of Bolinao, whose hands continue to transform raw fibers into works of fashion and craft.

Now, Olly+Fely is bringing these creations to New York, where the Accessories Council Trade Show describes the brand as embodying “whimsy and craftsmanship,” creating character-driven accessories that celebrate individuality through playful designs and thoughtful handmade details.

From the quiet weaving communities of Pangasinan’s islands to one of the world’s fashion capitals, the journey of buri reflects not only the revival of a traditional craft but also the growing reach of Filipino artistry.
FashionPhilippines New York 2026 is organized by the Center for International Trade Expositions and Missions in partnership with the Accessories Council. /jpv

articles.title: ‘Verde Island Passage Week’ set Sept. 21–25, aims for marine protection
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Environmental advocates, coastal communities, and fisherfolk will come together from Sept. 21 to 25 for the Verde Island Passage (VIP) Week 2026, with organizers…

image.caption: Photo taken in September 2021 shows colorful corals that attest to the uniqueness of Verde Island Passage as an area rich in biodiversity and thus needing protection from unbridled commercial activity and industrial development. The area mainly covers the waters off Tingloy and Mabini towns in Batan

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Environmental advocates, coastal communities, and fisherfolk will come together from Sept. 21 to 25 for the Verde Island Passage (VIP) Week 2026, with organizers renewing calls for stronger protection of one of the country’s richest marine biodiversity areas.
The Protect Verde Island Passage (VIP) Network announced that this year’s celebration will carry the theme “Tayo ang Alon: Sama-samang Pagkilos Para sa Karagatan, Kabuhayan, at Kinabukasan.”

The campaign seeks to highlight the role of communities and ordinary citizens in protecting the Verde Island Passage, which has been described as the “Center of the Center of Marine Shorefish Biodiversity” and the “Amazon of the Oceans” because of its exceptional marine biodiversity.

The network said the term “VIP” or “Very Important People” should refer not only to government officials and other influential individuals but also to fishermen, coastal residents, young people and communities whose food, livelihoods and future depend on the sea.
“VIP tayo,” the network said, emphasizing that protecting the passage requires collective action from people who live along and depend on its waters.
Organizers said the “Tayo ang Alon” theme recognizes that collective action can build a powerful force for the protection of the Verde Island Passage.
One of the major advocacy goals of the VIP Week is to push for the passage of the Verde Island Passage Protected Seascape (VIPPS) Bill in Congress and the Senate.
The network called on the public to support the proposed legislation and join efforts to strengthen protection for the passage.
“Ang VIP ay para sa VIP. At tayo ang VIP,” the group said.

The Verde Island Passage stretches between the provinces of Batangas, Oriental Mindoro, Occidental Mindoro, Marinduque and Romblon and is recognized as an area of exceptional marine biodiversity and importance to coastal communities. /jpv

articles.title: Estrada to pursue legal remedies as Sandigan drops Bonoan as coaccused
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Jinggoy Estrada said that he will pursue all available legal remedies after the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division dropped former Public Works and Highways Secretary Manuel…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Jinggoy Estrada said that he will pursue all available legal remedies after the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division dropped former Public Works and Highways Secretary Manuel Bonoan as a coaccused in the plunder case.
In a statement, Estrada said he respected the decision of the anti-graft court but stressed that he still had other legal options available.

“While I respect the decision of the Sandiganbayan, I wish to emphasize that there remain legal remedies available to me under our judicial system, which my legal team will carefully study and pursue at the appropriate time,” Estrada said Tuesday.
“I intend to avail myself of all remedies provided under our laws,” he added.
Estrada said the Sandiganbayan’s decision did not end his legal recourse, adding that he would continue to rely on due process and the rule of law.
“My faith in our judicial system remains firm. I will continue to stand by the truth and pursue every lawful means available to protect my rights and clear my name and honor,” he said.

His statement came as the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division dropped the plunder and graft charges against Bonoan, who was accused alongside Estrada and several Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials over an alleged scheme involving P573 million in kickbacks.
Bonoan had been the subject of a bid by the Office of the Ombudsman to discharge him as an accused and turn him into a state witness in other flood control corruption cases.

He had also testified before the Sandiganbayan in the case against former Sen. Ramon “Bong” Revilla Jr., where he claimed that all senators in 2024 had availed themselves of a “leadership fund” allotted by the DPWH under the 2025 national budget. /jpv

articles.title: Thousands pay homage to Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladic
articles.summary: SARAJEVO — Several thousand Bosnian Serbs paid tribute on Tuesday to former military commander and convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, who died while serving a life sentence for genocide.…

blocks.text: SARAJEVO — Several thousand Bosnian Serbs paid tribute on Tuesday to former military commander and convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, who died while serving a life sentence for genocide.

Mladic died on Thursday at the age of 84 in The Hague, where he was convicted of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the Bosnian war, including for his role in the Srebrenica massacre, Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since World War II.

Television images showed people gathered at the main square in central Banja Luka, the capital of Bosnia’s Serb entity, and them marching on the city’s principal boulevard holding up a banner proclaiming: “Commander, thank you for everything.”
Some lit smoke flares and waved flags of the Serb entity and then lit candles at a monument dedicated to Serb soldiers killed during the war and lined up to write messages in a condolence book.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos on Monday criticised Serbia’s plans to bury Mladic with state honours.
Mladic’s conviction for wartime killings as the former Yugoslavia descended into carnage after the fall of communism led the international press to dub him the “Butcher of Bosnia”.
The 1992-1995 war left around 100,000 people dead and 2.2 million displaced.
Mladic was the military face of a brutal trio, led on the political side by ex-Yugoslav president Slobodan Milosevic and former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic. /dl

articles.title: Senator Ed Markey wins Massachusetts Democratic primary
articles.summary:
Incumbent, 80, beats back challenge from Seth Moulton, who argued Markey was too old to be effective at his job

Senator Ed Markey won the Democratic primary in Massachusetts on Tuesday,…

blocks.text: Senator Ed Markey won the Democratic primary in Massachusetts on Tuesday, beating back a challenge from Seth Moulton, a congressman who tried to unseat him by arguing to voters his opponent was too old to be effective at his job.
Massachusetts is heavily Democratic, making the senator favored to win a third full term in the November general election, where he faces the Republican nominee John Deaton.

The 80-year-old incumbent, according to the Associated Press, easily defeated his 47-year-old rival, at a moment when Democratic voters agonize over the age of some lawmakers, a concern that was amplified by Joe Biden’s disastrous re-election bid in 2024, and Kamala Harris’s subsequent failure to keep Donald Trump from returning to the White House.

In primaries elsewhere in the country this year, Democratic voters unseated a handful of long-serving incumbents in favor of younger, progressive challengers who vowed to break from the party orthodoxy on issues like support for Israel.

But the dynamics in Massachusetts were somewhat of a reversal, with Markey being a longtime advocate for progressive causes and Moulton, who was born after Markey was first elected to the House in 1976, staking out more moderate positions on certain issues.

The senator is a champion of proposals to create a universal single-payer healthcare system and enact sweeping clean energy policies known as the “Green New Deal”, and had the backing of top congressional progressives, including Vermont independent senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren, also of Massachusetts.

Moulton, who first won election to a north-eastern Massachusetts district in 2014, has not endorsed single payer healthcare proposals, and shortly before Tuesday’s primary election apologized for saying that he did not want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete” – comments made after Trump beat Harris in the 2024 election in part by vowing to curb transgender rights.

The question of when a lawmaker is too old to continue serving loomed large when the candidates met for a debate in August. “I think everyone watching this debate can see that I’m more energized than I’ve ever been before in my life. I am crisscrossing the state. I’m fighting for families,” the senator said.

Moulton said his opponent had spent less time holding town halls and candidate forums, and pounced when the senator replied to a question about what AI tools he used by answering “whatever is inside of my iPhone and my iPad – whatever comes up”.

“Senator, if you don’t even know what you’re using on your phone or your iPad, this is why we need a new generation of leaders to regulate these technologies to make sure that they are safe,” Moulton said.

In the days before the primary, polls showed Markey with a sizable lead over Moulton. In 2020, the senator had fended off a challenge from congressman Joe Kennedy III, a member of the state’s best-known political dynasty.

articles.title: Prosecutors can seek death penalty against accused in Charlie Kirk shooting, judge says
articles.summary: A judge ruled on Tuesday that Tyler Robinson, the man accused of fatally shooting prominent U.S. conservative activist Charlie Kirk on a Utah college campus last year, should face trial on murder…

image.caption: Tyler Robinson, left, charged in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, speaks with defence attorney Staci Visser during a preliminary hearing on Tuesday. (Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

A judge ruled on Tuesday that Tyler Robinson, the man accused of fatally shooting prominent U.S. conservative activist Charlie Kirk on a Utah college campus last year, should face trial on murder ‌charges in a case eligible for the death penalty.
Kirk fatally shot during appearance at event on Utah campus last year

Utah District Court Judge Tony Graf made the ruling at a hearing where prosecutors laid out what they called "overwhelming" evidence that a capital trial of Robinson, 23, was warranted for the murder of one of the U.S. political right's most prominent figures. Defence lawyers had argued the shooting did not meet the standard for a death penalty charge.
An arraignment will follow the probable cause ruling. Robinson has yet ​to enter a plea.

Utah County attorneys accused the former apprentice electrician of firing ​the single shot that killed Kirk, 31, as he held one of his trademark campus debates that helped propel him to national prominence.
Robinson faces seven charges, among them aggravated murder for endangering the lives of others at ​the event. That count carries the death penalty in Utah.
'Great risk of death' to others, prosecutor says
Utah County prosecutor Ryan McBride presented video of ⁠what he said was Robinson taking up ⁠a sniper position at Utah Valley University in Orem on Sept. ‌10, 2025, before he shot Kirk.
He displayed pictures that he said showed Robinson created a "great risk of death" to others, with Kirk's security detail only feet away from Kirk when he was shot.
McBride said the four rounds in Robinson's rifle demonstrated that the shooter was prepared to fire more rounds if the first missed, further endangering others.

"He lay ⁠down in a prone position, and he would have seen this mass of people, of 3,000 plus people there for the event, took aim, put his crosshairs on Charlie Kirk, and fired," McBride told the court.
Defence argues shooting only endangered Kirk
Defence lawyer Staci Visser said the shooting endangered no one but Kirk, ‌arguing the crime did not meet the standard of aggravated murder.
Visser said the assailant did not engage with anyone else or reload the weapon, but simply shot the gun and ran away.
"There is one act. There is one shot. There is one bullet. There is one victim," Visser told the court. "There was no evidence that would suggest that anyone else was threatened."
During ​the hearing, the prosecutor cited test results that showed Robinson's DNA was on the alleged murder weapon. Defence lawyer Michael Burt questioned the reliability of that testing.

McBride alleged Robinson, who was ⁠in a relationship with his roommate Lance Twiggs, targeted Kirk for his political views against same-sex marriage and transgender rights. That argument could bolster ⁠the prosecution as it pursues the death penalty.
He cited a text message from Robinson in which he allegedly told Twiggs he ⁠shot ⁠Kirk because "some hate can't be negotiated out."
Defence attorney Richard Novak said it was ​unclear what Robinson referred to by "hate" and the ⁠wording did not imply he opposed Kirk's political views.
Among those in ​the packed courtroom were Kirk's parents, Robert and Kathryn, and his wife, Erika, who has taken leadership of the late activist's conservative youth organization.

items: Charlie Kirk's death has revealed simmering divisions in MAGA world
Vance vows to go after 'festering violence on the far left' while hosting Charlie Kirk's radio show

blocks.text: A co-founder ​of conservative youth organization Turning Point USA, Kirk ⁠was credited with energizing young voters behind U.S. President Donald Trump's 2024 re-election campaign.

His killing, captured in cellphone video that spread widely on social media, is among a series of attacks on U.S. political figures in recent years that have fuelled debate over political violence in a deeply polarized country.

articles.title: Federal judge tosses Trump lawsuit over young trans athletes in California school sports
articles.summary:
In a major LGBTQ+ rights victory, the justice department cannot force the state to ban trans girls from women’s sports

A federal judge has dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit…

blocks.text: A federal judge has dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit challenging California’s policy of allowing transgender youth to play on sports teams that match their gender, a major loss for Donald Trump and the Department of Justice (DoJ).

The justice department had been fighting for a year to force California to ban trans girls from women’s sports, with the president directly singling out one trans track and field athlete in online attacks and regularly mocking trans athletes in his speeches.

Since 2013, California has allowed trans girls to play on girls’ teams in schools, an LGBTQ+-inclusive policy that impacted a small fraction of the state’s youth. More than 20 states now have similar laws. California’s policy sparked minimal controversy for years until Republicans and anti-LGBTQ+ groups across the US made attacks on trans people a central part of their campaigns in recent election cycles.

In July 2025, the Trump administration sued California, alleging that its trans-inclusive sports policies violated Title IX, the federal law prohibiting sex discrimination in schools. The lawsuit focused on five trans girls who played sports, accusing them of taking opportunities away from other girls. The DoJ argued California was obligated to ban trans girls from girls’ teams while the state’s schools received federal funding.

On Monday, US judge Cynthia Valenzuela issued a major victory for California and trans rights, with a final order dismissing the DoJ’s suit and terminating the case. The judge argued that the US government failed to give notice to the state that its federal funding was contingent on schools banning trans girls from sports. The ruling noted the federal government has repeatedly shifted its guidelines on this issue over the last decade.

Although Trump issued an executive order last year calling for trans girls to be blocked from girls’ sports, the judge said that order did not constitute clear notice to California that it would lose funding if it maintained trans-inclusive policies.

The ruling came two months after the US supreme court’s conservative supermajority upheld Republican-backed laws in West Virginia and Idaho that barred trans girls from girls’ teams. Valenzuela noted the supreme court decision was narrow, with the justices concluding that those states could maintain their anti-trans laws, without saying every school must adopt similar restrictions.
The supreme court’s ruling did not call for a national ban on trans youth athletes nor did it address the question of whether Title IX permits trans girls to play on girls’ teams.

A DoJ spokesperson said Tuesday it was “evaluating our options for appeal”, writing in an email: “We are disappointed by the Court’s order and remain committed to enforcing President Trump’s agenda preventing boys from playing in girls’ sports.” The California Interscholastic Federation, which oversees school sports and was the target of the lawsuit, declined to comment.

California officials noted last year that out of the state’s nearly 6 million students in the K-12 public school system, it was estimated that there were fewer than 10 trans student-athletes actively participating in sports.
But youth targeted by the lawsuit and the Trump administration’s policy attacks have said the impact has been severe, with out trans students facing harassment at games and death threats.

Rainbow Families Action, a California group supporting trans youth, celebrated the ruling, saying: “This lifts a significant shadow that has been hanging over the joyous and expanding success story of girls’ and women’s sports in California.”

The group said the ruling sent a clear message that schools across the state must allow trans youth to continue playing on the teams that match their gender, noting school districts had been facing pressure over the last year to “defy California law and to pass illegal and harmful policies that comply in advance with [Trump’s] discriminatory executive orders that hurt transgender children”.

Trevor Norcross, father of a trans youth athlete targeted by the DoJ lawsuit, said the ruling was an “acknowledgment that the Trump administration has been overreaching since the beginning of his term”. He said he hoped the decision would help support trans youth athletes across the country: “While this is a great victory in California … the fight is not over in other states.”

articles.title: Trump nominates loyalist Hung Cao to be permanent navy secretary
articles.summary:
Acting secretary picked for top role as critics accuse president of overworking sailors during war with Iran

Donald Trump said Tuesday that he is nominating acting navy secretary Hung Cao…

blocks.text: Donald Trump said Tuesday that he is nominating acting navy secretary Hung Cao for the permanent job, giving the navy combat veteran the nod as concerns have emerged that some sailors have been stretched to the limit during the Iran war.
Cao has been serving as acting navy secretary since John Phelan departed the job unexpectedly and without explanation in late April.

Unlike Phelan, who had not served in the military or had a civilian leadership role in the service, Cao spent 25 years in the navy as a special operations officer and went on to serve with Seal teams and special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan.
“I am pleased to nominate a true WARRIOR,” Trump wrote on social media, prodding the Senate “to confirm this Warfighter, ASAP.”
Cao on social media called it the “honor of a lifetime to lead the great warriors of the Navy and Marine Corps team”.

Cao’s nomination comes as some, including Democrats in Congress, believe Trump has been overtaxing the navy. The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier’s nine-month deployment to support the Iran war has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea.

Concerns grew about the Lincoln’s deployment following reports of deteriorating mental health among the crew and shortages of supplies including food and hygiene products. Several Democratic lawmakers, including senators Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ruben Gallego of Arizona, are pressing for accountability from the Pentagon over conditions onboard the ship.

Cao served as navy undersecretary before his current role. He championed returning to duty service members who refused a Biden-era mandate to take the Covid vaccine. Cao, a Trump loyalist, also said he had no problem with the navy’s demonstration squadron, the Blue Angels, flying so low over a crowded Florida beach in July that chairs and tents went flying.
after newsletter promotion

Cao’s nomination also comes at a time of upheaval in the top ranks of the US military. In the latest example, army secretary Dan Driscoll submitted his resignation this week amid widespread reports of tension between him and defense secretary Pete Hegseth.

articles.title: Padilla, Lapid among motorists affected by NLEx traffic, flooding
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Sens. Robinhood Padilla and Lito Lapid were among the motorists caught in the massive traffic jam along the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) as severe flooding rendered parts of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sens. Robinhood Padilla and Lito Lapid were among the motorists caught in the massive traffic jam along the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) as severe flooding rendered parts of the expressway impassable in San Simon, Pampanga.
Padilla said it took him seven hours to travel from his home to the San Simon exit, after leaving at around 4:30 a.m. and getting out of the area at about 11:30 a.m.
“Nadaan po ako mismo sa NLEx kahapon… Pitong oras po… sa San Simon pa lang po ’yon, hindi po kami nakarating ng Pangasinan,” Padilla said during the Senate session on Tuesday.
(I personally passed through NLEX yesterday… It took seven hours… and that was only as far as San Simon. We didn’t even make it to Pangasinan.)
He said they initially expected the floodwaters to have subsided when they returned to NLEx later in the day, but found that the water had risen further.
“Makikita n’yo po sa video, mas tumaas pa ’yung tubig,” Padilla said.
(You can see in the video that the water rose even higher.)
Padilla said the flooding also left alternative routes, including MacArthur Highway, impassable.

Sen. Joel Villanueva, in his privilege speech, said Lapid was likewise affected by the traffic. He said the congestion stretched for about 10 kilometers, with some motorists reportedly spending as long as 22 hours on the road.

Villanueva called on the NLEx Corp. to consider waiving or refunding toll fees for motorists affected by the flooding. He also urged the operator to pursue long-term measures to address recurring flooding along the expressway.
The Inquirer sought comment from NLEx on the matter but has yet to receive a response as of posting time.
The NLEx operator has previously apologized to motorists stranded in sections of the expressway that became impassable because of severe flooding. /dp

articles.title: Zelensky warns airlines Russian skies not safe due to Ukraine drones
articles.summary: KYIV — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday warned airlines and passengers that Russian airspace would be “completely unsafe” and filled with Ukrainian drones for the…

blocks.text: KYIV — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday warned airlines and passengers that Russian airspace would be “completely unsafe” and filled with Ukrainian drones for the duration of the war.

“Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” he said in his nightly address.
“Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such — not a single civilian aircraft. There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin responded by branding Zelensky’s comments “a declaration of state terrorism”.
“They are asking us to resume negotiations… but you don’t negotiate with terrorists,” Putin said in a televised news conference.
More than four years after the start of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, both Moscow and Kyiv have intensified their deadly strikes.
At least 12 people were killed on Tuesday in Kyiv and the surrounding region during fresh massive overnight Russian strikes.
Air traffic at Russian airports is also regularly disrupted by the approach of Ukrainian drones, the number of which has increased in recent months.
“We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelensky said.
“Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation,” he added. “The sky over Russia is currently for drones… as long as the war continues.”

He said Ukraine would, however, clear its drones from Russian skies when its partners requested it, “for the sake of diplomacy, for the sake of negotiations… for specific periods of time and in specific destinations”.
Diplomatic efforts under US mediation to end the conflict have stalled since the outbreak of war in the Middle East in February. /dl

articles.title: Iran strikes back against latest US attacks
articles.summary: TEHRAN — Iran launched strikes on Wednesday targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan after vowing “severe punishment” in response to US attacks, including one that…

blocks.text: TEHRAN — Iran launched strikes on Wednesday targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan after vowing “severe punishment” in response to US attacks, including one that the Iranian Red Crescent said left four people dead at a wedding celebration.
US Marine Corps base Camp Titin in Jordan was targeted for an “intense ballistic missile attack”, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said early Wednesday, according to Iranian news outlet Tasnim.

The Jordanian army said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired from Iran, and did not confirm any injuries or hits on the US training camp located on the Gulf of Aqaba, near the borders with Israel and Saudi Arabia. Three other missiles landed in remote areas, it said.

Missile and drone attacks were also reported in Kuwait, where the army said they were responding to Iranian hostilities, and AFP reporters in Bahrain heard alert sirens for airborne attacks go off early Wednesday.

The latest round of conflict began when Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday, the first known strikes in several weeks, after which Tehran’s forces targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks.

More US strikes came on Tuesday, with Iranian state television reporting that explosions were heard in the country’s south along the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway and on an island in the Gulf, and that US forces hit an airport in the southern province of Kerman.

The Iranian Red Crescent said shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a home where a wedding celebration was taking place in the city of Kuhestak, killing four people, including a child, and wounding more than 50.
And the official IRNA news agency said that “four projectiles hit areas within the counties of Chabahar and Konarak,” without specifying whether there was any damage.

Asked if the US military had received any credible reports of civilian casualties from the Tuesday strikes, US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson, Captain Tim Hawkins, said “the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” referring to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards.

CENTCOM had earlier said on X that the strikes followed “recent attempted attacks by (the Revolutionary Guards) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region”.

US President Donald Trump said the “large and powerful” strikes were “in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait” and “the Iranians shooting eight missiles, all successfully knocked down, at our Military Base in Jordan”.
Earlier, Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi warned on X that Washington “will regret its new attacks”, saying that “severe punishment awaits the aggressors”.
Tankers attacked
After six months of war, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed and the United States persisting with a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington said its forces attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak on Sunday to prevent Tehran from planting mines in the strait’s key shipping lanes.
The Middle East war began in late February with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
A fragile ceasefire between the United States and Iran collapsed after attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies flowed before the war.
Greek maritime risk management firm Marisks said Tuesday that two crude tankers were hit by “unknown projectiles” late the previous day.
One of the incidents had been publicised earlier by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency, which added that no casualties or environmental effects had been reported.
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian meanwhile vowed Tuesday to match any US move to return to a deal aimed at ending the war.
He also warned that a return by the United States to “a policy of pressure and threats could derail the path of diplomacy”. /dl

articles.summary: Iran vows to prevent oil exports from the Gulf in response to US threats and sanctions, while the US military targets Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps assets

blocks.text: ATTACK. Iranian missiles are launched, as Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had carried out attacks against a U.S. base in Jordan and 21 other targets in the Gulf on Wednesday in retaliation for American strikes around the Strait of Hormuz, from a location given as Tehran, Iran, released June 10, 2026, in this still image taken from a video.
WANA via Pool/via REUTERS
Iran vows to prevent oil exports from the Gulf in response to US threats and sanctions, while the US military targets Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps assets

items: The US launched airstrikes on Iran, leading to Iranian retaliation and escalating tensions in the region, which have impacted global oil prices.
Despite recent hostilities, both nations have previously engaged in a month of relative calm, with Trump expressing skepticism about future agreements with Iran.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The US launched a barrage of airstrikes on Iran on Tuesday, September 1, prompting Iranian retaliation in the most serious escalation in weeks in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices and weighed on President Donald Trump’s popularity at home.

The strikes followed a weekend exchange of fire – the first since July – and attacks on Monday, September 1, on two tankers leaving the Strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping. Global oil prices rose more than $4 a barrel on Tuesday, settling at a five-week high.

Tehran remained defiant, warning that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by Trump to hit Iran “hard” and a warning from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Washington was about to impose new sanctions.

Five people were killed and 50 wounded at a wedding near Sirik, a coastal area on the Strait of Hormuz, the Iranian Red Crescent reported. The Mehr news agency said a four-year-old child was among those killed, while the IRNA news agency, citing a provincial official, put the number of wounded at 68.
There was no immediate US reaction to the reports.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement the US attacks would “tighten the lock” on the Strait of Hormuz, which carried one of every five barrels of the world’s oil before the war.
“If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be able to export oil,” Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf was quoted as saying by Iranian media.
Neither threats of strikes nor new economic sanctions appear to have materially changed the position of Tehran, which has been under heavy economic sanctions for half a century.
The second round of US strikes in three days followed a month of relative calm in which the US and Iran mostly held their fire while exchanging hostile statements.

Trump called Tuesday’s strikes retaliation for Iranian attempts to place sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz after the US military announced last week it had cleared a strategic shipping lane of Iranian mines, and for Iranian missiles fired at a US military base in Jordan.

Later, sirens sounded again in Jordan, state television reported. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it launched a heavy ballistic missile attack on the US Marine Corps base in Jordan and “killed a large number of US forces.”
Iran’s Fars news agency called it a retaliatory operation that fired missiles and drones.

There were no casualties so far from the Iranian attack on facilities in Jordan, two US officials told Reuters. This was based on initial information and could change as Iranian attacks continued, the officials said.

Jordan’s armed forces said its air defense systems dealt with 13 ballistic missiles that entered the kingdom’s airspace. The military said 10 missiles were intercepted and destroyed, while three fell in remote areas far from population centers.

Iranian media also reported the country’s military targeted a US base in Bahrain with a large-scale drone attack, and the Kuwaiti army reported its air defenses were responding to a hostile drone attack. Since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, Iran has responded with missile and drone strikes on US allies in the region.
Trump had warned Iran against doing so again following Tuesday’s assault.

“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!” Trump said in a social media post.
In an interview with Fox News, Trump played down the prospects of another ceasefire.
The US and Iran reached a deal in June that quickly fell apart, largely over interpretations of Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz.
“I think an agreement with them isn’t worth the paper it’s written on. We gave them a lot of chances,” Trump told Fox News.

The US military’s Central Command said it had completed a wave of strikes against IRGC targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites.
The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members.
More than 50,000 US service members are currently operating across the Middle East and remain vigilant, lethal, and prepared to continue executing operations directed by the Commander in Chief.

Iranian media reported multiple strikes, including a US missile attack near the city of Ahvaz and at the civilian Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, while explosions were heard in the southeastern port of Chabahar, the port city of Bandar Abbas on the Strait of Hormuz, and in Asaluyeh, a critical gas hub on the Gulf coast.
Iran’s state broadcaster also reported explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait.
The Fars news agency cited an IRGC spokesperson as saying the US “will regret its new attacks.”

The six-month-old conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US air bases in Jordan. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says Tennessee trip isn't sending wrong message amid trade war
articles.summary: Premier Danielle Smith defended her upcoming personal trip to the United States when asked if it was sending the wrong message amid an active trade war with Canada's southern neighbours.

image.caption: Premier Danielle Smith says her upcoming trip to Tennessee does not send the wrong message after trade negotiations broke down between Canada and the U.S. last month. (CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New
Premier Danielle Smith defended her upcoming personal trip to the United States when asked if it was sending the wrong message amid an active trade war with Canada's southern neighbours.
Smith was asked Tuesday about upcoming U.S. trip amid trade war
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith denied suggestions Tuesday that her upcoming trip to Tennessee could be sending the wrong message amid a trade war between Canada and its southern neighbour.

"I hope no one's surprised to hear that I believe it's my job to continue reaching out at all levels to various influencers in the United States and get our message across that we have an incredible partnership," Smith told reporters at an unrelated news conference in Calgary.
"It's an incredible economic partnership, trade partnership, defence partnership, and we want it to continue."

The premier is set to travel to Nashville later this week on a personal trip, and her office said she'll be taking time out to meet with the head of the city's chamber of commerce, state tourism commissioner Mark Ezell and the chief executive of a Nashville tourism marketing agency.

items: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith to meet with U.S. officials next week amid trade war

blocks.text: While Smith positioned the meetings as examples of her diplomacy efforts during the trade dispute, she also said a priority would be learning more about how Calgary can position itself as "Nashville north" and boost investment in the music industry.
"It is a personal trip, but being down there I thought I'd take advantage of some of the expertise that's down there," she said.
Smith said the Tennessee capital made changes 25 years ago to make itself a music industry haven and economic powerhouse and she wants to find out how.
"I want to find out a little bit about what that is and see if we can develop some excellent partnerships with the music industry so that we can do a transfer of talent and transfer of expertise."
Smith also said Alberta wants to expand its tourism economy and that it's a good time to discuss leveraging Calgary's assets.
Nathan Cooper, Alberta's senior representative to the United States, is set to join the meetings.

Smith has said she wants to see Canadian officials double down on diplomacy efforts and get back to the negotiating table with the United States before Ottawa implements retaliatory tariffs next week.

items: Retaliatory tariffs could raise costs for Canadian businesses already weathering the trade war

blocks.text: Ottawa's tariffs, set to take effect Sept. 8, are in response to 50 per cent tariffs that U.S. President Donald Trump ordered on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods starting Aug. 22.
Trade talks broke down in the final hours before the U.S. duties kicked in, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying the United States was asking for too much and offering too little.

articles.title: US officials defend Venezuela oil deal amid questions over rebuilding plan
articles.summary:
Government talks up pact but Venezuelan opposition alarmed that democracy yet to return after Maduro exit

Trump administration officials on Tuesday defended a highly contentious deal giving…

blocks.text: Trump administration officials on Tuesday defended a highly contentious deal giving the US control of a significant chunk of Venezuelan oil reserves, arguing that the sweeping agreement would help stabilize and rebuild democracy in the shattered South American country while giving Washington vital access to strategic crude reserves.
Last week, Donald Trump announced a “groundbreaking” deal that would give the US “majority” control over 65bn barrels – roughly one-fifth – of Venezuela’s oil reserves.

On Tuesday, US officials argued that the agreement would create a stable economic platform to restore Venezuelan democracy after nearly three decades of autocratic rule under former president Nicolás Maduro and his predecessor Hugo Chávez. But the pact, forged after months of secret talks, has provoked outrage among Venezuela’s opposition, already furious that democracy has still to return to the country eight months after the removal of Maduro by US special forces.
“They are inheriting a government that is generating revenue that can be used to rebuild that country,” a US official said during a conference call with journalists on Tuesday.

According to a White House factsheet released on Monday, the agreement granted the US-backed North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep) 100-year ‌rights over 17 oil fields in what it touted as “the biggest oil deal in world history”.
On Tuesday, said allowing Nabep, which is owned by the controversial Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, to take over some oil field would provide capital to “ramp up production rapidly”.

“That in turn will generate royalty revenue for the government – initially, the interim government for the time being – but ultimately for the republic, for the democratic elected government,” the official said.

“We can hand over a more stable Venezuela. But no matter what, a democratically elected Venezuela is still going to face challenges after 20 somewhat years of the disaster of Chavismo [the leftist ideology promoted by Chávez] and Maduro after the country was dismantled from the inside out, and it needs to be rebuilt.
“That’s going to take time. You don’t reverse 20 years of corruption, 20 years of kleptocracy, 20 years of no democracy, no freedom.”

The justification for the takeover of 17 oil fields previously controlled by Chinese and Russian companies came as Trump met oil refinery executives to discuss ways of converting crude into petrol and lowering prices for motorists at the pumps.

Chris Wright, the energy secretary, was due to fly to Caracas, the Venezuelan capital, on Tuesday to follow up last week’s deal, which Trump has hailed as “a historic transaction” to fill the US’s strategic oil reserves.

The oil deal has been given added urgency by Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran last February, which has caused fuel prices to soar after the Iranian forces retaliated by closing the strait of Hormuz, previously a passageway for 20% of the world’s oil supplies. Petrol prices now average about $4.10 a gallon compared with under $3 before the war started.

Increased petrol prices have filtered into the rest of the economy and led to significant drops in Trump’s popularity, with polls showing a majority of voters disapproving of his handling of the war and the economy.
The economic outlook formed the backdrop to the oil deal with Venezuela, first announced last Friday.
The agreement was backed by Venezuela’s national assembly – dominated by the ruling United Socialist party – on Tuesday after the country’s president, Delcy Rodriguez, defended it at the weekend.
“The benefits are endless,” claimed Rodríguez, a former vice-president whom Trump backed after ordering Maduro’s capture.

Opposition critics have complained that the Trump administration has made no attempt to promote a transformation to democracy or stage new elections since Maduro was detained by US forces and taken to New York to face criminal charges after a raid on his Caracas residence in January.

Instead, the White House has chosen to work with Rodriguez, Maduro’s former vice-president, despite her past vocal hostility to the US and previous roles in anti-opposition crackdowns in a regime that Washington believes has stolen recent elections.

The official said talks between the Venezuelan government and the opposition were set to resume later this month. “The last thing we want to see is a new democratic elected government inherit a country in crisis,” he said.
Joseph Gedeon contributed reporting

articles.title: More than a third of prenatal reports to NSW protective services not investigated, ombudsman finds
articles.summary: Other families have been unlawfully compelled to be case managed without consent, watchdog finds

blocks.text: More than a third of all reports raising concerns about the future welfare of unborn children were closed due to a shortage of allocated caseworkers, while families were unlawfully compelled to take part in prenatal case work, the New South Wales ombudsman has found.

In its findings after investigating the Department of Communities and Justice’s practice of responding to prenatal reports, which were released on Friday, the watchdog raised concerns about the number of reports about particularly high-risk children that were not referred on to further support services or a dedicated case manager due to a lack of resources.
Under the Care Act, people who suspect a child may be at risk of significant harm after their birth can make a prenatal report to the department.

“Our investigation found that DCJ closes a significant number of pre-natal reports without allocation and without referrals to support services, because of ‘no capacity to allocate’,” the NSW ombudsman, Paul Miller, wrote in the report.

According to the ombudsman’s report, DCJ data showed that out of 5,007 prenatal reports, 37% or 1,844 were closed without being allocated to a caseworker. Almost half of prenatal reports about unborn children screened as being at risk of significant harm (ROSH) were closed for the same reason while 50% were referred for case management by the department.
The investigation also revealed that child protection services wrongly assumed that its legislative powers were the same for both unborn children and children after birth.
Any active case management requires the consent and the knowledge of the pregnant woman or the families – something that was not routinely sought, Miller found.
“Any engagement by prospective parents with DCJ following a pre-natal report is, if there are no other children in the household, as a legal matter, entirely voluntary”, the report said.
“DCJ has no statutory power to compel parents to engage with it, including to attend interviews, permit home visits, respond to questions, undertake drug testing or accept service referrals.”

The report author acknowledged the “unavoidable tension” between making it clear that families should not be coerced into involvement with child protective services and the fact that their “non-engagement” can later be used as a factor against the family if welfare concerns are raised after the child is born.
Miller said that the legislation does not allow the department to conduct family meetings, home visits or checks for risks of substance abuse without a family’s consent during pregnancy.

“The law does not give DCJ the power to undertake any non-consensual casework during pregnancy. The law also does not allow DCJ to pre-emptively make and act on statutory decisions, such as by deciding that a child needs care and protection warranting removal or other statutory intervention, before the child is born.”

He stressed that the DCJ cannot lawfully substantiate ROSH before a child is born but that in some cases that was “routine”, as was the use of risk assessment tools which have previously been reviewed over concerns of racial biases.

Dr Jacynta Krakouer, a Noongar woman and the Aboriginal strategy and engagement lead at Adelaide University’s Australian Centre for Child Protection, said First Nations children were overrepresented in both the child protection system and prenatal risk alerts.

“In 2023-24, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare child protection data shows that 648 unborn reports were substantiated in NSW – 42% of these reports were for unborn Aboriginal babies,” Krakouer told Guardian Australia.
after newsletter promotion
While she said pregnancy was a unique opportunity to assist and support women and their families, she cautioned against assumptions a baby might already be at risk before they were born.
“There is a big difference between identifying concerns during pregnancy and making a formal finding that an unborn baby is already at risk of significant harm.

“At this point, parents haven’t even had the opportunity to demonstrate how they will care for that baby. We need to be very careful about predicting that someone will ‘fail’ as a parent before they have even had the opportunity to parent.”
She said that the structured decision-making tool used to assess Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families was not “objectively fair or accurate”.

“When previous child protection involvement becomes evidence of future risk, decades of greater surveillance of Aboriginal families can feed into decisions about the next generation. That risks creating a cycle where past involvement with child protection becomes a reason for further involvement with child protection.”

The ombudsman said the department had made a number of changes during the course of its investigation, including to explicitly state that the purpose of any engagement was to ensure families were better supported to reduce contact with the child protection system, and were fully informed about consent.
The DCJ told the ombudsman it was reviewing its prenatal birth alert system with the Aboriginal community controlled child safety sector.

articles.title: [In This Economy] Handa ka na ba sa ‘super El Niño’?
articles.summary: May ilang buwan pa tayo para maghanda. Gagamitin ba natin ang oras para rito, o sasayangin lang?

blocks.text: Ayon sa Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA), may 81% posibilidad na maging “very strong” ang El Niño mula Oktubre 2026 hanggang Enero 2027. May 97% posibilidad din na magpatuloy ito hanggang unang kalahati ng 2027.
Ito ang tinatawag na “super El Niño.” Pero forecast o pagtataya ito, at hindi ibig sabihing sabay-sabay na matutuyo ang buong Pilipinas.

Maaari pa ring umulan nang malakas sa kanlurang bahagi habang umiiral ang Habagat. Ngunit ngayon pa lang ay dapat nang paghandaan ang mataas na posibilidad ng kulang na ulan, tagtuyot, at matinding init—lalo na pagpasok ng dry season.

blocks.caption: Image from PAGASA, as of August 26, 2026.

blocks.text: Ayon sa mga eksperto, unang tatamaan ang agrikultura. Tinataya ng Department of Agriculture (DA) na maaaring bumaba nang 700,000 metric tons, o 3.5%, ang produksyon ng palay kung magkaroon ng malakas na El Niño, kaya maaaring lumiit ang kita ng magsasaka at magmahal ang bigas.
Hindi lang bigas ang problema. Kapag tinamaan ang mais, maaaring magmahal ang feeds, baboy, manok, at itlog. Kapag uminit o bumaba ang tubig sa mga palaisdaan, malalagay rin sa panganib ang mga isda.

Nakita na natin ito kamakailan. Sa huling El Niño event noong 2023 hanggang 2024, umabot sa P15.3 bilyon ang pinsala sa agrikultura, naapektuhan ang 333,195 magsasaka at mangingisda, at nawala ang 784,344 metric tons sa produksyon.
Kaya naman ang El Niño ay hindi lamang usapin ng panahon, kundi isa ring posibleng food inflation shock, o biglaang pagtaas ng presyo ng pagkain dahil kakaunti ang suplay.

Kapag tumaas ang presyo ng pagkain, pinakamabigat ang tama sa mahihirap dahil mas malaking bahagi ng kanilang kita ang napupunta sa pagkain lang. Lumiit din ang nabibili ng suweldo, kaya maaaring magtipid ang mga pamilyang Pilipino sa gamot, pamasahe, at edukasyon.
Puwede ring maapektuhan ang kuryente: tumataas ang paggamit ng bentilador at aircon kapag matindi ang init, habang maaaring humina ang hydropower kapag mababa ang tubig sa mga dam.

Noong 2024, umabot sa mahigit 19,000 megawatts ang peak demand sa kuryente, 11.2% na mas mataas kaysa 2023, na iniugnay ng Department of Energy sa init. Sa isang linggo ng Abril, tumaas nang 47% ang presyo sa agarang bentahan ng kuryente sa Luzon.

Kung mauulit iyan, hindi lang electric bills ang tataas. Asahan ang mas mahal na kuryente at tubig na dagdag-gastos sa mga tindahan, restaurant, pabrika, laundry shop, at iba pang negosyo. Lahat ng ito ay maaaring ipasa sa mga mamimili.

May epekto rin sa trabaho at kita. Mas nanganganib sa heat exhaustion o heat stroke ang construction worker, rider, magsasaka, vendor, at iba pang nagtatrabaho outdoors. Kapag pinaikli ang oras ng trabaho para sa kaligtasan, bababa rin ang kita ng maraming tao.
Maaaring magbago rin ang oras ng klase, opisina, at negosyo. Kapag walang pasok ang mga bata dahil sa matinding init, may mga magulang na kailangang lumiban sa trabaho o magbayad ng mag-aalaga.

Kapag kulang naman ang tubig, maaaring magkaroon ng rasyon o takdang oras ng suplay. Magastos ang pagbili ng container, water delivery, at bottled water, habang oras naman ang nawawala sa pagpila at pag-iigib.

Kung sabay na tumaas ang pagkain, kuryente, at tubig, maaaring bumilis ang inflation o pangkalahatang pagtaas ng presyo. Maaari nitong pigilan ang pagbaba ng interest rates o singil sa utang. Sa katunayan, noong August 27, binanggit ng Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas ang paparating na El Niño bilang isang dahilan kung bakit nito tinaasan ang “policy rate” nito (o interest rate na siyang basehan ng interes sa mga pautang sa buong bansa). Ginawa nila ito upang awatin ang nakaambang pagsipa ng inflation.
Hindi sanhi ng climate change ang El Niño, na natural na siklo sa karagatan at atmospera. Pero mas mainit na ang mundo ngayon, kaya maaaring lumala ang heat waves at iba pang climate extremes.

Para sa mga pamilya, ngayon pa lang ay gumawa na ng El Niño budget: maglaan ng dagdag para sa pagkain, tubig, kuryente, at gamot, bumuo ng maliit na emergency fund kung kaya. Iwasang mag-panic buying na lalo lamang nagpapataas ng presyo.
Ayusin ang tumutulong gripo at tubo. Alamin ang water-interruption schedule. Mag-imbak lamang ng sapat sa malinis at may takip na lalagyan. At huwag hayaang pamugaran ng lamok ang nakatenggang tubig.

Magplano rin laban sa init. Ilipat sa mas malamig na oras ang mabibigat na gawain, uminom ng sapat na tubig, at bantayan ang hilo, panghihina, pagsusuka, mainit at mapulang balat, o pagkawala ng malay (heat stroke).

Para sa magsasaka, sundan ang payo ng PAGASA, Department of Agriculture, National Irrigation Administration, at lokal na pamahalaan. Maaaring kailangang baguhin ang cropping calendar, gumamit ng binhing matibay sa tagtuyot at mabilis anihin, mag-ipon ng tubig-ulan, at kumuha ng insurance sa Philippine Crop Insurance Corporation.

Para sa negosyo, maaaring gumawa ng continuity plan. Sino ang alternate supplier, anong oras ligtas magtrabaho, gaano karaming tubig at kuryente ang kailangan, at paano poprotektahan ang manggagawa at mga produktong madaling masira?

Of course, hindi puwedeng ipasa sa mamamayan ang buong responsibilidad. Dapat i-publish ng gobyerno ang contingency plans para sa pagkain, dam, irigasyon, tubig, kuryente, kalusugan, at paaralan. Dapat may public dashboard rin upang makita ng lahat ang kakulangan sa ulan, reservoir levels, crop losses, power reserves, at ayuda.

Magandang binuhay muli ng DA ang Task Force El Niño noong Mayo. Ngunit kailangan pa ring siguruhin na maagang dumating ang binhi, irigasyon, insurance, cash aid, at transparent na plano sa pag-angkat ng pagkain—hindi kapag tuyot na ang bukid at mataas na ang mga presyo.
Para sa marami, mahirap i-imagine ang sobrang init dahil sa walang-tigil na ulan ngayong Agosto. Ngunit ilang buwan lamang ay ibang-iba ang panahon na mararanasan natin.

May ilang buwan pa tayo para maghanda. Gagamitin ba natin ang oras para rito, o sasayangin lang? Oo, hindi natin mapipigil ang El Niño, pero maiiwasan nating lumaki ang pinsalang pang-ekonomiya kung maghahanda ang lahat ng pamilya, negosyo, at gobyerno ngayon pa lang. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics (UPSE). His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler.com. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and Covid-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).
