articles.title: RCMP charge Calgary man for allegedly running $164M Ponzi scheme
articles.summary: The RCMP announced on Tuesday they had laid charges against Craig Michael Thompson, 49, for allegedly misappropriating investor funds from more than 1,000 victims via his company, Black Box…

image.caption: RCMP have charged a Calgary resident with fraud and laundering proceeds of crime after he allegedly misappropriated more than $164 million in investor funds. (David Bell/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

The RCMP announced on Tuesday they had laid charges against Craig Michael Thompson, 49, for allegedly misappropriating investor funds from more than 1,000 victims via his company, Black Box Management.
49-year-old charged with criminal offences relating to fraud and money laundering
The RCMP have charged a Calgary man after he allegedly misappropriated more than $164 million in investor funds from more than 1,000 victims.
Police allege that between March 2020 and April 2024 Craig Michael Thompson, 49, misappropriated the funds via his company, Black Box Management, in a large-scale Ponzi scheme.
Thompson was arrested by the RCMP’s Federal Policing Northwest Region’s Integrated Market Enforcement Team on July 31, and charged with fraud and laundering proceeds of crime.

Police said on Tuesday that Thompson, while representing himself as a one-man investment firm, received funds from Black Box investors with the understanding he would use the money for day trading. He would then send weekly email updates to investors about the performance and growth of their accounts.

After investigating the case, police said they found information in the email updates was allegedly plagiarized from online sources, and that out of the $164 million inbound funds, Thompson allegedly transferred more than $163 million to other external accounts, including his own personal trading account and an investment in a U.S.-based company.
Police allege their investigation also links Thompson to several other invoice businesses including Intelsense Investment Corp., Invader Management Ltd., and Attebyte Investment Corp.
When contacted by CBC News on Tuesday, Thompson’s lawyer said he and his client had no comment to provide on the charges.
Thompson is scheduled to appear at the Alberta Court of Justice in Calgary on Sept. 3.
Last summer, the Alberta Securities Commission convicted Thompson of securities fraud and ordered him to pay $8.8 million in penalties and costs for an alleged Ponzi scheme.

items: Calgarian who ran $150-million 'classic Ponzi scheme' ordered to pay $8.8 million in penalties

blocks.text: Thompson has not been convicted in criminal court.
On Tuesday, police said they are encouraging people who believe they may have been a victim of fraud related to this investigation to contact them.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Andrew Jeffrey is a multimedia journalist with CBC Calgary. He previously worked for CBC News in his hometown of Edmonton, reported for the StarMetro Calgary, and worked as an editor for Toronto-based magazines Strategy and Realscreen. You can reach him at andrew.jeffrey@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Farage faces questions over his claim of facing second standards investigation
articles.summary:
Reform leader said inquiry had been widened but watchdog is not believed to have decided whether to do so

Nigel Farage is facing questions about why he claimed his finances were the subject…

blocks.text: Nigel Farage is facing questions about why he claimed his finances were the subject of a second standards investigation, as he was sworn in again as Clacton’s MP.
The Reform UK leader said when he resigned in July that the standards system had become a “political tool” because “yet another standards investigation is under way” into his finances.

He argued he wanted the people of Clacton to be the judge of his actions, rather than “the establishment”, after revelations in the Sunday Times that his friend and convicted fraudster George Cottrell had paid for social media work, accommodation and security before the 2024 election.
However, it is understood the parliamentary standards commissioner had not launched another investigation or widened the scope of the existing one at that point.

The commissioner is believed still not to have decided whether to widen the inquiry as recently as two weeks ago, when it was reopened as Farage was returned as MP for Clacton with an increased majority.

The commissioner launched his first investigation in May into Farage’s £5m gift from the Thailand-based donor Christopher Harborne before the 2024 election, which was not declared on the MPs’ register of interests and was first revealed by the Guardian. Initially Farage said the money was given to pay for his security, then he described it as a reward for campaigning for Brexit.
At least two complaints were then submitted in July about Farage’s funding by Cottrell. Farage called a byelection on 7 July and the initial investigation was paused.

However, Westminster sources said the standards commissioner was assessing information. There is no official confirmation that he has widened his inquiry to include the Cottrell donations, and the commissioner’s list of investigations currently only includes the one launched in May.

The sources said the commissioner wanted to see further evidence that Farage had broken the rules in relation to donations from Cottrell in the year before the 2024 election, including his payments for social media work.

blocks.caption: Nigel Farage swears in as Clacton's MP at the House of Commons. He said on Tuesday he planned to spend less time in parliament while he toured the country. Photograph: House of Commons/Reuters

blocks.text: Farage has maintained the videos were personal and likened his public role before that election to the work of an influencer. However, a number of the videos were political in nature, campaigning on immigration issues.
Critics say these should be declared under rules that say donations related to politics must be registered in the 12 months before an MP is elected.
The standards commissioner declined to comment on the status of the investigation into Farage and whether any decision had been made on widening the inquiry.

If there is no second investigation nor a widened scope, it is possible the first investigation into Farage could conclude sooner than expected. The Times reported in July that the Reform leader would be interviewed within weeks but the byelection paused the process.

In relation to the investigation, Alex Burghart, the shadow chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, said: “The questions surrounding Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the donations from George Cottrell simply aren’t going away.

“Farage has already tried to run away with his farcical byelection in Clacton, but he can no longer hide from these questions. He needs to come clean … The public deserves answers and Farage can’t keep hiding.”

If the standards commissioner finds a breach of the rules, and the separate standards committee of MPs recommends a sanction of more than 10 days of suspension from parliament, Farage could end up facing a second byelection.

As he was sworn in again on Tuesday, Farage told GB News that he planned to spend less time in parliament and would be leaving more Westminster work to [the Reform deputy leader] “Richard Tice and the gang” while he goes on a tour of the country.

Farage will set his priorities for the year ahead when he gives his speech at the Reform party conference at the end of this week, where he is expected to attempt to draw a line under the focus on his finances.

articles.title: Burnham promises to bring optimism and ‘substantial change’ in first Commons speech as PM
articles.summary:
The prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the ‘series of wrong turns’ it had taken in the last 40 years

Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years.

In his first Commons appearance since he took over as prime minister around six weeks ago, Burnham told MPs he wanted to build a new sense of optimism so “we can make this next decade better than the last”.

The British people wanted “much more substantial change” on the big issues facing the country, he said. “That is what I will bring. Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should.”
The UK economy has taken a 6% hit from the effects of Brexit, according to economists’ analysis of internal Bank of England data on thousands of British companies since the referendum a decade ago.

Burnham’s first Commons appearance came as Keir Starmer, his predecessor, announced he would stand down as an MP, saying that he wanted to focus on international affairs instead, triggering a tricky first byelection test for Burnham in a London seat where the Greens will fancy their chances.

The cabinet was told on Tuesday that the government will have three key priorities: cutting costs of essentials like childcare and mortgages; the regeneration of communities; and greater public control of water, housing and energy.

Burnham’s deputy, Louise Haigh, will lead taskforces on each of those issues, the Guardian understands. He told his ministers they must be “relentless” in fulfilling his priorities. In his Commons statement, the prime minister also:

items: Hinted that he would commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying he had appointed John Healey as his chancellor “precisely because” of his position on military spending.

Opened the door to looking again at electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. “I do believe there needs to be a mandate to make that change. There are different views in this house, but I believe we will need to get a consensus at the next election. And if there is that consensus, then a change can be made in the next parliament.”

Announced he would attend the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey and continue pursuing green energy – but that he would be “pragmatic” on supply, amid expectations he will approve the Jackdaw gas field. “The mistake is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.”

blocks.text: Flanked by Healey and Haigh, Burnham suggested to MPs the Brexit vote had been a response to “a series of wrong turns” made by Britain in the 1980s onwards, that were then compounded by leaving the EU.

The prime minister, whose Makerfield constituency voted for Brexit, has previously argued it would be a mistake to rerun the referendum – but has said that he wants the UK to rejoin in his lifetime. He suggested the next UK-EU reset summit could take place in November.

“Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country de-industrialised. Austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this,” he said during a three-hour stint in the Commons.

“And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Change begins with honesty … Unless we are blunt about what went wrong, we won’t turn things around.
“Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain for 40 years. Too many places have been drifting.”

He added: “The government I lead will be relentless in giving people and places what they were promised 10 years ago: ownership and control, and from that control over their destiny comes change and growth.”

blocks.caption: Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of wanting to take the UK ‘back to the 1970s’. Photograph: House of Commons

blocks.text: Tory leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of “living in the past” over his attacks on Thatcher – who was in power from 1979 to 1990 – and four decades of neoliberalism.
after newsletter promotion

“The year is 2026 but the prime minister said everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. He is talking about a woman who became prime minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.”

In the statement, Burnham paid tribute to Starmer, saying he had created a platform for Britain to be fixed, “and we will use it well”. Just hours earlier, his predecessor announced he would be standing down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras, despite saying in July he planned to stay on until the next election.

“It has been a huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country,” he said. “I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs, including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.”

Starmer’s seat, long seen as a safe Labour hold, is likely to be targeted by the Greens, potentially for party leader Zack Polanski, who is a London Assembly member. “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years,” a Green spokesperson said.

Just as the Makerfield byelection was seen as a proof of concept for whether Burnham could beat Reform, so the north London seat will test his progressive credentials. Labour will choose its candidate to replace Starmer next Wednesday under an accelerated selection timetable.

Burnham’s first taskforce will be charged with finding bold solutions to tackling “everyday rip-offs”. The cost of living taskforce will look at parking charges, subscription traps and cowboy builders, as well as long-term fixed pressures like mortgages, food costs and childcare.

The second will assess the affordability and practicalities of the state taking over failing essential services, with Burnham believing that greater state control of essential services is the surest way to economic growth, as people’s hard-earned money would not be drained by ineffective profiteering by privatised services.

Government sources said that Haigh, the first secretary of state, wanted to look beyond sectors like transport and explore serious opportunities for greater state control in areas like energy and housing – if it would bring down ordinary people’s costs.

The third taskforce will explore more radical ideas to revive crumbling high streets and impoverished districts, such as potential legislative options on houses in multiple occupation, as well as devolving powers to mayors and councils to help them regenerate local high streets.

Burnham in particular is keen to explore how to replicate the regeneration of Stockport, which saw billions in investment in housing and event spaces, which the former mayor of Greater Manchester said should be a blueprint for towns across the UK.

Haigh will also explore whether it would be possible to revisit the Total Place pilots, an initiative during Gordon Brown’s government which mapped all public spending in specific local areas to see how joining up council, health, and social services could cut waste and serve communities more effectively.

articles.title: Briton among 119 more people rescued in Nepal after flash floods
articles.summary:
More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000 still missing in disaster triggered by glacial collapse

A British national was among 119 people rescued in Nepal on Tuesday, an…

blocks.text: A British national was among 119 people rescued in Nepal on Tuesday, an official said almost a week after deadly flash floods on the country’s border with Tibet.
An army spokesperson told reporters at a press conference that Tuesday’s rescue efforts had saved 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men.
“We have also rescued one British male during this search and rescue operation, and the search and rescue operation is continuing,” he said.
The British man is yet to be identified. The UK Foreign Office was contacted for comment.
The rescues mark a rare breakthrough in a devastating week for Himalayan communities on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border.
At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing.
Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday.
Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster.

The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday.
Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris.
Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region.
“Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33.

A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts.
The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster.
Scientists have said such disasters are more likely as the climate crisis affects mountainous and polar regions.
The UN’s top scientific advisory body said in 2023 that previously ice-bound landmasses – such as permafrost tundra and mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose.
Officials from Nepal, China and Tibet met in May to discuss strengthening their joint response to floods, weather and glacier-related hazards, Reuters reported on Tuesday.

articles.title: Iran: US launches fresh strikes as hostilities flare again
articles.summary: Explosions were reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz, as well as at an airport in southern Iran. US President Trump described the strikes as "large and powerful." Iran said the US will…

image.caption: US President Trump described the strikes as "large and powerful." Iran said the US will "regret" its latest attacks.Image: U.S. Navy/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz flared up again on Tuesday evening as the United States launched fresh strikes on Iranian targets in and around the strategic waterway.

"Explosions were heard again in Bandar Abbas city and Qeshm island," Iranian state television reported, adding that blasts were also heard on Lavan island, home to one of Iran's Gulf oil export terminals.
Oil prices rose in the wake of the latest attacks with US crude up by as much as 5%.

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."

US President Donald Trump said the strikes, which he described as "large and powerful," were retaliation for "failed" Iranian attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz and the firing of "eight missiles" towards a US military base in Jordan, all of which he claimed were shot down.

"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump wrote in his latest social media threat. "But it will not be the biggest attack of them all. That is waiting in the wings."
Iran: IRGC vows to respond to US strikes

An IRGC spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, about 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's joint military command said its armed forces would deliver what they described as "crushing and devastating blows" against the US, while state media said the army had launched operations against unspecified US targets in the region.

The Tasnim news agency said a "decisive operation by Iran's armed forces in response to the US enemy has begun. The US bases and interests in the region are being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones."
G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran
Meanwhile, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran.
"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina.
"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support."
He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with the IRGC.
"We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."
Iran's Pezeshkian meets Putin

The latest flare-up comes just hours after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said earlier on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate any US move that signals a return to the collapsed interim ceasefire deal.

Pezeshkian, speaking after the US and Iran had already resumed exchanges of fire for the first time in over a month, accused Washington of "reneging on its commitments" under the agreement, which fell apart in June, with both sides accusing the other of violating the agreement's terms.
Pezeshkian was speaking on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where he also met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday.
Putin reportedly told Pezeshkian that Russia stood in solidarity with Iran, and that the two countries would maintain their economic relationships despite the current turbulence.
Pezeshkian thanked Putin and criticized the US for having "no right" to impose sanctions on other countries.

articles.title: Ed Miliband promises ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK policy toward Israel
articles.summary:
Foreign secretary tells MPs he will try to stop illegal settlements carving up the West Bank

Ed Miliband has promised to “reset” Britain’s policy on Israel, saying he will try to stop…

blocks.text: Ed Miliband has promised to “reset” Britain’s policy on Israel, saying he will try to stop British companies helping build settlements in the West Bank.

Speaking to the Commons for the first time as foreign secretary, Miliband said he would set out measures to prevent UK involvement in projects such as the illegal E1 plan, which critics say would split the West Bank in half.
Tuesday’s comments came after Israel issued tenders for around a third of the 3,400 homes planned for the project. Miliband called the settlement “the crossing of a red line”.

He said: “It cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable. This government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution. We will act, and I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks.
“I want a comprehensive reset of our approach on these issues because it is necessary, it is high time.”
Ministers have been under pressure for weeks to place tighter sanctions on Israel, specifically in relation to the E1 plan.
Last month, Israel invited companies to bid for contracts to build 1,200 homes for the project between East Jerusalem and the settlement of Ma’ale Adumim.

blocks.caption: Ma’ale Adumim in the E1 area of the occupied West Bank, where the Israeli government plans to build thousands of homes. Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/Shutterstock

blocks.text: A group of former British diplomats called on the government in May to threaten action against any companies bidding to build any illegal settlement “designed to divide the West Bank in two and destroy Palestine’s viability”. They warned that E1 was part of Israel’s “systemic West Bank annexation”.
Other governments have condemned the project. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz – usually one of Israel’s staunchest defenders – called it a “big mistake”.
The UK joined a group of 20 other countries, including France, Germany and Italy, as well as the European Union, to issue a joint statement calling E1 “unacceptable”.

The statement said: “The E1 settlement will undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank and harming the territorial contiguity of the Palestinian territories.”
Miliband said: “We need to look, and we are looking indeed, at our wider economic relationship with the occupied territories and the different tools we have to tackle it.
after newsletter promotion

“I want to be very clear: we do not want British companies financing, constructing, or advertising new settlements. The work we are now undertaking is how we can stop that. And as I say, I’ll have more to say soon.”
Ministers are under pressure to go further and ban trade in goods and services with people or organisations linked to illegal settlements.

James Naish, the Labour MP for Rushcliffe in Nottinghamshire, said: “Does the foreign secretary accept that this pace of expansion shows that current UK measures are failing to change Israeli government behaviour, and that a trade ban is now the necessary next step?”

Stephen Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, indicated this could be included in the government’s measures. He said: “We have absolutely condemned the settler violence, the settler terrorism that we have seen, absolutely our condemnation of the proposals for E1 and all illegal settlements, and indeed we have joined other countries around the world in condemning this proposal and been very, very clear with the government of Israel that this must stop.

“The prime minister has been very clear that we need to do more, including looking at further sanctions, both those involved in the violence in Gaza, but also looking at measures to ban trade in goods with illegal settlements.”

The Israeli embassy to London responded by referring to previous comments by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools. The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.”

articles.title: Fertility program offers future choices for 12-year-old N.W.T. cancer patient
articles.summary: Fort Good Hope, N.W.T., resident Chloe Dixon was diagnosed with a soft-tissue sarcoma in the summer of last year. While treatment for cancers like hers can impact a person's fertility, a relatively…

image.caption: Fort Good Hope, N.W.T., resident Chloe Dixon was diagnosed with a soft-tissue sarcoma — a rare form of mouth cancer — in the summer of last year. (Submitted by Paul Dixon)

blocks.text: North·New

Fort Good Hope, N.W.T., resident Chloe Dixon was diagnosed with a soft-tissue sarcoma in the summer of last year. While treatment for cancers like hers can impact a person's fertility, a relatively new procedure in Canada is giving Chloe the choice of having children in the future.
Chloe Dixon says she was shocked to hear about the procedure but is happy to have choices for her future
Fort Good Hope, N.W.T., resident Chloe Dixon, 12, was diagnosed last summer with rhabdomyosarcoma, a rare, aggressive cancer.
During the wave of discussions with her family about treatment options, doctors brought up a new procedure that could give Chloe the chance to have children when she grows up.
Chloe said she was initially shocked when the doctors told her about the program.
“I thought it was definitely a good idea to do it,” Chloe said. “I'm 12, I don't know much about that. But I thought it was the safer option.”
Many cancer treatments can damage a patient's fertility.

As first reported by the Toronto Star, a fertility program between The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) and Mount Sinai Fertility Clinic in Ontario is giving pediatric patients options for their reproductive future.

Through ovarian tissue cryopreservation, doctors remove one ovary, which is then processed, frozen and stored. If the patient decides to become pregnant later in life, the tissue can be implanted again.
Since her diagnosis, Chloe has stayed in Toronto to undergo multiple surgeries and chemotherapy at SickKids.
A chance at reproductive autonomy

Dr. Kriti Kumar, a pediatric oncologist at SickKids, co-leads the collaborative fertility preservation program between Sinai and SickKids. She said offering a choice is important for a person’s reproductive autonomy.
“When we give therapy that we know can be harmful to fertility, it's really important that we have these options available to patients," she said.
While adult patients can freeze mature eggs, that option isn't available for kids

Kumar said a person born with ovaries has a finite number of eggs at birth. That number naturally declines. Some cancer treatments like surgeries, radiation and chemotherapy can cause the eggs to decrease faster, leading to an early onset of menopause.
“These young girls can go through menopause in their teens, in their 20s and in their 30s and that can affect their actual fertile window,” she said.
Kumar said discussions about tissue preservation often happen soon after a cancer diagnosis.
“We really want to make sure that we're giving patients and families as much time as we can to really think about this,” she said.
Fewer than 20 pediatric patients have undergone the procedure through the SickKids program so far. Because the program is relatively new, no patient has had their tissue reimplanted yet, Kumar said.
As pediatric cancer survival rates continue to rise, doctors are focusing more on long-term post-cancer quality of life, she said.

“We want to make sure that we're not just curing them and then saying, 'Go out in the world and fend for yourself,'” she said. “We want to really make sure that they're thriving and really living full lives.”
‘A great option’

Paul Dixon, Chloe’s father, said the family was overwhelmed when doctors first presented the option to them. The discussions happened alongside a wave of other information about Chloe’s cancer diagnosis and treatment plan.
“After we sort of settled in on it and thought about the future and whatever else is going on, then it was a great option,” he said.
He added he was grateful hospital staff included Chloe in all of the medical information sessions alongside her parents. Chloe underwent the tissue preservation procedure in August 2025.
“I know that I have a bit more of an opportunity to have kids in the future. But yeah, I feel like it was a bit of a weird conversation,” Chloe said.
She is currently in the maintenance phase of chemotherapy and is looking forward to starting school.
“Ultimately, things are going well,” Dixon said. “Hopefully Chloe has the same type of future as any other child that hasn't gone through cancer treatment.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Yumna Iftikhar is a Pakistani Canadian journalist covering the impact of federal policies on minority communities. She also writes about climate change and Canada’s energy transition journey. Yumna holds a Master of Journalism from Carleton University. She can be reached at yumna.iftikhar1@cbc.ca
With files from Shannon Scott

articles.title: US launches new airstrikes on Iranian targets as hostilities flare
articles.summary: Move from Washington quashes hopes that exchange of fire last weekend might not presage ⁠wider renewal of hostilities

blocks.text: The US launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets on Tuesday, quashing hopes that an exchange of fire last ⁠weekend might not presage a ⁠wider renewal of hostilities.

Oil prices had ​already risen after that first exchange of direct attacks since July and after reports of two tankers being hit leaving the strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping.

Tehran remained defiant, warning ⁠that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard” in response to the renewed Iranian strikes, and a warning from Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, that Washington was about to ⁠impose new sanctions.

“Today at 12 p.m. ET (1600 GMT), U.S. forces began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran,” US Central Command posted on X. “The strikes follow ​recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of ‌Hormuz and against American service members deployed to ‌the region.”
Iran’s state broadcaster said there had been reports of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait.
The state-linked news agency Nour ‌News said there had been reports of explosions in the port city of Bandar Abbas and in Chabahar, a port on the southern coast.

The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US airbases in Jordan.

Although he warned of a US response to the Iranian strikes, the US president also told reporters on Monday that they did not signal a return to full-scale war, and a senior Iranian source told Reuters they were a “limited ‌and contained confrontation”.

However, Trump made dire threats against Tehran on social media. He warned that if Iran retaliates against the US’s latest strikes, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran”.

The ominous last part of Trump’s message was starkly reminiscent of threats the US president has made in the past that could amount to war crimes if carried out, including threatening to destroy critical civilian infrastructure such as power plants and bridges, threatening to bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages”, and an April threat that “a whole civilization will die tonight” if a peace deal wasn’t reached.
In Iran, the Fars news agency quoted an IRGC spokesperson as saying the US “will regret its new attacks”.

More recently pledges by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.

Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, had said early on Tuesday ​that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was intended to halt the conflict.

The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since US and Israeli strikes began on 28 February. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period – which passed without further agreement.

“I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the ⁠memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, at ​a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which includes Russia ​and China.
But Iranian officials have shown no public ​sign of bowing to pressure.

“If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be ​able to export oil,” Mohammad Baqer QalibafIran’s parliament speaker was ​quoted as saying by Iranian media. If ​the US intensified its “siege”, he said Tehran would respond militarily.
Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told a press conference in Tehran that Washington was “addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”.

“As long as they act in this manner, they will certainly get no result other than what they have achieved so far,” he added, warning that Tehran would “use all our capabilities, whether on the battlefield or through our diplomatic apparatus”.
Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
articles.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 6,000 confirmed cases, with nearly 3,000 deaths. As the virus spreads, authorities are racing to contain one of the deadliest…

image.caption: The Ebola outbreak has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain itImage: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it.

"Around 60 health zones are now affected, every week more are added to the list. And the same pattern is repeated everywhere: initially, there is resistance and denial, followed by gradual acceptance," DW correspondent Jonas Gerding reported from Bunia, the capital of the Ituri province, the epicenter of the latest Ebola outbreak in Congo.
"Unfortunately, a lot more people will die until this Ebola outbreak gets under control," he added.
Health experts have said the situation is particularly worrying in eastern Congo, where conflict and insecurity are making it harder for response teams to reach affected communities.
Ebola outbreak in DR Congo outpaces efforts to contain it

"This outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record. It is growing faster and wider than the response to contain it, but it can be stopped," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told journalists last week.
The United Nations has appealed for more funding as humanitarian agencies struggle to keep pace with the increasing number of cases.

"International attention, political focus and resources are still lagging behind the reality unfolding on the ground," Guterres said, warning that the world "must also overcome another virus — the virus of indifference."
Vaccination campaign gathers momentum
As researchers continue trials aimed at developing a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain, Congolese authorities have rolled out a vaccination campaign focused on front-line health workers.
The vaccine was originally developed for a different Ebola variant, but officials hope it will provide some protection against the current outbreak.
Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said more than 50,000 doses had already arrived in the country.

"We will cover all the provinces that are around Ituri, moving in a ring towards the center of the outbreak, that is to say towards Ituri. But we have enough doses for all healthcare providers," he said on August 28.
Some health workers remain confident despite uncertainty over how effective the vaccine will be against the Bundibugyo strain.

"It is a vaccine that has already proven itself. We are talking about Ebola Bundibugyo, of Ugandan origin. But the vaccine that they want to administer to us was the vaccine that had succeeded for the Zaire type," said health worker Arnaud Batumbu.
"Since both cases involve a viral disease, I hope the vaccine will work for us now as well," he added.
Communities seek protection
Residents in hard-hit areas say they are ready to take the vaccine if it is properly explained to them.
"I will be ready to get vaccinated if only someone explains to me the importance of this vaccination," Clemency, a student in Tshopo province, told DW.

blocks.caption: Health workers are worried about the spread of the virusImage: Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Others are calling for wider access. "Children need to be vaccinated too. They go back to school; there are many of them in class," said local resident Carine Lobwadji
Some community members also fear vaccine supplies may not be enough.

"I have learned that this is an insufficient quantity. I ask the authorities to add other doses for Tshopo and that we vaccinate everyone, especially those who will voluntarily agree, since some are afraid," said Onyeka Treasure, a photographer.
Violence hampers response
The latest outbreak is unfolding against a backdrop of violence and mass displacement in eastern DRC, complicating efforts to stop transmission.
Ebola response teams have reported attacks while carrying out their work, including during operations to safely handle Ebola-related deaths.

"We demand greater security so we can operate in the field and do our work without endangering our lives," Floribert Magene, a member of an Ebola response team, told The Associated Press on Monday after an attack in Ituri province.
Magene said his team was assaulted near Mambasa while responding to a call to secure a body.
Economic toll grows
Beyond the health emergency, the outbreak is worsening economic hardship for many families.
Schools have reopened in towns such as Bukavu and Bunia, but many parents are struggling to afford basic school supplies.
DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts
Stationery shop owner Furaha Mpangu Esperance told DW that demand has collapsed as families prioritize food and other essentials.

"In any case, it doesn't work. The situation is serious because there are no customers. We have even lowered the prices but there is no one to buy. Before, we even sold 10 boxes, 20 boxes a day. Today not even three boxes, not even two! The situation is critical," he said.
To reduce disruption to education, the government has proposed radio-based learning for children unable to attend school.

"For us, it's a double objective: to ensure that children continue to go to school, despite the epidemic, and to ensure that distance learning is the device that will help them," Education Minister Raissa Malu told DW.

blocks.caption: Schools have enforced protective measures, like hand-washingImage: DW

blocks.text: Teachers, however, say many areas lack the infrastructure needed for effective distance learning.

"We, the teachers, are ready, but we don't have the tools. In sensitive areas, even picking up frequencies is quite a problem," said Patrick Girinegi, president of the Ituri teachers' inter-union alliance. "The first-grade children can't read, nor do the parents. Several schools don't have printers or computers. How will it go?"
Many students and parents would rather see classrooms remain open with stronger health measures in place.

"It's easy for me to understand when it's my teacher himself who explains it to me. Saying that the child stays at home to listen to the radio, I don't think it's going to work. We [must] find ways to go to school without contaminating ourselves," said Viviane Tshipamba, vice-president of the Ituri children's committee.

Despite the challenges, health authorities point to a positive sign: more than 1,360 people have recovered from Ebola so far. For many Congolese, those recoveries offer hope that with stronger support, increased vaccination rates and improved security, the outbreak can still be brought under control.
Marcus Loika, Gaston Mukendi and Mitima Delachance contributed to this article.

articles.title: Germany blames Russia for drone attack at Leipzig airport
articles.summary:
Government says ‘dangerous behaviour’ is part of effort by Moscow to cause damage with hybrid attacks

The German government has blamed Russia for the drone attack on Leipzig airport last…

blocks.text: The German government has blamed Russia for the drone attack on Leipzig airport last month, calling it “dangerous behaviour” and part of a systematic and concerted effort by Moscow to “cause great damage” through a large number of hybrid attacks.

The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, and the foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, ended weeks of speculation and the government’s hesitancy to blame Russia, saying in a brisk 10-minute briefing in Berlin that all indications were the Russian state had provided the knowhow and equipment for the planned attack and “low-level agents” were recruited to carry it out.

A drone loaded with explosives was discovered at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August attached to the wing of a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used to transport weapons to Ukraine. It failed to detonate but could have caused a catastrophe, authorities said.

Russia will face a package of penalty measures, Wadephul said, adding that the German government saw “a need for appropriate and necessary action in this situation”. It would respond “to this hybrid attack in Leipzig with proportionate and measured, yet equally resolute, action”, he said. “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.”

He added: “The dangerous behaviour of the Russian Federation is part of attempts at destabilisation, disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression.” Berlin regretted the abysmal state of its relations with Moscow, he said.

blocks.caption: Germany’s foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, said Germany was ‘a daily target of hybrid warfare’. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The EU expressed “full solidarity” with Germany over the attack, and Nato assured Berlin that it would defend its members.

The Russian ambassador had been summoned to the foreign ministry at that very moment to be informed of the consequences, Wadephul said. The Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed later this month, and Russian House, a sprawling cultural and science institute in the centre of Berlin, which is alleged to house Russian spies and to have been the launchpad for a number of hybrid attacks carried out in Germany over the past few years, is to be turned out of its rented building.

A clampdown on Russia’s shadow fleet – illegal ships carrying Russian oil and other supplies in the Baltic and North seas – is also planned. Sweden and Finland track and disrupt the shadow fleet but Germany does not, so vessels regularly opt to sail via German waters in its foreign economic zones.
New lists of people on a blacklist would be drawn up and tighter border controls of Russians entering Germany would be carried out, Wadephul said.
Parallel to these moves, Berlin is also backing the European Commission’s 22nd package of sanctions, to cover a further 1,600 companies and organisations with a Russian connection.

Responding to ​Germany’s announcement, ‌Russia’s foreign ministry ​spokesperson, ​Maria Zakharova, said Moscow would respond to what she called Berlin’s “anti-Russian action”, according to the Interfax news agency.

The government has previously said it does not intend to directly involve Nato by invoking article 4 of the alliance. However, its Nato and European partners were informed about the investigation and agreed on the planned consequences, Wadephul confirmed.
The Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, promised “full solidarity” with Berlin.

Rutte said Berlin had put forward clear evidence of Moscow’s role in the “hybrid attack” and welcomed the measures announced in response, while von der Leyen vowed to “keep the EU united despite these escalating and serious acts”.

blocks.caption: Police officers walk across a field at the airport searching for evidence. Photograph: Sebastian Willnow/DPA/AP

blocks.text: Tuesday’s announcement marks the first time the German government has concretely named Russia as responsible for the attack.
It marks the lowest point for decades in relations between Russia and the EU’s largest member, which were already at a very low ebb over Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
It comes before a critical election in the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg Vorpommern, in which the war in Ukraine and relations with Russia have been a focal point.

The far-right populist Alternative für Deutschland, which is pushing a pro-Russia agenda as it seeks to win an absolute majority in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt this weekend, has accused the government of double standards over its treatment of Russia. Urging the government to prove Russia’s involvement in the Leipzig incident earlier this week, it said the same rigour should be applied to investigations into the attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukraine is alleged to have been responsible.

The drone in the Leipzig incident was carrying 600 grams of explosives and was discovered in the security area of ​​the airport close to Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes on the night of 4-5 August. The explosive device detonator appeared to have failed. A second drone was believed to have been part of the planned attack but investigators have since thrown doubt on that theory. Traces of the military explosive hexogen were found on the edge of the airport on 14 August along with a further drone, investigators confirmed. Had the devices exploded they could have caused a catastrophe, German officials said.
The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who last week said whoever was behind the attack “will pay”, did not attend the briefing to the press and public on Tuesday.

Konstantin von Notz, the Green party’s security policy expert and commissioner for intelligence oversight, criticised the government before the announcement for what he described as its failure to stand up to Vladimir Putin in the face of the growing hybrid threat from Russia. “The federal government must finally stop being hesitant, reticent, and timid. Things must be called by their name, and decisive action must be taken,” he said in an interview with the RND network.

Even within his own Christian Democratic Union party, Merz has faced calls to be tougher towards Russia. On Tuesday, the party’s foreign policy expert, Roderich Kiesewetter, urged the chancellor to take a tougher line against Russia, accusing successive governments of exercising “extreme caution with regards to Russian state terrorism on German soil”.

Citing sources in German intelligence, Bild Zeitung said direct connections had been made by investigators between other drone and explosives finds and other incidents in Germany and across Europe, including in Romania, Italy, Poland, Bulgaria and the UK. A cache of weapons discovered recently in a Berlin forest are thought to be connected to Russian activities in Romania. Investigators in various countries are believed to be working in parallel with each other.

articles.title: US launches more strikes on Iran as state media reports explosions
articles.summary: US Central Command accused Iran of targeting commercial shipping and American service members deployed in the region.

blocks.text: American forces resumed strikes against Iran on Tuesday, US Central Command said in a statement.
It accused the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of "recent attempted attacks" against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and "American service members deployed to the region".

Centcom said US forces began striking IRGC targets at 12:00 ET (16:00 GMT). Iran state media reported the country's deputy governor for security as saying four projectiles had hit the counties of Chabahar and Konarak.
The IRGC said the US would regret the strikes, as US President Donald Trump warned that Iran would be hit again at "a much harder and higher level" if it retaliated.
The attack follows the first known US strikes on Iran since late July earlier this week, when forces attacked two rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait.
Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported that several explosions were also heard on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, as well as Konarak and Bandar Abbas.

Donald Trump confirmed the "large and powerful" strikes, which he said were in response to Iran shooting eight missiles at a US military base in Jordan, adding the country had "failed" at adding sea mines to the Strait.

Regarding his threat of a further attack in the case of Iranian retaliation, he added: "It will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran."
IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said that severe punishment awaited the US and the country would regret the new attacks.

articles.title: Russia attempted attack at airport last month using explosive-laden drone, Germany says
articles.summary: The German government is blaming Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives, and announced it would shut down a Russian consulate, among…

image.caption: A police investigator works on the tarmac near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 5 near Leipzig, Germany, after what Germany now says was an attempted drone attack by Russia. (Jens Schlueter/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The German government is blaming Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives, and announced it would shut down a Russian consulate, among other measures against Moscow.
Germany says it will shutter Russian ​cultural centre, Russian consulate in response

The German government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives, and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate, among other measures against Moscow.
The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on the evening of Aug. 4 and the device was defused. German officials said at the time that the incident posed a new level of danger.
Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption across Europe with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said on Tuesday that authorities found elements such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonator that are "known to us from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine."
He said that the device pointed to "a high degree of technical expertise" and painstaking planning, but that the execution of the plan appears to have been left to "low-level" agents.

items: Kremlin denies reports CIA director warned Russia about attacking NATO countries
Could an explosive drone at a German airport signal a growing Russian threat to NATO?

blocks.text: Dobrindt told reporters in Berlin that intelligence points to "people being involved who acted on behalf of Russian state entities," though he didn't specify which ones.
"Taken together, the police investigations, the pattern and intelligence findings prove a Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig airport."

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that "with the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership decided deliberately to do significant damage again to our already massively burdened bilateral relationship."
He said that the Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed effective Sept. 18 and the contract under which the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin is operated will be rescinded.
Germany promises increased pressure on 'shadow fleet'

Germany will propose the addition of more people from Russia to European Union sanctions lists "in the context of hybrid attacks," will step up entry controls for people from Russia and "increase pressure on the shadow fleet," a reference to tankers suspected of shipping Russian oil in violation of international sanctions. The EU has sanctioned hundreds of "shadow fleet" ships.
Russia's Foreign Ministry told the Interfax news agency that Moscow "would respond" to what it described as Germany's "anti-Russian decision."
Leipzig/Halle is a major hub for international freight and for providing support to Ukraine. The planes that regularly use it include Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.

It is also home to NATO's Strategic Airlift International Solution, or SALIS, which is currently operational almost every day in delivering equipment to NATO battle groups along its eastern flank from Finland to Romania and supporting EU and alliance nation missions.

In 2024, an incendiary device ignited at a logistics centre at the airport and set fire to a freight container before it could be loaded onto a cargo plane, part of a plot that Western security officials suspect was organized by Russian intelligence.

articles.title: The Atari brand was long tarnished in gaming. Its new leadership 'burned it down' to rebuild
articles.summary: As video games become an increasingly digital-first hobby, the people keeping the Atari name alive are going back to their roots, by offering new versions of their 1980s classics.

image.caption: Packaging and box art for the Activision series of games for Atari's 2600+ retro revival console are seen at the Gamescom video game conference in Cologne, Germany last week. (Jonathan Ore/CBC)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
As video games become an increasingly digital-first hobby, the people keeping the Atari name alive are going back to their roots, by offering new versions of their 1980s classics.
The classic games company is re-releasing classic Activision games on its 2600+ revival console
As video games become an increasingly digital-first hobby, the people keeping the Atari name alive are going back to their roots, offering new versions of their 1980s classics.

Last week at the Gamescom conference in Germany, Atari Interactive announced a collaboration with Activision to re-release 39 games from the latter company's early years on physical cartridges, including Pitfall, River Raid and Megamania.
They can be played on the Atari 2600+, a recreation of the original 2600, which launched in 1977. The newer console supports wireless joysticks and can connect to modern TVs through HDMI.

The 2600+ was released in 2023, along with re-releases of classics such as Pac-Man, Galaga and Dig Dug. It can also play original cartridges for the Atari 2600 and 7800 consoles — if you can find them in your parents' homes and dust them off. The newly released versions are also backward compatible, meaning they can be played on the original consoles, if you still have a working one.

"The audience for these games seems to have not stopped consuming these games. So people who have old games in their closet, when these were released, people were buying these to play their old games," said Mike Mika, studio head at Digital Eclipse, one of Atari's labels.

Mika says the Activision releases are particularly meaningful because they represent a reunion of sorts more than 40 years in the making. Activision was formed in 1979 by programmers who had worked at Atari but disagreed with the company's policy of not crediting its developers or awarding them bonuses on bestselling games.
Now owned by Microsoft as part of Activision Blizzard, the studio is one of the video game industry's largest and is behind franchises such as Call of Duty and Candy Crush Saga.
"Now we're working with Activision to bring those games that were the beginning of all that back to Atari," Mika told CBC News.
Atari brand rises from the ashes

The Atari name has had a tumultuous history since its heydey bringing video games into North American homes in the 1980s. The brand passed through multiple publishers and holding companies in the '90s and 2000s and is now owned by Luxembourg-based Atari SA, formerly the French-based company Infogrames.

In the 2010s, owner Frédéric Chesnais attempted to revive the brand by engaging in "deeply unsavoury businesses" including gambling and blockchain, according to a report by Gamesindustry.biz, as well as proposing a chain of Atari-themed hotels.
In 2021, the company split in two, with American investor Wade Rosen taking over the gaming division, while Chesnais focusing on other ventures, including a new Atari Token cryptocurrency.

Rosen soon took over as CEO and has gradually sold off or phased out many of the company's non-gaming ventures, instead focusing more on the retro gaming market and bringing the brand closer to its roots.

Atari acquired studios including Vancouver-based Nightdive Studios and Digital Eclipse. It also launched the Atari 2600+ console, along with other hardware such as joysticks, paddle controllers and the Intellivision Sprint, a revival of another '80s-era competitor to the 2600.
Atari president Ethan Zoubek said the brand's iconic logo "was slapped on things opportunistically" and "the soul of it was diminished" in the process.
"When we came in five years ago we really, in many ways, burned it down and built it back up."
Part of rebuilding the brand Mika said, involved earning back the trust of retro Atari fans — some of whom have continued playing and homebrewing games since the '80s.

That included recruiting people who worked with the company during its heyday, including hiring Hiro Kimura, the artist behind the original Atari 2600 box art of Pac-Man, to compose new art for the game's 2025 re-release for the 2600+, according to Atari's VP of strategic operations Matthew Burnett.
Atari 50, a compilation of classic games paired with an extensive documentary developed by Digital Eclipse, released in 2022 to wide critical acclaim.

For the Atari x Activision collection, the studio also recreated fabric patches included with deluxe versions of each game. Activision originally offered these patches as a mail-order bonus for players who sent in photos of their high scores.
A renewed love for physical games and hardware

Atari's retro releases remain something of a niche in the wider games market, though its focus on recreating the experience of playing old games on cartridges could benefit from renewed interest in physical media.

Some gamers have expressed frustration that the upcoming Grand Theft Auto VI game is being released only as a digital download, rather than on disc. Sony has also faced backlash after announcing it will stop producing discs for its PlayStation games beginning in 2028.
Atari's games, meanwhile, come in the same black plastic cartridges as they once did, along with box art, instruction manuals and, in some editions, the recreated patches.

"My daughter now, who's 16, is hardcore into vinyl [records]," said Mika. "Physical is more important to the younger generation now, surprisingly to me, and now we're getting that kind of interest for these kinds of things too in games."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jonathan Ore is a writer and editor for CBC Radio Digital in Toronto. He regularly covers the video games industry for CBC Radio programs across the country and has also covered arts & entertainment, technology and the games industry for CBC News. You can reach him at jonathan.ore@cbc.ca

articles.title: ‘Where’s Newfoundland?’ ask shocked residents looking at Hilroy exercise books
articles.summary: As a new school year approaches, parents and students are out buying new school supplies — but one classroom staple has people in Newfoundland and Labrador demanding answers.

image.caption: Hilroy Canada's glossy exercise books don't include Newfoundland or Cape Breton on the cover. (Elizabeth Whitten/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New
As a new school year approaches, parents and students are out buying new school supplies — but one classroom staple has people in Newfoundland and Labrador demanding answers.
New design is missing Newfoundland, Cape Breton

Hilroy Canada exercise books are known for the map of Canada on the cover. The design for a glossy version of the notebook also features the map but it's missing some of Canada’s geographical features — namely Newfoundland and Cape Breton.
When handed a book by CBC News, Victor Aucoin, a teacher, initially admired the design but on closer inspection asked, “Where’s Newfoundland?” before laughing.
“There’s no Newfoundland. Oh, so we don’t exist in Canada, OK! That’s nice to see,” he said.
“The most beautiful island on Earth and… we didn’t make it to Canada,” he added, shaking his head a little. “What a sin.”
Aucoin said given the province's economic importance to the country, it was shocking to see the island missing, adding he won’t be buying these books.
“I know in my classroom if some children come in, I will ask them to tell their parents to contact Hilroy and file a complaint, as I will as well.”
He added his mother is from Cape Breton.
“Wait till I call her and tell her Cape Breton is no longer part of Canada. She’s going to be pleased. No Newfoundland. No Cape Breton,” he said, again shaking his head.
Aucoin reiterated the situation is unacceptable and he would be contacting the company to tell them to take the new exercise books off the shelves.
“This is an uproar.”
It's not clear when the design was released. CBC News has contacted ACCO Brands, which owns Hilroy, for an interview but did not hear back by publication.
‘It’s bananas’
Johnathan Goodyear, also looking over the new design, said it was “kind of crazy” that Newfoundland is missing and wondered how it happened. He’d like to see the company recall the exercise books.
“It’s bananas," he said.
Goodyear added Newfoundland and Labrador has contributed a lot to Canada, especially on a military front, so “knocking us off is pretty rough.”
Some people worried the omission could have a detrimental impact on students learning about the country.
Goodyear is concerned it could leave students unaware of the country’s geography.
“It’s kind of a big deal.”
Rose Wilkinson said Newfoundland should be included in the cover and worries people don’t know where Newfoundland is.
“I feel like most people don’t think of it as a place [in] Canada because it’s so small," she said.
Dace Gruchy, who initially admired the new design for its bright colours, was also unimpressed when he noticed Newfoundland was missing from the cover.
“That’s mad disrespectful," said Gruchy. “We should be on this ‘cause we’re part of Canada.”

articles.title: Jurors in Lindsay Clancy trial deadlocked but judge asks them to keep trying
articles.summary: The Massachusetts mother is facing murder charges for killing her three children at their family home in 2023.

blocks.text: Jurors in the trial of Lindsay Clancy are deadlocked after three days of deliberations, but a judge has asked them to keep trying.
Clancy, a resident of Massachusetts, is facing murder charges for killing her three children at their family home in 2023.

Her lawyer does not dispute that the 36-year-old former nurse killed the children, but argues that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time and was unable to distinguish right from wrong.
The Massachusetts mother is charged with three counts of first-degree murder, as the prosecution argues she made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them.
The jury, made up of nine women and three men, began deliberating last week after hearing weeks of testimony from dozens of witnesses.
On Tuesday, audible gasps could be heard in the courtroom as Judge William Sullivan read out a note from the jury indicating that it was deadlocked.
Clancy, who was left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window shortly after the killings, appeared stoic as she sat in a wheelchair beside her lawyer.
It is not uncommon for jurors in high-profile trials to struggle to reach a decision, and judges have protocols for such situations.
A deadlock among the jury such as this one happens in "complex and emotionally charged trials", Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, told the BBC.

"If the deadlock persists, the judge might issue an additional 'dynamite' instruction [known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge in Massachusetts] to encourage the group to consider alternative perspectives and strive for an agreement while upholding their genuine convictions," Cucolo said.
But it is "typically a last-ditch effort" from a judge, she said.
The judge can declare a mistrial if the jury is not able to agree on a verdict.
Clancy is accused of strangling her kids - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months - with fitness bands in their Massachusetts home in January 2023.

The defence argues that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis, a severe mental health condition that can develop after childbirth, and that she should therefore not be held criminally responsible for the killings.
If found guilty of first-degree murder, the intentional and premeditated killing of another person, Clancy will face a mandatory life sentence in prison without the possibility of parole.

She could also be found guilty of a lesser charge, including second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or manslaughter - unintentionally killing "by wanton and reckless conduct". In either of those instances, she would face time behind bars.

If she is found not guilty by reason of insanity, she will not be set free - she would instead be sent to a psychiatric hospital where her status would be periodically reviewed. She could stay in hospital for the rest of her life.

articles.title: Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase
articles.summary:
Six employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capital

Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately…
articles.byline: Luke Harding and Dan Sabbagh in Kyiv

blocks.text: Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv.

Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said its workers died when a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities, it added, during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and the Kyiv region. At least 12 people died, with a dozen wounded, including three children.

“An unbearably difficult night for the entire railway family. Railway staff have been working at the scene since early this morning. The attack has caused significant damage. Rescue workers are still putting out a number of fires,” said Ukrzaliznytsia’s chair, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.

blocks.caption: Boryspil, in the Kyiv region. Trains were evacuated and travellers stranded during Russia’s days-long air assault on Kyiv Photograph: Jelle Krings

blocks.text: The grim strike took place as Russia escalated its attacks on the Ukrainian capital. It has carried out continuous raids for six days, beginning last week, in an attempt to disrupt daily life and demoralise the city’s inhabitants. The onslaught took place hours before Ukrainian children began a new school year.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured. One wounded railway employee, Volodymyr, was taken to hospital on Tuesday, with people urged to donate blood if they were B positive – his group. “Our colleagues are by his side,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding it would support victims’ families.

Ukraine’s railway network is Europe’s third largest, with 15,000 miles (24,000km) of track. It has been a lifeline for the country’s wartime civilians, transporting four million people and an estimated 120,000 pets. It has brought world leaders to Kyiv, including Joe Biden and Andy Burnham, who arrived last week on an overnight service from Poland.

blocks.caption: Railway workers repairing overhead lines after a Russian strike. Photograph: Jelle Krings

blocks.text: Serhih Leshchenko, a member of Ukrzaliznytsia’s supervisory board, described the railway as the “backbone of Ukraine’s economy”. It was the main logistical supplier for the country’s army and industry, and every week transported 600,000 people, he told the Guardian. With 170,000 workers, it was also Ukraine’s biggest company.

For these reasons Russia was trying to destroy railways, he added. In the first year of the war it attacked bridges, which could be easily replaced. Next, it targeted rails and electricity substations. Ukraine then switched to using diesel engines. This year, Russia started “direct attacks on civilian locomotives”, he said – an insidious tactic, at a time when Ukraine is short of air defences.

Several drivers have been killed and locomotives targeted inside depots. Leshchenko said that if a Shahed drone came within 50km of a train, it had to be evacuated, and could only continue once the threat has passed. So far this year Russia has hit the network more than 1,500 times – a higher figure than in the whole of 2025. Overall, 249 carriages and 492 locomotives have been damaged.

Once known for their punctuality, trains now suffer regular delays, sometimes lasting as long as 12 to 15 hours. Amid air raid sirens, passengers are forced to disembark and take cover, including during winter. Writing on Facebook, the Ukrainian journalist Tetiana Zaiets described how she hid in April when Russian drones flew overhead.

blocks.caption: A destroyed railway bridge in the Lyman district in eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk oblast. Photograph: Jelle Krings

blocks.text: “It was hell. The train stopped at night somewhere in central Ukraine. I don’t even know the name of the town. Half asleep, I just heard the conductor say ‘evacuation’. We took only our personal belongings and valuables with us. It was raining outside. Thank you to the conductors for handing out blankets,” she posted.

She added: “That’s how we held out for two hours. While kamikaze drones were buzzing overhead, we crawled under a goods wagon. The last carriage in the train was full of children. They were being taken back from hospital. They were crying in their sleep. I thought I’d ended up in some sort of horror film. But no, this is our life.”
Since the incident, Zaiets said she was too frightened to travel by train. “Until the war is over, I won’t be using it,” she said, stressing she respected Ukraine’s “courageous” railway workers.

Last week, an enemy drone hit a train in the Odesa region with 600 people on board, including 15 children. “The train was stopped, we were kicked out. We heard explosions, everything was burning. It was scary,” one passenger, Andriy, told the website Suspline.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Refugees arriving in Lviv on evacuation trains from Kharkiv and Kryvy Rih make their way through the train station. Photograph: Jelle Krings

blocks.text: Another passenger, Eva, said she was evacuated twice, and “dropped off in a field”. “We sat there and heard something flying. Then we saw a drone very close by.” She managed to collect her belongings and was eventually picked up by a bus, she said.

Leshchenko admitted the Russian strikes were hurting Ukraine’s economy and had slowed the export of grain from its under-fire Black Sea ports. He said Kyiv needed air defences from western partners, so it could protects its trains from marauding missiles and drones. “If the whole country is under attack, they will attack railways for sure,” he said.

Up until this year more than 90% of Ukrainian trains arrived on time. This was in part down to the fact engines never go especially fast, rolling at 55mph. Carriages are clean and comfortable: the best way of getting around a vast country. Stewards look after night train customers and bring them morning tea in filigree holders. There is a trolley on day trains, and patchy wifi.

blocks.caption: A wounded Ukrainian soldier is evacuated on a train. Photograph: Jelle Krings

blocks.text: On international services, border guards scrutinise male passengers, while dogs roam up and down corridors. Since the invasion, men between 18 and 60 have been forbidden from leaving the country, with some exemptions. On trains from Kyiv to Przemyśl, a railway hub in eastern Poland, most travellers are women. Since 2022 about six million people have departed abroad, many exiting by train.

In recent days Russia has launched over 1,500 drones at Ukraine, 800 of them jet-fuel models, which are harder to shoot down. In the past, Moscow would send a swarm of drones a couple of times a week, usually at night. Now the attacks continue without a pause, with one or two drones dispatched every hour, paralysing ordinary life. Air raid sirens in Kyiv are non-stop.

Pertsovsky, Ukrzaliznytsia’s boss, described the loss of his employees on Tuesday as “terrible”. “We are in touch with their loved ones. Everyone is with them to get through this extremely difficult time. The night is bitter with impossibility,” he wrote.
