articles.title: 'I have fired 40 of my agents for being corrupt', says Nigeria's anti-corruption chief
articles.summary: The EFCC boss says more than five of the dismissed officials are already facing prosecution.

blocks.text: Nigeria's anti-corruption agency has dismissed more than 40 employees for alleged corruption and financial misconduct over the past three years.
The disclosure was made by Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) chairman Ola Olukoyede at an event assessing the agency's achievements since he took the helm in October 2023.
He said more than five of the dismissed officials were already facing prosecution, while case files are being prepared against others.

The EFCC investigates financial crimes, including fraud, money laundering and corruption - regularly pursuing cases against politicians, public officials, business figures and others accused of misusing public funds.

"In the past two-and-a-half years or three years of my service, I've asked them to dismiss over 40 staff on account of corruption and financial malpractice," Olukoyede told journalists at the briefing in the capital, Abuja.
He went on to explain that as part of the reforms he had overseen at the agency, the EFCC's Department of Internal Affairs had been renamed "the Department of Ethics and Integrity".
To fight against conflicts of interest, a policy on gifts and hospitality had also been introduced.
It requires officers to declare gifts above a certain threshold - which he did not specify - including gifts received from relatives abroad.
"You must be sure that your hands are clean. You can't be fighting corruption when your hands are soiled with corrupt practices," Olukoyede said.
The BBC asked the EFCC for more details about the alleged corruption involving its former staff members, but the agency said this information was not available.
It was keen to point to its other achievements over the last three years - highlighted at Monday's briefing, external.
Olukoyede, 56, said he had overseen a record-breaking time for the EFCC, recovering 1.23 trillion naira ($925m, £683m), with a conviction rate of more than 75%.
"The commission received 49,673 petitions, investigated 39,615 cases, filed 14,476 cases in court and secured 10,872 convictions between October 2023 and July 2026," he said.
In the first half of 2026 alone, it had recorded 1,370 convictions from 1,889 filings, the EFCC chairman added.
"These results reflect diligence, resilience and a prosecutorial approach anchored on evidence and courtroom outcomes."
Other figures disclosed at the event show that the EFCC's caseload is increasingly focused on cybercrime and fraud rather than just corruption cases against high-profile officials.

articles.title: Vance calls Michigan Senate candidate El-Sayed 'evil' at campaign rally
articles.summary: El-Sayed faces Trump ally Mike Rogers in what has quickly become a senate race characterised by personal attacks and insults between the two.

blocks.text: US Vice-President JD Vance has described Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as "a very, very evil" person at a campaign rally in Michigan, accusing him of being a divisive figure.

He also warned El-Sayed to "keep my wife's name the hell out of your mouth", after the candidate appeared to suggest that Vance's late grandfather would not accept Second Lady Usha Vance, who is Hindu.
El-Sayed shot back at Vance later on Monday, accusing the Trump administration of pushing "evil" policies and "starting wars abroad when there's peace".
The 41-year-old candidate is facing Trump ally Mike Rogers in what has quickly become a senate race characterised by personal attacks and insults between the two.

Speaking at a rally for Rogers in a Detroit suburb on Monday night, Vance repeatedly accused El-Sayed - who is Muslim - of being a divisive figure with little interest in bringing communities together.
"I realise that there's something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today," Vance said, adding that he was seeking to "destroy" the country.

"My message to Abdul El-Sayed is: You can pal around with terrorist sympathisers, and you can say that America deserved 9/11, or you could empathise not with the children who were targeted at Temple Israel, but with the attacker," the vice-president said.
During his primary, El-Sayed campaigned alongside controversial far-left influencer and Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who once suggested that the US "deserved" the attacks in New York and Washington.
While El-Sayed never said those words and has since distanced himself from Piker, Vance repeatedly linked the two together during his speech.
In an interview with CNN later on Monday, El-Sayed took his own jabs at Vance, accusing the vice-president of a series of "evil" policies during the Trump administration.

"Evil is ripping healthcare away from working people in exchange for tax breaks for billionaires," El-Sayed said. "Evil is making people pay more for groceries and gas while pushing for trade wars and actual war. Evil is dividing people for your own gain. Evil is selling out your morals for a little bit of power."

He also sought to clarify his previous comments about the Vance family and the Second Lady, saying that he was seeking to demonstrate that Vance "believes in a political philosophy that says that some people are somehow more American than others".

The Michigan Senate race is among the most high profile of the upcoming midterm elections and takes place in a key battleground state that former President Joe Biden won in 2020 and Donald Trump won in 2024.
A survey released earlier this week by Michigan firm Epic-MRA suggests Al-Sayed has a narrow four-point lead over Rogers, a former law enforcement officer with long experience in politics.

articles.title: Mark Carney tells US to ‘start being serious’ amid escalating trade war
articles.summary: Canadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insults

blocks.text: Mark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada.

Days before Canada is due to retaliate against Trump’s sweeping tariffs with its own duties on US goods, the Canadian prime minister criticized US officials for insulting his country. “It is beneath their office,” he said.
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions” about trade, Carney said.
Trump signed an executive order last week directing the US federal government to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America – a move that has been rejected by Canadians.
The US president’s most senior trade negotiator has meanwhile downplayed the potentially disastrous effects of a US trade war with Canada, declaring the spat to be “more their emergency than ours”.

The US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, argued that Canada was more vulnerable after the breakdown in talks set the stage for sweeping tariffs between the two neighbors, telling Politico: “There are no negotiations happening on trade right now.”
The comment comes just more than a week after US-Canada trade talks imploded. The US levied 50% tariffs on $20bn in Canadian goods.

Canada, the US’s second-largest trading partner, announced it would impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of American goods starting on 8 September. Now, US residents are poised to feel extreme pressure from Trump’s tariffs and Canada’s retaliatory measures, including on day-to-day items.
Greer appeared to blame the escalating trade war on Canadian officials, telling Politico: “It’s not clear Canada wants a deal.
“If Canada believes that prohibiting and banning American goods and services is appropriate, then obviously that’s something that the United States should consider as well.”
Unacceptable asks from Canada included lighter taxes on heavy-duty trucks, according to Greer, who said such requests torpedoed the trade talks.

Canadian officials, on the other hand, attributed the collapsed negotiations to a White House disagreement over who was directing trade talks. Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, also said that American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant”, but added: “In Quebec, these are rights.”

Trump, for his part, has argued in recent weeks that Canada “wants the benefits” of being a US state, without being one – a preoccupation of the US president – as he lashed out at the country’s leaders. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” claimed Trump. “No more!!!”

Greer suggested that negotiations broke down after a misunderstanding around what was, and wasn’t, on the table. “Was that political? I don’t know,” he told Politico. “Was it economic? … I’m not sure how much economic sense it makes because the choice is not between the current tariffs and … you know, duty-free trade. Like, that is that. Those weren’t the options.”

articles.title: 'Tapusin na yan!': Prosecution to finish confidential funds article next week, says Chua
articles.summary: Saying they don't want an overly lengthy impeachment trial, members of the House prosecution panel intend to conclude its presentation on the confidential funds misuse article against Vice President…

blocks.text: Saying they don't want an overly lengthy impeachment trial, members of the House prosecution panel intend to conclude its presentation on the confidential funds misuse article against Vice President Sara Duterte next week.
According to solon-prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, the team is already looking to shift to the two remaining articles of impeachment.

“Masasabi natin, baka by next week ay matapos na, hopefully, ang confidential funds, and we will move on to the next article,” Chua said Tuesday afternoon, Sept. 1 during the prosecution's post-hearing press conference.
(We can say that, hopefully, we could finish the confidential funds article by next week, and we will move on to the next article.)

On Tuesday, Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Colonels Manaros Boransing II and Magtanggol Panopio testified about Army certifications that were used in the Department of Education’s (DepEd) response to state auditors.

In an effort to shorten its witness list, Chua said two other military officers would no longer be presented since their expected testimony would largely repeat the points already placed on the record.
“Iisa lang naman iyong sasabihin nila. To shorten—ayaw naman natin ng protracted hearing. Gusto natin matapos na rin ito.”
(They would only be saying the same thing. To shorten [the proceedings]—we don’t want a protracted hearing. We also want this to be finished.)
Chua said prosecutors already covered the central points involving the Youth Leadership Summits (YLS) and the military certifications.

Respondent Duterte is being accused--among other things--of misuing a total of P612.5 million worth of confidential funds released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and Department of Education (DepEd).
On Wednesday, Sept. 2, the prosecution expects to present former DepEd undersecretary and chief-of-staff Michael Wesley Poa, as well as a representative of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA)

Poa, currently Duterte’s defense lawyer, is expected to address the chain behind the military certifications, while the PSA witness will cover its checks of names appearing in confidential-fund records.

After those witnesses, the Manila solon said the remaining article I lineup would be short. “Ang natitira na lamang si Mr. Edward Fajarda, and probably isa—or at most, dalawa,” he said, referring to DepEd’s former special disbursing officer (SDO).
“The only one remaining is Mr. Edward Fajarda, and probably one—or at most, two [more witnesses].”
He said the prosecution will make its final lineup decision after Wednesday’s hearing. The panel previously finished its presentation of evidence on article IV, or the death threats article.
Defense's turn next
Chua reminded impeachment trial watchers that once the prosecution finishes all four articles of impeachment, the defense must present its own case.
“May target kasi tayo. We have to understand, after us mayroon pang defense; sila naman ang magpe-present. Siyempre ayaw naman natin na umabot pa ito by next year,” he said.
(We have a target. We have to understand that after us, there is still the defense; they will be the ones to present [their case]. Of course, we don’t want this to extend into next year.)

"Sana, hopefully, by November tapos na lahat (Hopefully, everything will be finished by November), so by December we can have the decision of the impeachment court whether or not to convict the Vice President," Chua said.

articles.title: How different would Lindsay Clancy's murder trial look if it happened in Canada?
articles.summary: Canada has an infanticide provision in the Criminal Code that applies exclusively to a mother who kills her newly born child while her mind is "disturbed."

image.caption: Lindsay Clancy watches jury members as Judge William Sullivan polls them before they start deliberations during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., on Monday. (Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children, infanticide and suicide.

As jurors deliberate whether or not Massachusetts mom Lindsay Clancy is criminally responsible for killing her three children, some observers have questioned whether the trial that has gripped the public for the past five weeks could have played out differently had it happened somewhere else.
That's because, unlike Canada, the U.K., and parts of Australia and Europe, the U.S. doesn't have infanticide provisions in its criminal code.

In Canada's Criminal Code, infanticide applies exclusively to mothers who kill their newly born children — defined as a person under the age of one year — while suffering from a "disturbed" mind as a consequence of birth and lactation.
It's a criminal offence, but carries a lesser sentence than murder or manslaughter, so legal experts say it is sometimes argued as a partial defence to the latter two charges.

The major difference is the sentence, with infanticide punishable by a maximum of five years, said Isabel Grant, a University Killam Professor in the Allard School of Law at the University of British Columbia who specializes in criminal law.

"Women who kill as a result of not recovering from childbirth should not face life imprisonment — that doesn't really serve anyone's interests if there was truly a postpartum illness at play," Grant, who has published extensively in the area of homicide, including infanticide, told CBC News.
"The United States has taken a much harsher approach to these cases than in Canada, with young women being sentenced to extraordinarily long periods of incarceration in some of these cases."

Clancy, 36, is accused of killing her three children in 2023 while her then-husband was running an errand. Over the past five weeks, jurors at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., have heard that she strangled Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and eight-month-old Callan with exercise bands in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.

items: Why Lindsay Clancy, on trial for the deaths of her 3 children, has so many supporters
What is postpartum psychosis, the illness at the centre of Lindsay Clancy's murder trial?

blocks.text: She then attempted to take her own life by jumping out of a second-floor window, which left her paralyzed.

Clancy's defence doesn't dispute the killings. But they argue she isn't criminally responsible because she had bipolar disorder and was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and little-understood mental health condition that can affect a new mom's sense of reality.
Prosecutors argue Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder because she plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the killings.

Jurors could find Clancy guilty of murder or manslaughter or acquit her if they find that she wasn't criminally responsible due to psychiatric illness. Clancy’s sentence could be as severe as life in prison, or, if acquitted, she could remain confined in a mental health facility or be released.
How social media drives toxic obsession with the Lindsay Clancy case
Could Clancy have used infanticide defence?

Arguing for the lesser charge of infanticide in cases of this nature isn't a perfect solution, but is, on the whole, "far more just and merciful than the life sentences so common in the United States," Michelle Oberman, a professor at Santa Clara University School of Law and author of When Mothers Kill, recently wrote in the New York Times.
However, even if the U.S. had similar provisions to Canada, it may not have changed much for Clancy's case because of the ages of her older children, experts agree.

To qualify for the reduced sentence, the accused must meet all the criteria of the legal definition of infanticide, said criminologist Kirsten Kramar, author of Unwilling Mothers, Unwanted Babies: Infanticide in Canada.

The accused must be the woman who gave birth to the child killed, the child must be less than one year old at the time of the act or omission and the mother must be suffering from a disturbed mind as a consequence of birth and lactation, Kramar told CBC News.

Technically, in Canada, Clancy could have raised infanticide as a defence for the murder of Callan, who was eight months old, said Grant, the criminal law professor at UBC. But the killing of Clancy's older children could not be defended as infanticide even if she hadn't recovered from the birth of the youngest child when she killed them, she added.
"That is a shortcoming in the Canadian law."

Given what Grant called the extensive evidence of Clancy's serious mental health problems, "it is possible she would have been charged with manslaughter for the older children and infanticide for the infant but that would be a significant determination," she said.

Jurors have heard that Clancy was prescribed 13 psychiatric medications across different providers, and her attorneys say Clancy did everything she could to seek help, including going to the emergency room, calling a suicide hotline and checking herself into a psychiatric hospital.

Whether or not the charges might have changed, Grant says she suspects that, in Canada, "we would probably have less information about the case before it gets to trial, the trial would not be televised and she would have the option of being tried by a jury or judge alone."
That sentiment was echoed by Oberman, in the New York Times, who wrote these "tragedies can avoid becoming true-crime dramas" because they typically avoid going to public trial.
"Ms. Clancy’s trial, with its high-stakes drama and surrounding media frenzy, does little to honour her children," she added.
The judge in Clancy's trial told jurors to keep deliberating Tuesday after they said they could not reach a unanimous decision.
About Canada's infanticide legislation

Canada's infanticide legislation was passed in 1948, amended in 1955 and upheld in a few recent landmark cases. It's both an offence and a partial defence. Researchers have called its use "rare and complex."

Its purpose was to address situations where women — usually young, unwed women — felt compelled to kill their babies due to societal pressures, such as the stigma attached to unwed motherhood or the fate of the baby, said Kramar.

items: Jail time necessary for ‘public condemnation’ of rare P.E.I. infanticide case, judge rules
Infanticide convictions upheld for Meredith Borowiec, who dropped 3 babies in dumpster

blocks.text: "These were considered altruistic killings that did not merit the death penalty," Kramar said.
In Canada, capital punishment was abolished from the Criminal Code in 1976.
"It provides for mitigation of punishment that recognizes the social conditions of motherhood and that the killing is not done out of malice towards the baby," Kramar said.
Lawyers have previously noted the wording is intentionally vague so it can be handled case by case.
P.E.I. woman gets 1 year in jail for rare infanticide case

In 2011, the law was upheld by Ontario's top court in the case of a Guelph woman convicted of infanticide after smothering two of her children. In 2016, the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the infanticide convictions for a Calgary woman who left three babies in a dumpster.
Most recently, in January, a Charlottetown woman who inflicted life-ending injuries on her three-month old daughter was sentenced to one year in jail after pleading guilty to infanticide.
Cassie Acorn was originally charged with first-degree murder, but a psychiatric evaluation determined she had a “disturbance of the mind” — namely postpartum depression — at the time of the crime.

During sentencing, provincial court Judge Jeff Lantz spoke about how many cases of infanticide involve mothers who did not want to be pregnant, gave birth in secret and then either killed or abandoned the infants to their death.
Acorn wanted the child to be born, Lantz said, but also recognized she was an abuse survivor with a cognitive disability who found herself overwhelmed with postpartum depression.

articles.title: Germany says Russia behind attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
articles.summary: Investigators believe an explosives-laden drone was deliberately targeting a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August.

image.caption: The airport is ​a cargo and military logistics hub used by NATO and Ukraine's Antonov Airlines for military suppliesImage: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The German government on Tuesday said Russia was "responsible" for an attempted drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.

"The federal government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig," said Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday afternoon, adding that the attack fitted the pattern of a "long series of destabilization operations" against Europe.
Leipzig airport attack: What has Germany said?

"The means used — such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine," added Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.

Authorities discovered a drone fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism on the evening of August 4 in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport between Ukrainian cargo aircraft and believe a second drone may have collided with a DHL aircraft nearby.
Last week, German media reported a third drone, also loaded with explosives, had also been discovered at the airport.
German federal prosecutors described the incident as a "serious attack on Germany's transport and logistics infrastructure."
"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," said Dobrindt.

Over the weekend, German chancellor Friedrich Merz had promised that a formal response to the incident would be made public in the coming days. He did not go into further detail but said that Germany's European Union and NATO allies would "not be surprised."

Earlier on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Wadephul vowed a measured response to the discovery of the drone, but stopped short of holding Russia directly responsible for the incident until his press conference with Interior Minister Dobrindt.
EU top diplomat points finger at Russia

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said earlier on Tuesday that it was "clear" that Russia was involved in the drone incident, but declined to comment further until Germany had identified those it believes were responsible,
Kallas said Russia was becoming increasingly provocative, raising the question of what could be done to deter Moscow from escalating tensions any further.

articles.title: Leptospirosis survivor: Don't wade, bathe in floodwater
articles.summary: With the continuous onslaught of the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat), cases of leptospirosis in the country are expected to rise as several communities remain submerged in floodwaters.

blocks.text: With the continuous onslaught of the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat), cases of leptospirosis in the country are expected to rise as several communities remain submerged in floodwaters.
In a “24 Oras” report by Oscar Oida on Tuesday, leptospirosis survivor Jimmy Dunva warned the public about the dangers of wading and bathing in floodwater.
Dunva recalled suffering a severe case of the disease when he was rushed to the hospital for treatment, where doctors informed him that he had only a few days left to live.
“‘Di na po ako makalakad nung mga araw na ‘yon, kumbaga po namamanas na po yung mga paa ko,” Dunva recalled.
(I couldn’t walk during those days because my feet were already swollen.)

“Bale po, two days na lang po before nalaman na [leptospirosis] na po talaga ‘yung sakit ko, two days na lang mamamatay na daw ako kasi malubha na po talaga ‘yung [leptospirosis] ko nung time na ‘yon,” he added.
(It was just two days before they confirmed that my illness was actually leptospirosis. They said I only had two days to live because my condition was already that severe at the time.)
However, unlike other severe cases that ended in death, he survived his ordeal through dialysis.
Dunva recounted the grueling distress he experienced while fighting leptospirosis, particularly the terrifying uncertainty of not knowing how much longer he would live.

“May sinuguran po ako na baha na, ‘di ko namalayan na may sugat ako non nung time na ‘yon. Ang hirap po magkaroon ng [leptospirosis], kumbaga hindi mo alam kung mamamatay ka na o mabubuhay ka pa… akala ko talaga noon, mamamatay na po talaga ako,” Dunva said.

(I waded through a flooded area, unaware that I had a wound at the time. Having leptospirosis is extremely hard—you don't know whether you'll live or die. I honestly thought I was going to die back then.)
He shared that he cannot help but feel sad whenever he sees people bathing or swimming in floodwaters, as if they do not take the dangers of leptospirosis seriously.

“‘Pag nakakakita po ako sa mga balita po ng mga nakalusong pa sa baha na parang feel na feel pa po nila—na ‘di nila alam na ‘yun po ang magiging sanhi ng [pagkakaroon ng leptospirosis] po natin,” Dunva said.
(Whenever I see news reports of people wading through floodwaters seemingly enjoying themselves, it saddens me because they don't realize that is exactly how you contract leptospirosis.)
Unlike Dunva, Villardo Villaranda Jr., a barangay councilor, did not survive leptospirosis. He fought the disease for barely three days before passing away.
In Oida’s report, relatives of the 50-year-old councilor expressed deep grief over his sudden death.

“Nag-complain siya sa akin na three days, ‘yung three days po na may symptoms na siya. Then after, pina-check up ko po siya two and a half days lang po ‘yung nilaban namin sa ospital, after noon nawala na po siya,” said Evelyin Lagan, Villaranda's sister.
(He complained to me after experiencing symptoms for three days. I had him checked, but we only got to fight for two and a half days in the hospital before he passed away.)
Doctors suspect that the victim may have contracted leptospirosis while riding his motorcycle through flooded areas.

“Ang explanation sa amin ng doktor, kahit daw po hindi siya sumulong sa baha, ‘yun daw pong tubig na nasa kalsada pa rin kahit humupa na ito, naco-consider pa rin siya na part siya ng tubig baha na pumasok sa sapatos niya po,” Lagan recalled.

(The doctor explained to us that even if he didn’t directly wade through deep floods, the stagnant water left on the road after receding is still considered floodwater, which may have seeped into his shoes.)
Villaranda was also placed on dialysis, but the intervention came too late to save him.
“Nahirapan na po siyang huminga. Actually, tinapat naman na po kami ng doctor na severe na ‘yung case niya kasi lahat ng symptoms ng leptospirosis nag-manifest na po sa katawan niya,” Lagan added.
(He had difficulty breathing. Actually, the doctor was frank with us that his case was already severe because all the symptoms of leptospirosis had manifested in his body.)
According to the latest data from the Department of Health (DOH), there were 5,486 cases of leptospirosis recorded nationwide from January 4 to August 27.
The highest number of cases was recorded in NCR, Region 2, and Region 3.
These figures are expected to rise further, given that numerous areas were submerged in floodwaters during the heavy monsoon rains over the weekend.
The DOH stated that it has already deployed additional health professionals to hospitals that typically receive leptospirosis patients.

Authorities continue to remind the public never to take leptospirosis lightly and to seek immediate medical consultation upon experiencing symptoms after wading through floodwaters. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 20: Army officers deny certifying DepEd's confidential fund spending
articles.summary: Army colonels Manaros Boransing II and Magtanggol Panopio denied that they issued certifications attesting to the propriety of the Department of Education"s P15 million confidential fund spending in…

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 11:21pm

Day 20 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte started with Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero saying that the pictures circulating on social media supposedly showing hostile witness and Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio wearing an earpiece, were generated using artificial intelligence (AI).
In addition, Escudero reminded the parties that every witness "must testify solely from his or her own knowledge, free from coaching or influence from counsel or any other person."

Army colonels Manaros Boransing II and Magtanggol Panopio denied that they issued certifications attesting to the propriety of the Department of Education’s P15 million confidential fund spending in 2023.

In separate testimonies before the witness stand, Boransing and Panopio said such certifications were only issued to attest to the successful conduct and attendance of participants in the Youth Leadership Seminar and Information Education Campaign, not to testify on any expenditure.

While Boransing and Panopio both said that they were not aware that their certification would be used by the DepEd to liquidate confidential funds, they had varying reactions once they were made aware of the purpose. Boransing said he had no reaction as he was busy with other more important matters, while Panopio was somehow surprised.

Panopio also testified that the "confidential" information provided by the DepEd in relation to the conduct of the abovementioned youth activities may have included data on teenage pregnancy and the personal life of students.
Defense counsel Sheila Sison countered that these certifications were made by the military with full knowledge that it would cover “any legal purpose it may serve.”

Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III did not question Boransing and Panopio but made a manifestation that an alias may be used as a pseudonym for entertainment purposes, but if there is no actual person behind the name, it could be considered a “fictitious name” or “fake name.”
He cited Republic Act No. 6085, which regulates the use of aliases.

“It’s only allowed in the Philippines for pseudonyms, solely for literary, cinema, television and other entertainment purposes. Therefore, if there is a person behind the alias, then it is an alias,” he said.

This was the same point raised by private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia when she was being asked by Senator-judge Robin Padilla last week if she is aware that Philippine revolutionary heroes also used aliases.

Divinagracia tried to explain to Padilla that the use of aliases is a non-issue for the prosecution because the prosecution’s impeachment case against the Vice President did not allege that the names of confidential fund recipients were aliases, but Padilla quickly cut her off by arguing that it cannot be a non-issue because it was the prosecution who was putting forward the unusual names.

It was former OVP special disbursing officer Gina Acosta who earlier testified that the unusual names of recipients of the confidential fund of the OVP, as stated in its acknowledgement receipt submitted to state auditors, which included Timon Pusa, Miggy Mango, Antonio Pagong, among others, might have been aliases.

Also on Day 20, Escudero reminded his colleague, Senate Minority Leader Alan Cayetano, that the burden of proof always lies with the prosecution as accusers in this case, after Cayetano suggested that presumption can shift depending on the evidence presented.

“For the record, to clarify, the burden of proof never shifts. The burden of evidence may shift, but the burden of proof does not. The burden of proof still lies with the prosecution, but depending on how the issue is presented, the burden of evidence may shift, but the burden of proof never shifts,” Escudero said.
The House prosecution team then said that given the testimony of the Army colonels, the Vice President’s camp is clearly lying about how it spent its P15.5 million DepEd confidential fund allocation.
As this developed, defense team lawyer and former DepEd Undersecretary Michael Poa stepped down from his post as spokesperson.

This is because Poa is expected to take the witness stand, being the one who asked for military certifications to justify the DepEd’s P15.5 million confidential fund expenses in 2023 that were used to pay for rewards to informants. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: France targets Shein and Temu with fast fashion fees
articles.summary: The levy on "ultra-fast fashion" items could reach almost €20 per garment by 2030.

blocks.text: France has started imposing fees on fast fashion items which could reach almost €20 per garment by 2030, as the government tries to curb sales of cheap clothing sold by e-commerce sites.
The levy, which came into force on Tuesday, follows a new law passed in June to regulate so-called "ultra-fast fashion" companies such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress.
The e-commerce giants, known for selling large volumes of cheap apparel, have been criticised by French officials for driving a surge in ultra-fast fashion.
China's commerce ministry has described the French law as discriminatory and a trade barrier, saying it could violate World Trade Organization (WTO) principles.
French minister Mathieu Lefevre said the "harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion" on the environment and economy were "well known".
In July, Lefevre's office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European companies.
Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two factors: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.
The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.
For 2026, the charges range from a €0.50 (£0.43) levy on underwear to €2 (£1.71) for T-shirts, to €9 (£7.71) for jeans and €12 (£10.28) for a jacket.
The levy could reach up to €19.50 (£16.71/$22.60) per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50% of the product's pre-tax price.

articles.title: Harmful haze from Indonesia fires to affect western PH – Pagasa
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The haze possibly linked to ongoing fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia may be swept over the western portions of the country due to strong winds brought by the southwest monsoon, or…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The haze possibly linked to ongoing fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia may be swept over the western portions of the country due to strong winds brought by the southwest monsoon, or “habagat,” the state weather bureau said.

Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration weather specialist Benison Estareja said during the 5 p.m. weather advisory that, based on its satellite image, the haze may affect the western section of Visayas and Mindanao, as well as Mimaropa.
He explained that the air particles came from Kalimantan in Indonesia and are being pulled by the southwest monsoon.

“Itong mga papupusaw na kulay galing po dito sa may Kalimantan sa may central part ng Sabah dito sa may Indonesia ay inaasahan pong kikilos dahil unti-unting tinutulak nga nitong southwest monsoon or habagat patungo dito sa western side ng ating bansa,” he explained.

(“These fading colored areas—originating from the Kalimantan region in the central part of Sabah, Indonesia—are expected to move, as they are gradually being pushed by the southwest monsoon toward the western side of our country.”)

Estareja advised the public to constantly monitor the air quality index (AIQ) of their respective areas in the Department of Environment and Natural Resources – Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) issued advisories.

The DENR-NCR reported early Tuesday that several areas in Metro Manila recorded high PM2.5, which refers to fine particulate matter measuring 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter, wherein AIQ reached up to “acutely unhealthy levels”. /cb

articles.title: Solons clash over bill setting 5-year barangay, SK terms
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — House lawmakers on Tuesday differed over a bill seeking to set five-year terms for barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials, which would postpone the upcoming elections…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — House lawmakers on Tuesday differed over a bill seeking to set five-year terms for barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials, which would postpone the upcoming elections for their posts to 2028 in turn.
The exchange was between Act Teachers party-list Rep. Antonio Tinio and Asenso Pinoy party-list Rep. Henry Oaminal, one of the proponents of the proposed measure, House Bill No. 10971.

During the interpellation of the bill’s committee report at the House plenary session, Tinio questioned the rationale behind the term extension, pointing out that Republic Act No. 12232, enacted in 2025, already set the term of barangay and SK officials to four years.

“Since the said law was passed, several stakeholders including grassroot leaders such as barangay officials and SK officials expressed to us that a four-year term would not be sufficient,” Oaminal answered.

“It is within the plenary powers of Congress to constantly evaluate laws that are previously passed to determine if they are still sufficient to meet the ever-changing needs of our constituencies,” he added.
In response, Tinio said the proponent’s answer was “very telling.”
“Natural, kung sino ang elected official, itinanong mo na OK lang ba i-extend term natin, s’yempre, sasabihin nila yes,” the Act Teachers party-list maintained.
(It’s only natural that, if you ask elected officials if they want to extend their terms, they’d say yes, of course.)
“Hindi ba mas mahalagang constituency ’yung mga botante mismo? Mayroon bang lumapit sa mga kongresista, sa mga komite?” he added.
(Aren’t our constituencies, the voters, more important? Has anyone approached our congressmen, our committees?)
Tinio pressed Oaminal on whether the barangay and SK officials’ constituents had been consulted on the matter, to which the latter—speaking for his own constituents—answered in the affirmative.

“A lot of barangay projects, when a barangay leader starts it, and a new barangay leader is elected, more often than not, the barangay project started by the previous leader is abandoned,” the Asenso Pinoy party-list explained.

He further maintained that barangay projects normally took over three years to complete and that over 70 percent of barangays operated with only a P5-million budget annually, although it is not immediately clear where his data was sourced.
Oaminal further cited the 2025 Supreme Court decision, which stated that Congress had the power to set the terms of barangay and SK officials.

Citing concerns on the right to suffrage, however, Tinio suggested that the proposed measure instead allow the upcoming 2026 BSKE to proceed this November but apply the five-year term to barangay and SK officials afterward.
Tinio further cited that some SK officials were supposedly already above the age limit of 24.
After Tinio’s interpellation, the period for sponsorships and interpellations was terminated, and the House plenary suspended consideration of the bill.
Similar measures postponing the November 2026 BSKE and fixing the term of barangay and SK officials at five years were approved by the Senate panel on local government last week. /cb

articles.title: NSW government to resume pill testing at music festivals but rejects calls for wider community rollout
articles.summary:
Use of sniffer dogs and searches will continue despite health and harm reduction groups arguing they could lead to riskier drug taking

  • Get our

blocks.text: Drug testing will resume at New South Wales music festivals from October, but will not be rolled out into the wider community despite calls from peak health and harm reduction groups, while the controversial use of sniffer dogs and searches will continue.
On Wednesday the state government announced NSW Health will consult with the music festival industry and harm reduction organisations to roll out pill testing at up to 15 music festivals each year.

There will be no change to the use of sniffer dogs at music festivals, a government spokesperson confirmed, which has been found to prompt risky drug taking. Police, security guards, bag searches and sniffer dogs at music festivals can lead to riskier drug use as people may “pre-load”, or take all of their substances at once, to avoid detection.
Detection of drugs through sniffer dogs has also been used by police to justify strip-searches, which courts and legal experts have found to be unlawful.
The testing rollout follows a 12-month trial which ended in February and which saw 1,480 drug samples tested across 12 NSW music festivals.
The trial was free and anonymous, and meant festival goers could hand over a small sample of substances they intended to use to health staff to test for purity, potency and contaminants.

An independent evaluation led by the University of Sydney, also made public on Wednesday, found people changed their approach to drug taking after getting their drugs tested, particularly when substances differed from what they expected.

Unexpected substances were found in 8% of samples, while high-dose MDMA was found in 4% of MDMA samples where a dose could be calculated. High doses of MDMA increase the risk of organ failure and death, especially in hot environments or when combined with other substances.

A range of unexpected psychoactive substances were detected through the testing, including ketamine analogues (human-made substances which copy ketamine’s chemical makeup, but can produce different and dangerous effects) and heroin.

The University of Sydney evaluation also surveyed people about their views towards pill testing and found “a consistent concern … was the conflict between policing activities (such as drug detection dogs) and access to the service site, which may have dissuaded potential service users from accessing harm reduction services”.
A report from a landmark summit into how to reduce drug-related harms, published in 2025, recommended NSW consider ceasing the use of drug detection dogs and strip-searches at music festivals.
The chief executive of Unharm, Dr Will Tregoning, said the searches need to be scrapped.
“Drug detection dogs are intensive operations that have a track record of clearly contributing to increased overdoses,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

“People see the dogs and take all of their drugs at once out of fear of being detected, and we know police have been strip-searching people at an industrial scale. These searches are also deeply traumatic for people, and affects predominantly young people.”

Ahead of the announcement, peak health and harm reduction groups including the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, the Alcohol and Drug Foundation, and Unharm wrote to NSW’s premier, Chris Minns, and health minister, Ryan Park, on Tuesday calling for pill testing services to be offered in the community.
The ACT and Victoria have both moved beyond festivals to fund community drug checking, where staff provide people with the results along with non-judgmental health and harm reduction advice.
“Drug checking at festivals reaches people who can get to a festival. It cannot reach the people dying at home,” the letter says.
“We ask you to commit to a next phase of drug checking in NSW that includes community-based services, designed for the communities they serve and independently evaluated from the start.”
The letter said that 72% of fatal drug overdoses in Australia happened at home in 2024.
Minns told budget estimates in August that there were no plans to roll out testing to the community.

articles.title: ES Recto defends FL Liza's birthday dinner: 'Not raining at the time'
articles.summary: Executive Secretary Ralph Recto defended President Marcos Jr. amid public backlash after videos circulated showing him singing at First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos" birthday celebration.

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 10:44pm

Executive Secretary Ralph Recto on Tuesday defended President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. amid public backlash after videos circulated showing the chief executive singing at his wife First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos’ birthday celebration.
In an ambush interview, Recto expressed belief that it was not raining during the First Lady's birthday party.
“Pagkaalam ko birthday ng First Lady ‘yun. Nag-dinner lang sila. At noong mga panahong ‘yun, hindi naman umuulan,” the Executive Secretary said.
(What I knew was it was the First Lady’s birthday. They just had dinner. And at that time, it was not raining.)

Asked if there was anything insensitive regarding the event, Recto stood firm. “Like I said, noong panahong ‘yun, birthday ng First Lady. They had a small party at hindi naman umuulan noong weekend na ‘yun.”
(Like I said, at that time, it was the First Lady’s birthday. They had a small party and it wasn’t raining that weekend.)
The First Lady turned 67 on August 21. She earlier also received backlash for posting about taking a "birthday sabbatical" amid the widespread flooding.
Over the recent weekend, continuous heavy rains brought by the Southwest Monsoon or Habagat caused flooding in Metro Manila and several areas in Luzon.

Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said the President continued to monitor the flooding situation and ordered concerned agencies to respond accordingly to the impacts of the inclement weather. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Highlights: Day 20 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Sept. 1, 2026
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Two Philippine Army officers took center stage at Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Tuesday as they testified about military certifications that the Department…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Two Philippine Army officers took center stage at Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Tuesday as they testified about military certifications that the Department of Education (DepEd) used to support its liquidation of P112.5 million in confidential funds in 2023.

Col. Manaros Boransing II told the Senate impeachment court during Day of the impeachment trial that the Army did not receive any funds from Duterte’s offices—whether regular or confidential—to finance the 2023 Youth Leadership Summit (YLS) or the Information Education Communication (IEC) campaign.
Boransing, however, said DepEd could have used its own regular budget for the programs, although he had no knowledge of whether confidential funds were used.
Col. Magtanggol Panopio, meanwhile, testified that a certification he issued for the youth summit was not a valid supporting document for liquidation before the Commission on Audit (COA).
Panopio said he was shocked to learn that DepEd had used the certification to justify its expenses and told Sen. Joel Villanueva that he personally believed the use of the document was improper.
The two officers were presented by the House prosecution to shed light on how military certifications were obtained and used by DepEd under Duterte’s leadership.
Their testimonies are expected to form part of the prosecution’s case on the alleged misuse of confidential funds under Article I of the Articles of Impeachment.

Meanwhile, Presiding Officer Sen. Francis Escudero issued a blanket prohibition on Tuesday barring witnesses at the impeachment trial from possessing or accessing earpieces, mobile phones, smartwatches, and similar communication devices while testifying.

Escudero made the announcement to correct misinformation about previous witness, OVP Assistant Chief of Staff Lemuel Ortonio, after the court determined that a viral image allegedly showing Ortonio wearing an earpiece during his testimony was AI-generated and false.

Sen. Vicente Sotto III also weighed in on the ongoing debate over suspicious names on OVP confidential fund acknowledgment receipts, stating that a name may be considered an alias only if there is an actual person behind it.
Sotto said that if no real person exists behind a name, it must be treated as fictitious or fake, not merely an alias.
Signatories on the receipts included names resembling food brands, fruits, and local politicians, such as Mary Grace Piattos, Miggy Mango, and Kristine Applegate Estrada.

After the session, public prosecutor and Manila Rep. Joel Chua said the prosecution may have three or four witnesses remaining under Article I, covering the confidential fund allegations, with defense lawyer Michael Poa set to take the stand next.
Poa, who stepped aside temporarily from his role as defense spokesperson out of deference to the court, is expected to face questions about military certifications he helped obtain for DepEd.
Chua said the prosecution would decide on its next set of witnesses after Poa’s testimony, estimating about one week before they rest their case on Article I. /dp

articles.title: DA, NIA ask for more funding in 2027 as response to El Niño effects
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Agriculture (DA) and National Irrigation Administration (NIA) on Tuesday appealed for budget increases in some of their projects to respond to the possible…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Agriculture (DA) and National Irrigation Administration (NIA) on Tuesday appealed for budget increases in some of their projects to respond to the possible impacts of El Niño in the country.

During the House committee on appropriations’ briefing on the budget proposal of the two agencies, committee chairperson Rep. Mikaela Suansing asked both agencies if they allotted contingency funds under the 2027 National Expenditure Program for possible effects of El Niño on farmers and fisherfolk.

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said that his agency needs budget increases for the Presidential Assistance for Farmers and Fisherfolk (PAF), noting that the distribution rate of PAF for this year stood at 57.67 percent and may be exhausted by next month due to the effects of southwest monsoon to the livelihoods of farmers and fisherfolk.

He added that the agency needs another P8.7 billion for the fertilizer assistance funds for farmers and additional P10 billion to P12 billion for fisherfolk under the programs of the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources.

Meanwhile, NIA Administrator Eduardo Guillen asked the House lawmakers for an increase in the agency’s quick response fund (QRF). He shared that the NIA only has P300 million allotted for its QRF this year, which he said will not be enough.
Suansing then asked them to categorize the items allotted for El Niño response, noting that this is for them to give special consideration to their requests.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration earlier said that a moderate to strong El Niño is present in the Tropical Pacific. Citing climate models, it added that El Niño will persist until the first half of 2027 and may reach a very strong state until the end of 2026. /cb

articles.title: War and sanctions deepen Iran's fuel crisis
articles.summary: Long lines at fuel stations are spreading across Iran as war damage, import constraints and new US sanctions squeeze supplies.

image.caption: In cities across Iran, drivers are reporting hours-long waits at filling stationsImage: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Only days after Washington announced a new round of economic sanctions on Iran, the country's gasoline shortage has become increasingly visible on the streets.

In cities across Iran, drivers are reporting hours-long waits at filling stations. Videos circulating on social media show some people arriving before midnight or sleeping in their cars to secure fuel the following morning. Some stations have closed before serving everyone in line.

The situation is even more difficult for diesel. Truck drivers say queues at filling stations near major cities can stretch for kilometers, forcing them to wait overnight simply to obtain enough fuel to return to work.

Iran already faces a gasoline deficit of roughly 15 million liters a day. War damage, difficulties importing refined products and a tightening US blockade have made an old structural problem much harder to manage.
Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?
Hours in line for a few liters
A resident of Karaj, west of Tehran, told DW that some filling stations were limiting individual purchases to around five liters.

"I'm in the gasoline line right now. It took about 45 minutes just to get this far," he said. "Yesterday I went to several stations. Some were closed, some had no gasoline and others had very long queues."
He said he returned at 6 a.m. the next morning hoping to avoid the crowds but again found a long line.
He suspects the shortages are partly being used to prepare public opinion for higher gasoline prices, a claim that cannot be independently verified.
For truck drivers, waiting means losing income.

"Our whole life is either spent in the diesel line or on the road," one driver said. He described sleeping at a station while waiting for a tanker that might arrive around midday and supply only a few dozen trucks.
Another driver said he had been waiting since 8 a.m. after failing to obtain diesel the previous day.
For drivers whose earnings depend directly on keeping their vehicles moving, every lost day adds to rising insurance, tire, oil, repair and maintenance costs.
Is Iran changing its gasoline?
The shortage has coincided with the use of methanol in domestically produced gasoline.
Vahid Ghaneifard, chief executive of Persian Gulf Star Oil Company, recently confirmed that the refinery had begun testing methanol as an oxygenate in its gasoline.
The company says methanol makes up around 0.5% of the mixture. Iran's refining authorities say the national fuel standard permits methanol concentrations of up to 3%.
Officials insist the trial complies with technical requirements.
But the timing has fueled public suspicion.
Videos shared online show motorists holding bottles of unusually clear fuel and claiming that gasoline quality has deteriorated.
Why Iran fuel crisis hits different in Europe than the US
Some have alleged that water or excessive alcohol is being mixed into supplies. The allegations have not been independently corroborated.

There has, however, been at least one confirmed incident involving water contamination. In Rafsanjan, local authorities acknowledged that water had mixed with gasoline at a filling station after videos showed cars and motorcycles experiencing problems following refueling.
Officials said the incident resulted from a technical fault and was being investigated.
Distrust over fuel quality grows
For motorists already facing shortages, isolated incidents can reinforce wider fears.

A Tehran resident told DW he had spent about 1 billion tomans — roughly $5,250 (€4,529) at current exchange rates — repairing his car after its crankshaft failed. He believes poor-quality gasoline caused the damage, though such a connection has not been independently established.
He said he was reluctant to publicly protest.
Another resident in Rey, south of Tehran, told DW that motorists had gathered outside a filling station after several cars were allegedly damaged following refueling.
The concern is not simply technical, as it reflects a deeper collapse of trust between consumers and authorities at a time when the government is also discussing higher gasoline and diesel prices.
Tehran argues that the current subsidy system encourages excessive consumption and smuggling and imposes an unsustainable burden on state finances.
But consumers point to other issues such as inefficient cars, inadequate public transport and incomes that have failed to keep pace with inflation.
Can new US sanctions cut off Iran's oil revenue?
Is a price increase in the works?
Economist Hassan Mansour believes the government is once again preparing the political ground for higher energy prices.

Officials have repeatedly argued that Iranian gasoline prices are artificially low, that large volumes are smuggled abroad and that the economy consumes far more energy per unit of output than comparable countries.
The proposed solution is to bring domestic fuel prices closer to international levels.
"Once again, the government finds itself preparing the ground for raising the price of energy carriers," Mansour told DW.
But the problem runs deeper than subsidized gasoline.

Mansour points to the financial condition of Iran's oil industry. Budget documents indicate that the National Iranian Oil Company has tens of billions of euros in debt to the central bank and commercial banks, while the company also owes substantial sums to the National Development Fund and faces major tax liabilities.
When these debts cannot realistically be repaid, Mansour argues, they weaken state finances and contribute indirectly to currency instability and inflation.
Raising gasoline prices could therefore serve both as a demand-management measure and a source of additional revenue.
How the Iran war has deepened Saudi-UAE rivalry
A politically dangerous choice
The government has few easy options.
While imports are harder to finance and transport, domestic production is struggling to keep pace with consumption.
Increasing output quickly requires investment and technology, while reducing consumption means either rationing fuel more aggressively or raising prices. Yet both carry political risks.
Iranian authorities remember what happened in November 2019, when a sudden gasoline price increase triggered nationwide protests followed by a deadly crackdown and an internet shutdown.
Today the economic environment is considerably more fragile.
War has damaged infrastructure, international sanctions are tightening and household purchasing power has fallen sharply. Long fuel queues are now adding another source of frustration.
For Tehran, raising prices might help reduce the gasoline deficit.
But doing so while people are already waiting overnight for fuel could turn an energy shortage into another crisis of public anger, which is something far more difficult to control.

articles.title: Robin Padilla says trip via NLEX to San Simon took 7 hours, Lito Lapid misses impeachment trial
articles.summary: Senators were among those who experienced the horrendous traffic jam on both lanes of the North Luzon Expressway caused by flooding in the San Simon area.

blocks.text: Senators were among those who experienced the horrendous traffic jam on both lanes of the North Luzon Expressway caused by flooding in the San Simon area.
According to Mark Salazar's report on "24 Oras," Sen. Robin Padilla told the Senate plenary about his seven-hour trip from his home to San Simon in Pampanga.
Sen. Joel Villanueva, on the other hand, narrated how Sen. Lito Lapid missed the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte because of the congestion on the expressway.
Padilla shared the long hours they spent queuing on NLEX and presented a video documenting his ordeal from Monday.

“Umalis po kami ng 4:30 ng umaga galing po sa aming bat cave, sa tahanan… Nakalabas po kami ng San Simon 11:30 na ng tanghali. Pitong oras po… sa San Simon lang po 'yon, hindi pa kami nakarating ng Pangasinan,“ Padilla shared.
(We left at 4:30 in the morning from our home… We only managed to exit San Simon at 11:30 in the morning. That was seven hours… just in San Simon alone, and we hadn’t even reached Pangasinan yet.)

“Hindi din po passable doon, 95% ng mga lugar ng San Simon ay lubog. Pagbalik po namin ng NLEX, iniisip namin baka bumaba na ‘yung tubig. Makikita niyo po sa video mas tumaas pa 'yung tubig,” he added.
(It was impassable there; 95% of San Simon was submerged. When we returned to NLEX, we thought the water might have receded. But as you can see in the video, the floodwaters rose even higher.)
Padilla called the experience on the expressway unfair, emphasizing that motorists pay tolls to use it.

“Nagbayad ka naman. [Sana] una na lang sinabi na nila na hindi ganon ang mararanasan namin dahil expressway nga eh. Pero ganon pa man po, wala din naman talagang dadaanan dahil doon po sa McArthur Highway ay lubog din,” Padilla said.

(You paid for it. They should have warned us that this is what we would experience on an expressway. But even then, there was really no alternative route because MacArthur Highway was also submerged.)
Villanueva said Lapid's ordeal at the San Simon segment of NLEX prevented him from attending the earlier impeachment trial.
“Reports showed the traffic stretching as far as 10 km, Mr. President, 10 kilometro po. Some motorists reported spending up to 22 hours,” Villanueva said.

“Gusto natin malaman, Mr. President, at itanong sa NLEX Corporation, nabigyan ba agad ng tulong ang ating mga kababayan nating na-stranded? May tubig po ba, may pagkain [o] portalets at medical assistance po ba?” he added.
(We want to know, Mr. President, and ask NLEX Corporation: Was immediate assistance provided to our stranded motorists? Was there water, food, portable toilets, or medical assistance?)
Villanueva similarly pointed out the toll motorists pay to traverse NLEX, urging expressway management to consider waiving fees or offering refunds to those trapped in the traffic.

“Ang NLEX po, hindi libre ang pagpasok ho diyan. Dapat ikonsidera ng NLEX management ang pag-waive o pag-refund ng toll fees para sa mga motoristang matinding naapektuhan. Nagbabayad ka ng toll, naiipit ka pa sa baha,” the senator said.
(Entering NLEX is not free, so NLEX management should consider waiving or refunding toll fees for severely affected motorists. You pay a toll, only to get trapped in a flood.)
He also stressed that traffic advisories regarding conditions on NLEX must be issued promptly, and that sufficient personnel should be deployed to assist stranded motorists.

The senators’ discussion of the NLEX traffic ordeal led to broader concerns regarding anomalous flood mitigation projects across the country, as well as the status of a previously proposed flood control master plan.

Senator Vicente “Tito” Sotto III noted that a comprehensive master plan had been developed under the leadership of former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Rogelio "Babes" Singson.

“Secretary Babes Singson of the Department of Public Works created and formulated a flood control [plan] from north to south. They started the study sometime in 2011, and by 2015 it… became a master plan and they were about to execute,” Sotto said.
“Unfortunately, there were elections in 2016 and the program, I believe, was sidelined,” he added.
Padilla questioned which agency would be entrusted to craft such a master plan moving forward.

“Napakaganda po ng mungkahi ng ating idolo rin, dati pong Senate President Vicente Sotto. ‘Yun pong masterplan, ang tanong ko lang po, sino po bang gagawa na naman niyan? DPWH po ba ang gagawa? Medyo di po ba tayo napapaso na ba?” Padilla said.

(The suggestion of former Senate President Vicente Sotto is very good. My only question regarding that master plan is: who will draft it this time? Will it be the DPWH again? Haven't we been burned enough?)
For her part, Senator Risa Hontiveros brought up the proposed mega-dike project that local government units in Pampanga have long been requesting.

“Fino-follow up ng mga barangay captain noon mula sa Pampanga ay ‘yun daw meg adike na matagal nang ipinapanukala, panahon pa yata ni dating Pangulong Macapagal Arroyo. Ano na po ba ang nangyari doon?” Hontiveros said.

(What the barangay captains from Pampanga were following up on back then was the mega-dike project that has been proposed for a long time, back during the administration of former President Macapagal-Arroyo. What ever happened to that?) –Jean Mangaluz/NB, GMA News

Haakon's wife, Queen Mette-Marit, was absent from the formalities as she continues to recover from a lung transplant.

articles.title: MapQuest app reaches No 1 on US Apple list after defying Trump’s Lake Ontario order
articles.summary:
Navigating app surpasses Google and Apple Maps on top-downloaded US chart after posting ‘we’re not changing it’

A pioneering online mapping app that defied

blocks.text: A pioneering online mapping app that defied Donald Trump by refusing to rename Lake Ontario has become the most in-demand navigation tool in the US.

MapQuest, which was openly dismissive of the president’s 27 August executive order directing federal agencies to refer to the smallest of the Great Lakes as “Lake America” amid a trade spat with Canada, leapfrogged rivals Google Maps and Apple Maps to top the most-downloaded list, as first reported by TechCrunch.
The app held the No 1 spot on Apple’s App Store as of Tuesday morning, the Guardian confirmed.
Google quickly capitulated to Trump’s demand, showing Lake America to US customers, while Apple is reportedly mulling a decision under pressure from the White House to make the same change.
But MapQuest, a 30-year-old company that bills itself as “the OG” (original) of the internet mapping era, appears to have been rewarded for standing firm.

TechCrunch said the app’s downloads had “soared” in recent days to become the fourth most popular of all apps in the US, excluding games – and to lead the Apple app store’s navigation chart, with Google at No 2.
In Canada, meanwhile, MapQuest was the second-most downloaded app overall by Sunday night.

It comes as polls show Trump’s efforts at renaming the lake found favor with only 14% of Americans, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday. And that survey found only slightly more, 20%, approved of higher tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on Canadian goods, with 57% opposed.

MapQuest’s general manager, Doug Berger, said in a statement that usage of its app was running at about 50 times its usual rate. As a bit of fun, he said, the company was also offering subscribers the chance to generate their own name for the lake.

That was courtesy of a tool it first introduced after Trump rebranded the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” among US federal government agencies in 2025 – to which Google also acquiesced in the American market.
Berger said in a statement: “We took the same approach we did with the Gulf of Mexico: be part of the conversation, and give people an app that keeps the names they’re familiar with.
“Hundreds of thousands of people signaled to us this weekend that we got it right, by downloading our app.”
MapQuest has maintained its defiance, and some might say mockery, of Trump’s Lake Ontario order since an original “We’re not changing it” post on social media on 27 August.

The following day, in an all-capital letter post similar in style and language to those favored by the president, it wrote: “Our maps are big and beautiful. People come up to us and say we’ll get them places. And we do!”

It also responded to a poster who expressed surprise that MapQuest still existed and was not “in the same grave” as RadioShack, the once prominent US technology and electronics company that went through two bankruptcies and shuttered its retail locations a decade ago.
“Understandable but the other OG, @RadioShackUSA, is still here too,” MapQuest replied, noting its continued existence as an e-commerce operation.

On Tuesday morning, Apple Maps continued to show the body of water spanning the US-Canada border as Lake Ontario, despite the insistence on Monday of Doug Burgum, Trump’s interior secretary, that he was “confident” it would soon show Lake America after the president contacted the company directly.
On Google, its map for US users reflects the change – but remains Lake Ontario, a name it has had for about 400 years, for users in the rest of the world.

Elsewhere, protests continue to escalate. A giant “Lake Ontario – Now and Always” sign in English and French was erected over the weekend near Grimsby, Ontario. Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, told ABC News: “No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”

On Monday, three Democratic US representatives, Tim Kennedy and Joe Morelle of New York, and Debbie Dingell of Michigan, introduced legislation called the Hands Off Our Great Lakes act, seeking to block the Republican president’s federal order to rename the lake, and prevent future changes.
