articles.title: Lost island in northern B.C. lake — that appeared and disappeared — located, B.C. Hydro says

image.caption: A photo of this floating island of trees in the Williston Lake reservoir in northern B.C. was taken by a local boater and shared with resident Rocky Avery, who posted it to social media. (Submitted by Rocky Avery)

blocks.text: British Columbia
B.C. Hydro says mini forest bigger than a Canadian football field landed ashore in the Williston Reservoir after drifting some 30 kilometres northwest of its last known location.
Newly formed island found along shore of Williston Reservoir after drifting for 30 kilometres
A newly formed island in B.C.'s largest lake has been located.

B.C. Hydro said Monday that the forested land mass, bigger than a Canadian football field, landed ashore after drifting some 30 kilometres northwest of its last known location in the middle of Williston Reservoir.

The island's curious appearance, and seemingly sudden disappearance in the massive man-made lake in northern B.C., has captured international attention and intrigue since boaters first made the discovery in August.
B.C. Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer said satellite imagery dated Aug. 15 shows the island resting in the north entrance of the Ospika Arm, where the Ospika River flows into the reservoir.
He said the island appears to be intact, and that it has moved even further away from the W.A.C. Bennett Dam connected to the reservoir.
"For it to disappear and now to reappear, that just creates a lot of excitement," Gammer said.
"It's great to know that we found it and it's not causing any trouble right now and hopefully that's the way it stays."

items: An island mysteriously appeared — then disappeared — on B.C.'s largest reservoir

blocks.text: The island's origin still hasn't been confirmed though B.C. Hydro believes record high water levels likely caused it to break off somewhere along the reservoir's sprawling shoreline.
Gammer said strong winds would have moved it through the open waters over the last month.
"It's certainly not current. The water does very slowly move to the east to the [dam]," Gammer said. "The wind is really what's going to drive things."
Island in Canada mysteriously appears, then vanishes
The Williston reservoir was created in 1968 and is the seventh-largest in the world.
John Clague, an earth sciences professor at Simon Fraser University, said decades of erosion have left the banks of the reservoir vulnerable to landslides.
He said the reservoir is "notorious" for having strong winds that can create waves and currents that undermine shallow rooted trees along the shoreline.
B.C. Hydro estimates the island to be around 70 metres wide and 140 metres long, or about 9,800 square metres in area.
"This has to be a world's record in terms of size for floating wood mats with trees that were quite healthy and growing nicely and now are part of an island," said Clague.
B.C. Hydro will want to get a better understanding of where it came from and how it formed, Clague said.
"There should be a big scar along the shoreline."
Clague said he's surprised how far the island has travelled, and B.C. Hydro will want to investigate to understand where it came from and how it formed.

That's quite a distance for it to travel and not essentially fall apart," he said. "It's a big piece of real estate, but it's thin. It's not like an iceberg that extends further beneath the water in an ocean."
The island's whereabouts have been a curiosity for residents in northern B.C. as well as interested observers from around the world.
Video of the island bobbing in the middle of the reservoir first went viral in local Facebook groups in early August.
After a decade spent running fishing charters on Williston Lake, Marianne Anderson said she has never seen anything like it.
She said a local fishing guide showed her the video of what looked like a giant carpet of trees, bobbing in the middle of the lake.
The next time fishing guides were in the area, the island was gone.
"It looked unreal," she said.
LISTEN | An island mysteriously appeared — then disappeared — in northern B.C.:
Radio West3:57A floating island in northern B.C.'s Williston Reservoir

Finlay Farquhar, a radio engineering assistant based in the United Kingdom, said he was able to track the island's new location using open-source satellite websites after reading about it on social media.
He also found it nestled on the shoreline in the Ospika Arm.
"Quite curious, and it was really quite surprising that there'd been a floating island," Farquhar said. "I was quite surprised by how far it moved."
Gammer said B.C. Hydro was able to locate the island after independently confirming new reports of its location.
Gammer said it's possible the island might move again if strong winds break it free from shore.
"It's nothing that's going to require us to take some serious action," he said.
"We will monitor this just to see what happens, whether it breaks apart and if we then have a debris field instead of one big chunk, that may cause us to take some other action."
He said the island is unstable and boaters should be cautious.

"Go ahead, boat up to it, get near it, take your own pictures, get your drone out, whatever you'd like to do to image it," he said. "But we really warn people about trying to climb on it, as tempting as it may be."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Matt Preprost is a reporter with CBC British Columbia based in Fort St. John. He has covered the B.C Peace region and Northern Rockies since 2013. Email him at fsj@cbc.ca
Katie DeRosa

articles.title: Ex-president Duterte requests ICC chamber to require resubmission of charges
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte"s defense team has requested the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to direct the Prosecution to resubmit the document containing the charges (DCC)…

blocks.text: Former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team has requested the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to direct the Prosecution to resubmit the document containing the charges (DCC) for allegedly violating Duterte’s right.
In an 11-page document dated August 31, Duterte’s team argued that the DCC violates the former official’s right to be informed in detail of the nature, cause, and content of the charges against him.

Due to this, it appealed to the chamber to order the Prosecution to refile a document that frames the charges “in terms of counts with a defined scope, being crimes under the ICC Statute, and with an exhaustive list of underpinning acts.”
“The accused cannot even begin to make strategic decisions about how to approach this case, because he does not know what case he has to meet,” it said.

“The Duterte charges are a literal moving target; a non-exhaustive, illustrative list of events whose proof beyond reasonable doubt may or may not trigger liability for thousands of others, and whose evidential value remains entirely unclear,” it added.
In April, the ICC confirmed the charges against Duterte cover 49 incidents, which are divided into the following three counts:

Count 1: Murder as a crime against humanity in Davao City during the mayoral period of at least 19 victims, between 2013 and around June 2016, through indirect co-perpetration, ordering and/or inducing, and/or aiding and abetting;

Count 2: Murder as a crime against humanity of ‘high-value targets’ in locations across the Philippines during the presidential period of at least the 14 victims between around July 2016 and July 2017, through indirect co-perpetration, and/or ordering and/or inducing and/or 25(3)(c) (aiding and abetting); and

Count 3: Murder and attempted murder as crimes against humanity in barangay clearance operations in locations across the Philippines during the presidential period of at least the 45 victims (43 murders and two attempted murders) between around July 2016 and September 2018, through indirect co-perpetration, ordering and/or inducing, and/or aiding and abetting.
Duterte’s team noted that it received a notice of details of eight additional incidents submitted by the Prosecution, bringing the total list of incidents to 57.
“[C]onsistent practice has been for charging documents to be divided into topical headings, usually geographical areas with corresponding time periods, or overarching events,” it said.

“Under each topical heading, the counts are then listed together with the legal and factual basis being alleged in support of each. In this way, the accused is duly notified of the allegations in detail, as required,” it added.
According to his defense team, the framing of the DCC is “entirely different and entirely novel.”
“The topical headings have been elevated to the status of counts allegedly committed over an extended period and across a large geographical area,” it said.

The defense team said that a “count” has only ever denoted an individual crime under the ICC Statute. Meanwhile, it said the specific charged acts were relegated to the “status of non-exhaustive and illustrative-only incidents without legal characterization.”
“The Prosecution’s decision to frame the charges in this entirely novel way makes it impossible for the defendant to know what case he has to meet at trial,” it said.
The defense said that it would need to be ready to defend against any unlawful killing over a seven-year-plus period.

“Keeping in mind that the Prosecution had disclosed around 5,000 documents as at the date of the confirmation decision, which has now increased by over 400% to over 25,000 items at the date of writing, the Defence team has no chance of even reading this full volume of disclosure before the start of the trial, let alone being aware of every alleged murder or killing contained therein and being ready to defend against them,” it said.
Aside from this, the defense team said the current charges put the Trial Chamber in an impossible position.

It said that the Chamber must examine whether the act is part of the widespread or systematic attack, considered as a whole with due regard to the nature of the act at issue, its aims and consequences and knowledge of that nexus by the perpetrator of the act.

“Where there are no pleaded underlying acts, but rather only ‘non-exhaustive’ and ‘illustrative’ examples of alleged conduct by perpetrators, the Prosecution can circumvent these requirements,” it said.

“Meaning, that the trial could end with the Prosecution having done nothing more than establishing a certain number of ‘illustrative incidents’ but without any of the requisite contextual elements necessary to link the charged acts back to the charged counts,” it added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Ford government to begin ripping out, reconfiguring Toronto bike lanes following court of appeal ruling
articles.summary: The Ford government is going ahead with bike lane removal and reconfiguration on some of Toronto's busiest roads, the province announced Tuesday.

blocks.text: Toronto
The Ford government is going ahead with bike lane removal and reconfiguration on some of Toronto's busiest roads, the province announced Tuesday.
Vehicle lanes on sections of Bloor Street W. to be 'immediately' restored, province says
Ford government to begin Toronto bike lane removal. Here's what you need to know

Tuesday's news release says that the provincial government is going to begin the process of "restoring motor vehicle lanes" that were previously removed to make bike lanes on Bloor Street, Yonge Street, University Avenue, Queen's Park, Queen's Park Crescent and Avenue Road.

The release says the province has also issued a request for proposals to "study and provide design options" for restoring vehicle lanes along some "sections" of Toronto's busiest streets. These proposals would look into options for retaining or reconfiguring bike lanes, according to the release.

items: Ontario Court of Appeal says Ford can rip out Toronto bike lanes
Ontario aware bike lane removals may not reduce congestion, could make people less safe: internal documents

blocks.text: "The province is also immediately beginning to restore motor vehicle lanes on Bloor Street W., starting east of a 600-metre section at Clissold Road where vehicle lanes were restored in December 2025," the news release said.

The announcement comes after Ontario's court of appeal ruled in August that the Ford government can rip out 19 kilometres of protected bike lanes in Toronto, reversing a lower-court decision made in July 2025.
Restoring vehicle lanes stops congestion, transport minister says

When asked about bike lane removals at an unrelated news conference Tuesday, Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria was firm in saying that bike lanes in areas like Bloor Street W. is the reason for gridlock and congestion in the city.
"Getting these bike lanes out of the way, restoring vehicle lanes, will allow us to get people moving quicker and faster in one of the busiest cities in the world," he said.
Sarkaria went on to say that he had spoken to "many community members" about the bike lanes. He said their instalment has impacted local business and is causing less people to go downtown.
"We need to restore the vehicle lanes to stop the congestion," he said.

In a separate interview Tuesday with CBC News, Sarkaria said the 600-meter section the province is looking to "immediately" remove along Bloor Street W. would "require the least amount of work" to bring back car lanes.
When asked about how the province will decide to remove or reconfigure the bike lanes it identified, Sarkaria said "the vehicle lane gets the priority."
"In some circumstances where both could coexist, we'll consider that and look at that," he said.
Where will cyclists go if Toronto loses major bike lanes?
When asked about safety concerns once the bike lanes are removed, Sarkaria said the rules of the road will still apply to cyclists and drivers.

"We expect, just like the hundreds of thousands of other streets in Ontario where both the vehicles and cyclists can coexist, that that will continue to happen on the streets that we are specifying right now," he said.
Sarkaria also said secondary streets, such as King Street and College Street, would be better alternatives to the bike lanes the province looks to remove or reconfigure.

items: Ontario aware bike lane removals may not reduce congestion, could make people less safe: internal documents

blocks.text: Internal documents from the transportation ministry that were made public as part of a court challenge to Bill 212 — the legislation that gave the province sweeping control over municipal bike lanes — cast doubt on some of Sarkaria's statements.

Those documents include a report prepared by engineering and urban planning firm CIMA+, which said collisions for all road users could increase upwards of 54 per cent if bike lanes are removed, based on existing research.

A 2024 briefing note on from the cabinet office committee also said the proposed bike lane removals may not achieve "desired outcomes," saying that current data and research "does not confirm that removing bike lanes that occupy a lane of traffic would significantly alleviate congestion."
Ontario appeal court says Ford can rip out Toronto bike lanes
Bike lanes a municipal election issue

Bike lanes are already proving to be a contentious municipal election issue. Mayoral candidate Brad Bradford previously vowed to remove the Bloor Street W. bike lanes should he become mayor, despite initially being one of the councillors who voted in favour of them.

Mayor Olivia Chow, who is seeking re-election this fall, issued a statement Tuesday saying the province should be focused on dealing with Trump and helping families and workers, rather than "picking endless political fights with the City of Toronto."
"I resist any argument that pits road users against each other because it makes everyone less safe. Pedestrians, cyclists and drivers all deserve safety on our roads," Chow said.

items: Tell us what’s at stake for you in Toronto’s municipal election
Bradford vows Bloor Street W. bike lanes are 'coming out' if he's mayor

blocks.text: Mayoral candidate Chris Alexander said the province's actions are evidence of "governance failure" at city hall, and as mayor he'd table a transportation plan that "actually works."

"A competent city works with the province and designs solutions that have neighbourhood support. Toronto needs to get things right the first time, instead of getting stuck in costly court battles for years," Alexander said.
Ontario Green Party leader Mike Schreiner also weighed in on the province's announcement, calling it "performative politics" that "doesn't address the root cause of congestion."
"What we actually need is more dedicated bike and transit lanes and investment in transit that allow for more people to get around more affordably and efficiently," he said in a social media post.
With files from Lane Harrison

articles.title: As glaciers melt, can communities be protected?
articles.summary: Rising temperatures are increasing the risk of floods and avalanches in mountain regions. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet shows the urgent need for solutions, and the tools that could help save lives.

image.caption: Thousands are still missing following last month's devastating floods in Nepal and TibetImage: Sunil Sharma/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: High mountain glaciers formed in the ice age are retreating and becoming unstable as the burning of fossil fuels heats the climate and leads to a decline in snowfall.
The instability creates the conditions for large glacial sections to collapse, triggering ice and rock avalanches that can dam river valleys before tidal waves of water are released.

Following the glacier collapse that triggered what is know as a mountain tsunami in Nepal and Tibet on August 26, thousands are still missing and feared dead. Unlike the 2025 glacier avalanche that destroyed the town of Batten in Switzerland — where nearly all inhabitants were evacuated — a lack of early warning systems in the Himalayas left locals and tourists at the mercy of flash floods.
How much is climate change to blame?
The causes of glacier collapse are part of a complex web of interrelated changes to high mountain landscapes due in part to rising global temperatures, say scientists.

Levan Tielidze, research fellow in Glacial Geomorphology at Australia's Monash University, says the Himalayas are not, as is often imagined, a "frozen and relatively stable environment," but "dynamic systems in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, rock slopes, rivers and monsoon processes interact."

"As the climate warms, these components are changing simultaneously, meaning hazards can cascade from one process into another," he told DW. When rock, ice and water interact in more unpredictable ways on the world's highest peaks, the resulting debris flows "can transform into a catastrophic flood far downstream," Tielidze added.

Almost 25 years ago, in what was then the biggest glacial collapse in history, one glacier crashed onto another in the Caucases Mountains of North Ossetia in the Russian Federation. The event caused avalanches of ice and debris that slid more than 24km (15 miles) and killed around 125 people.
"The Kolka Glacier disaster was one of the early warnings of the increasing occurrence and potential severity of such glacier-related hazards," Tielidze told DW.
Meanwhile the UN says glaciers in Nepalese mountains have declined by one-third in 30 years, which has added to their instability.

Some research suggests that even if emissions from burning fossil fuels were low enough to prevent the planet from heating by more than 2 degrees Celsius (36 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to pre-industrial times, the wider Hindu Kush Himalayan region could lose up to half its glacier cover — compared to 2020 levels — by the end of the century.

For Dipesh Chapagain, senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, there is "ample scientific evidence linking greenhouse gas emissions to global climate change, which in turn is driving glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and ice avalanches."
"These changes are increasing both the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters in mountain regions," he added.

Chapagain has studied hundreds of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region — caused when meltwater from glaciers and snow creates a lake that eventually bursts and sends extreme flash floods downstream. The number of these events per decade has increased fivefold since the 1950s.
Pakistani villagers face climate change, melting glaciers

The glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet shares similarities to a GLOF event; however the former was very different as it skipped the "intermediate lake-formation stage entirely … and directly triggered the flash flood," said Chapagain.

The avalanche also generated seismic activity equivalent to about magnitude 5.2 before the momentum of the water-rich debris flow that entered the river system saw it travel roughly 100 kilometres, noted Tielidze.
"These hazards are becoming so difficult to classify," he added, in reference to the way mountain rock, ice and water are interacting in more unpredictable ways due to climate change.

blocks.caption: Riverside communities in Nepal were destroyed by the unprecedented flash flood and mudslide  Image: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP

blocks.text: Is it possible to adapt to more extreme glacier collapse impacts?

The 2025 glacial collapse in the Swiss Alps that destroyed the entire village of Blattan resulted in one fatality. Detailed surveillance of glacier deformation and the surrounding terrain allowed authorities to evacuate the population before the catastrophic collapse.
But this is less possible in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, which contains more than 63,700 glaciers, notes Tielidze.
"In the Himalayas, we need to move beyond monitoring only individual dangerous lakes," he said.
"We need integrated systems combining satellite observations, seismic detection, glacier and slope monitoring, river gauges, weather forecasts and automated warnings."
For rapidly evolving events such as the Nepal disaster, detecting seismic movement could give downstream communities "precious minutes of warning," he added.

blocks.caption: The destroyed village in Blatten, Switzerland, was in the path of an avalanche of rock, ice, and debris triggered by the collapse of the Birch GlacierImage: Laurent Gillieron/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chapagain says the transboundary nature of glacial hazards in the Himalayas makes "cross-border and regional cooperation on disaster preparedness" just as urgent as early-warning systems.
However, currently available adaptation technology and capacity may be insufficient to "respond to a disaster on the scale we've just witnessed on the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal," he added.

"What we have learned from this is we can adapt to climate change but not to climate apocalypse," said Shreya K.C., the Kathmandu-based advocacy working group co-coordinator of the Loss and Damage Youth Coalition, in a statement.
A rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions that are at driving glacial melt and instability will need to accompany any adaptation measures.

"We cannot engineer our way out of unlimited warming," said Tielidze. "Some mountain hazards will remain unpredictable and some changes will eventually exceed the capacity of communities and infrastructure to adapt."

articles.title: Months before ICC trial, Duterte wants prosecution to refile cases vs him
articles.summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte wants the prosecution to refile a document that 'frames the charges in terms of counts with a defined scope, being crimes under the ICC Statute'

blocks.text: Former president Rodrigo Duterte wants the prosecution to refile a document that 'frames the charges in terms of counts with a defined scope, being crimes under the ICC Statute'

MANILA, Philippines – Just a few months before his scheduled historic trial, former president Rodrigo Duterte asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to order the prosecution to refile the cases against him.

“The [defense] accordingly requests the Trial Chamber to order the prosecution to re-file a document before the Pre-Trial Chamber that frames the charges in terms of counts with a defined scope, being crimes under the ICC Statute, and with an exhaustive list of underpinning acts, which represent the entirety of the charges against the accused,” said the Duterte camp’s motion dated August 31.
In the motion, Duterte’s lead counsel Peter Haynes argued that the prosecution’s document containing the charges or DCC “is not fit for [its] purpose” and should be struck out.
This is the Duterte camp’s latest bid to challenge his case before the ICC after recent legal defeats.
Just last April, the ICC pre-trial chamber confirmed all three counts of Duterte’s crimes against humanity case, thus sending him to trial that will start in November.

Even on the issue of jurisdiction or whether the ICC was the right platform for the cases, Duterte did not score a win. The ICC Appeals Chamber junked his jurisdiction challenge and cleared the way for the trial.
The latest defeat was in May, when the pre-trial chamber denied Duterte’s request to appeal the ruling that confirmed his ICC cases.

blocks.caption: ICC denies Rodrigo Duterte’s latest attempt to delay trial

blocks.text: In their August 31 motion, the Duterte camp said the prosecution’s DCC was framed around “illustrative non-exhaustive incidents.” They argued that the way the charges were framed violated Duterte’s right to be informed in detail of the nature, cause, and content of the charges against him under 67(1)(a) of the Rome Statute.
They said the only effective remedy to this is for the prosecution to refile the charges that properly inform Duterte about his case.
According to the defense, the prosecution’s decision to frame the charges that way makes it impossible for Duterte to know what case he has to meet at the upcoming trial.

“The Prosecution’s desire and intention to add further incidents is noteworthy as it plainly indicates that the Prosecution, at least, does not believe that it needs to prove all or most of the incidents. However, with a trial due to start in three months, the [defense] has no idea what is regarded as necessary proof of a ‘count’ on this DCC,” said the motion.
Duterte’s camp further argued that the prosecution’s charge document — which has broad topical headings rather than charged crimes — would allegedly be unacceptable in any criminal jurisdiction.

“The accused cannot even begin to make strategic decisions about how to approach this case, because he does not know what case he has to meet. The Duterte charges are a literal moving target; a non-exhaustive, illustrative list of events whose proof beyond reasonable doubt may or may not trigger liability for thousands of others, and whose evidential value remains entirely unclear,” the camp added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Woman killed in Times Square stabbing, suspect shot dead by police
articles.summary: Police say the double stabbing, which injured another person, was random and the suspect had a mental health history with police.

blocks.text: A 32-year-old woman was killed and another victim is in hospital following a stabbing in Times Square, New York City late on Wednesday afternoon.

The suspect, a woman wielding two knifes, was shot by police. All three people were taken to hospital, where the female victim and the suspect were later pronounced dead, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani told a news conference.
Mamdani said the second victim is in a "stable condition". He also thanked NYPD officers for preventing a "horrific attack from becoming even worse".
New York Police Department (NYPD) Commissioner Jessica Tisch called the attack "an unprovoked double stabbing" that took place within approximately 20 seconds of each other.

Citing preliminary information, Tisch said the NYPD call centre received several 911 calls at approximately 16:24 local time (21:00 BST) reporting a woman armed with two knives was stabbing people along Seventh Avenue in Times Square.
Police believe the incident began near West 41st Street and Seventh Ave.
The suspect approached a man who had just exited the subway and was standing with his wife waiting to cross the street, Tisch told a news conference.
"A witness at the scene told investigators that he observed the subject remove two knives from a red Target bag before approaching the first victim.
"The subject waved the knives before stabbing a 68-year-old man in the right side of his abdomen, in what appears to be a random and unprovoked attack."
The 68-year-old was taken to Bellevue Hospital and is now stable.
The suspect continued up Seventh Avenue towards 42nd Street, which is where she stabbed the second victim, who did not survive after being taken to hospital.
The suspect continued on Seventh Avenue, which is when police tried to get her to drop her weapons, speaking to her for four minutes, the NYPD commissioner said.
"During the encounter she told the officers 'I'm not dropping anything, I'd rather kill both of you'. She repeated 'I will kill you'", Tisch said.
The suspect waved knives towards the officers, who then used Tasers, which were "ineffective" and did not stop her from heading towards them.
NYPD officers then shot the woman, who was later also pronounced dead at Bellevue Hospital.

The suspect was later identified as 49-year-old Pamela Cisneros of Queens, New York City. She had never been arrested but had a "documented mental health history with the NYPD, with one incident in 2018 and one in 2019", Tisch added.
A tourist from Boston, Melinda Puzon, told the BBC's US reporting partner CBS News that she heard the shots and saw "so many people on the street".
"It's very shocking."

articles.title: Sexual assaults happening almost every day in Ceuta, prosecutors say
articles.summary: Most migrants have returned to neighbouring Morocco, but as many as 5,000 remain in the Spanish exclave.

blocks.text: Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave at the end of July.
That number meant there was almost one case every day, Ceuta's chief prosecutor Silvia Rojas said.
She told El País newspaper migrant girls were "particularly vulnerable because of their irregular status in the territory".

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
There have been scenes of violence in recent days as tensions flare up between migrants and local residents.
Sánchez called the second meeting of his national security in a week on Tuesday to tackle the issue.
Between 1,400 and 1,600 of the estimated 5,000 migrants still in Ceuta are children, according to Rojas.
Among the suspected attackers are four Moroccans, three Spaniards and a Belgian, Efe news agency reports.
Rojas said many victims did not file a report, either out of fear of because of their "current situation in Ceuta".
The Spanish Society of Epidemiology has warned that violence against women "cannot be considered an isolated event".
Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said a multi-million euro aid package had been approved by the cabinet that would help provide essential services and cover care for unaccompanied children.

The territory's conservative mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas, has called on Spaniards to take part in demonstrations across mainland Spain in support of Ceuta on Wednesday, which coincides with the city's annual holiday.
The Spanish government is facing bitter criticism from its opponents for its handling of the crisis. The hard-right Vox party said Sánchez had not "lost control of Ceuta - he has handed it over".
Arantxa Campos, president of the Ceuta Employers' Confederation, told the BBC: "We can't do anything unless these people leave.
"We don't have a plan from the government. We don't have anything. We don't even know when they're going to finish screening everyone."

Unlike his political opponents, Sánchez has been careful to avoid blaming Morocco for stoking the surge of migrants. He said on Monday that no intelligence reports pointed to "any involvement in one way or another" from the Moroccan authorities.

Instead he focused on disinformation on social media "associated with both Russia and Israel and an international far-right movement that always uses migration, not only to attack Spain but also Europe", although he appeared to indicate they had stoked the crisis after 31 July.
He told Cadena Ser it did not mean "it must come from a state actor".

Russia and Israel have both denied any involvement. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused the Spanish prime minister of "a blatant lie" and Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman demanded proof to support Sánchez's allegations.

A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.

Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.

The opposition People's Party (PP) has criticised Sánchez for "exonerating" Morocco and pointing the finger in other directions. Borja Sémper, a spokesperson for the party, said tens of thousands of people could not have moved towards the Ceuta border without Morocco's knowledge.
Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.

articles.title: Will impeachment trial prosecutors resign? Not anymore, says Chua
articles.summary: The House prosecution team's core of 11 solon-prosecutors will remain intact in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial. Thus, said prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, with the…

blocks.text: The House prosecution team's core of 11 solon-prosecutors will remain intact in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial.
Thus, said prosecutor Manila 3rd district Rep. Joel Chua, with the revelation shelving a proposal for some of them to resign from the panel so they could speak publicly about the merits of the case.
“We have decided, wala na lang munang mag-resign,” Chua said Tuesday, Sept. 1 following day 20 of the high-stakes proceedings.
The panel considered a reshuffle after the Senate impeachment court reiterated the sub judice rule, or the limits on public comments about matters being tried.

One option was for selected House prosecutors to leave the panel and serve only as spokespersons. “Noong una, isa iyon sa mga naging discussion kung ganoon ang mangyayari. Kasi iyon ang talagang unang option,” Chua said.
(At first, that was one of the discussions, if that was what would happen. Because that was really the first option.)
The idea drew support from lawyers working with the team. “May mga suggestion ang ibang private prosecutor at public prosecutor na may ilan mag-resign para maging spokesperson."
(Some private prosecutors and public prosecutors suggested that some members resign so they could serve as spokespersons.)
But Chua said the prosecution members ultimately chose continuity. He noted that changing the structure of the team at this stage would require finding replacements.
“After considering everything, total isang buwan na lang kung masusunod iyong ating target...Too late na kung magbabawas tayo at magdadagdag pa,” Chua said.
(After considering everything, there’s only about a month left if we follow our target...It’s too late if we start removing and adding members.)
As such, the team will keep public briefings focused on schedules, witness sequencing, and other procedural updates.
More importantly, Chua said the prosectors "will just try to explain things in a way that does not touch on the merits [of the case]".

That was also why Chua, a public prosecutor, appeared at Tuesday’s briefing. He said reporters could still ask about what comes next without forcing prosecutors into a public discussion of the evidence.
“Baka may magtanong tungkol sa procedural aspect outside the merits of the case, so I can answer that,” said the veteran lawmaker from Manila.
(Someone might ask about the procedural aspects outside the merits of the case, so I can answer that.)
The approach allows the public to receive practical updates while the same prosecutors continue their work inside the impeachment court, Chua said.
It also preserves the team’s current assignments as the prosecution tries to finish article I on confidential funds and move to the remaining articles of impeachment against Duterte.
Fifteen private prosecutors are helping the solon-prosecutors gain a conviction from the respondent, free of charge.

articles.title: Mladic's death, Bosnia and Serbia's unfinished reckoning
articles.summary: The death of Ratko Mladic did not close a dark chapter of European history; it reopened old wounds. The ideology that created him lives on. The Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war, not the divisions…

image.caption: Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic (pictured here in 1994) was convicted of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre and other war crimes by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in 2017Image: Pascal Guyot/AFP

blocks.text: The death of Ratko Mladic should have closed one of the darkest chapters in European history.

Instead, it has reopened old wounds, proving that both the Dayton Peace Agreement that ended the 1992-95 Bosnian War and the three decades of international engagement that followed never came close to addressing the causes that led to the conflict.

When Mladic, the former commander of the Bosnian Serb army, died on August 27, 2026 in a prison hospital in The Hague, his conviction for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes — including the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and the siege of Sarajevo — had been final for nearly a decade.
Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead

What was never settled, however — and what, it seems, was never even seriously attempted — is the question of how a society lives with a man who remains a convicted criminal in the eyes of an international court but is viewed by some as a hero and symbol of the Serbian people.
For this reason, the reactions that followed Mladic's death came as no surprise.
Mladic openly mourned in Republika Srpska

In Serbia and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska, one of the two semi-autonomous entities created within Bosnia and Herzegovina by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, Ratko Mladic's death was mourned as the loss of a national hero, not the end of an era of crimes — a narrative that stands in direct contradiction to the facts established by international courts.

Senior officials in Republika Srpska, which covers around 49% of the territory of the former Yugoslav republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, called on citizens to gather in squares and light candles "for the salvation of the general's soul."

blocks.caption: Senior officials in Republika Srpska called on people to gather in squares and light candles 'for the salvation of the general's soul'Image: Radivoje Pavicic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Milorad Dodik, still the most powerful political figure in Republika Srpska despite stepping down as its president last year after a six-year ban on holding public office imposed by Bosnia's constitutional court, called his death a "murder," suggesting it was "an organized approach that was meant to lead to a fatal outcome."

That Mladic is not perceived as a man convicted of genocide but as a symbol of "a time and a struggle" was confirmed by Drasko Stanivukovic, mayor of Banja Luka, the de facto capital of Republika Srpska.
Institutional support in Belgrade
In the Serbian capital, Belgrade, this stance received institutional backing.
Serbia's justice minister announced a funeral with the highest state and military honors.
President Aleksandar Vucic accused the Hague tribunal of "uncivilized behavior" for not allowing Mladic to spend his final days outside his prison cell.

Moreover, former interior minister Aleksandar Vulin spoke of Mladic in the same breath as other Serbian national heroes, invoking a narrative that links the First World War to the 1990s, saying, "From Gavrilo Princip to Ratko Mladic, the best Serbs are killed tied up."
A very different response elsewhere in Bosnia

In the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the other main entity in Bosnia, where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, news of Mladic's death was met with unanimous condemnation of the deceased, given that Mladic was finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, a town in eastern Bosnia where around 8,000 men and boys were killed in July 1995.

Bosnia's foreign minister, Elmedin Konakovic, framed the official Serbian response as Serbia's conscious choice: "No one is forcing Serbia to treat Mladic as a hero, nor to attribute his crimes to it. Serbia is choosing this itself," he said.
Representatives of victims and survivors pointed out that any public glorification is a direct insult to the families of those killed.

The European Commission, responding to questions about the announced state funeral, said that "glorifying convicted war criminals is contrary to the most basic European values" and that such practices have no place in either member states or candidate countries.

blocks.caption: 'No one is forcing Serbia to treat Mladic as a hero [...]. Serbia is choosing this itself,' said Bosnia's foreign minister, Elmedin KonakovicImage: Denis Zuberi/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: The European Movement in Serbia warned that a state funeral would amount to "institutional glorification" and a "serious moral, legal and political attack on Serbia" and urged the Serbian government to abandon the plan.
How can this happen?
But how is it possible that a man who has been finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica is still honored as a military commander?
The answer is not simply that he is viewed by some as a national hero. It is structural, and it begins with the Dayton Peace Agreement itself.
The 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina by turning existing front lines and territorial control into the constitutional architecture of a new state.
One of the fundamental elements of the agreement was Republika Srpska, which is recognized by all signatories and embedded in the constitutional structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

That division was not an administrative technicality, it reflected the political reality on the ground at the time negotiations were held, including territories under the control of forces commanded by Ratko Mladic.
The compromise was necessary to stop the bloodshed. The problem is that since 1995, it has never been accompanied by a mechanism for dealing with the past that would match the political compromise.

Dayton created a complex constitutional architecture — a state divided into two entities and the Brcko District with a total 14 governments and parliaments at state, entity and cantonal level — for a country of just 3 million people.

It is a system built to prevent war, not a system built to produce common citizenship, and was described by the Council of Europe's Venice Commission as long ago as 2005 as "neither rational nor efficient."
In such a system, where ethnic identity is built into the very logic of power, denial or relativization of crimes is not a marginal phenomenon, it is a political resource.
In other words, each side sees itself as a victim, which makes joint recognition of committed evil as a precondition for reconciliation impossible.
The price of missed responsibility
Bosnia and Herzegovina has state-level legislation that criminalizes the public denial, gross minimization or justification of genocide and the glorification of persons convicted of such acts.
The Dayton Peace Agreement 30 years on
In reality, however, enforcement of this legislation remains uneven.
Serbia has no such law, and its public authorities, instead of distancing themselves from Mladic's legacy, openly embrace it.
This is not just a symbolic difference, it is the difference between treating the wartime legacy as something shameful to be overcome or as a resource to be politically exploited.
The role of the international community
The international community, which stopped the war in 1995 through force and diplomacy, subsequently retreated into the role of administrator of the status quo.

The Office of the High Representative, the international envoy empowered to impose laws and remove obstructive politicians under the Dayton Agreement, did indeed impose laws and remove obstructive politicians for decades, but in doing so only stabilized the system without dismantling its causes.
The result is twofold: a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 30 years since the end of the war and the fact that an ideology that gave rise to that war is still very much alive.

articles.title: Philippines prepares for unprecedented 5-million tons rice imports
articles.summary: The Philippines will import a record-high five million metric tons (MT) this year, as it turns to foreign supplies to offset a projected shortfall in domestic production caused by El Niño, according…

blocks.text: The Philippines will import a record-high five million metric tons (MT) this year, as it turns to foreign supplies to offset a projected shortfall in domestic production caused by El Niño, according to the Department of Agriculture (DA).

“As we are facing El Niño, we are projecting that we might need to import up to five million MT for this year,” said Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel during his agency’s budget hearing on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The projected import volume this year is nearly four percent higher than the current record of 4.81 million MT set in 2024.
Total rice imports as of Aug. 13 reached 3.46 million MT, already higher than the 3.39 million MT recorded last year, according to the Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI).
Tiu Laurel said the additional rice supply will serve as a buffer as the country’s rice production losses are estimated to reach 900,000 MT within the year.
He said the decline represents the “worst-case scenario” of a strong El Niño in the fourth quarter of the year, which is projected to damage several hectares of rice farms.
“What we are all doing this year is precautionary. It is better to be prepared and have enough supply rather than risk having a shortage,” said Tiu Laurel.
Tiu Laurel noted that increased rice imports for the year will also serve as a supply cushion for the first quarter of next year in order to get ahead of a potentially weaker harvest season.
Considering this, the import volume for 2027 may go down to the normal range of between 3.8 million MT and four million MT.
While the country relies on foreign supplies to meet domestic demand, Tiu Laurel said the main objective of the government continues to be increasing local output.
He told lawmakers that the DA is focused on rolling out mechanization measures, expanding irrigation, and developing new rice seeds to further boost productivity.
The agency is also preparing to implement a program requiring traders to first invest in rice mills and processing facilities before they allowed to purchase rice from abroad.
It is estimated that around 80 percent of rice importers in the country are engaged solely in importing and have yet to commit investments in the local rice sector.
“That is one of the plans to make the industry self-sustaining and competitive in the international market,” said Tiu Laurel.
Based on BPI data, Vietnam has maintained its position as the country’s top rice supplier with imports reaching 2.56 million MT, or 74 percent of the total volume, as of Aug. 13.
Other top sources of rice include Thailand with 378,404 MT, Myanmar with 286,052 MT, Pakistan with 107,485 MT, and Cambodia with 87,802 MT.
The DA’s proposed budget for next year is ₱198.45 billion, down eight percent from the allocation of ₱215.69 billion for this year.

Under this budget, the agency wants to prioritize programs that raise farm and fishery productivity, improve infrastructure, reduce post-harvest losses, strengthen logistics and market access, and expand the use of technology.

articles.title: Thailand shortens visa-free stays for dozens of nations from Sept. 15
articles.summary: BANGKOK, Thailand — Thailand will halve the length of visa-free stays for tourists from more than 60 countries and territories to 30 days, effective September 15, the foreign ministry said Tuesday.…

blocks.text: BANGKOK, Thailand — Thailand will halve the length of visa-free stays for tourists from more than 60 countries and territories to 30 days, effective September 15, the foreign ministry said Tuesday.
Tourism is vital to the Southeast Asian nation’s economy, but officials say the move is part of an effort to curb crime involving foreign nationals.
A string of recent arrests has included foreigners accused of drug offences, sex trafficking and operating businesses such as hotels and schools without proper permits.

Under Thailand’s current tourism scheme, travellers from more than 90 countries — including Europe’s 29-nation Schengen area, China, India, the United States and several South American countries — are eligible to visit for up to 60 days without a visa.

The reduction to 30 days visa-free applies to over 60 countries and territories, including China, the United States and 27 EU countries, the Thai foreign ministry’s consular affairs department said on Tuesday.
The visa-free status for around 20 other countries was unclear, with a foreign ministry official declining to comment on Tuesday.
Visitors from Peru, Brazil and South Korea will be granted 90-day visa-free stays, up from 60 previously.
Tourists will be able to extend their stays once, at the discretion of an immigration officer, a government spokeswoman told AFP in May when the cabinet approved the measure.
Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said that month that the plan to trim visa-free visits was part of a crackdown on individuals abusing the visa system by committing crimes in the country.
Thailand has attracted 20.9 million foreign tourists since the beginning of the year, down three percent on the same period in 2025, according to the latest official figures.

articles.title: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review
articles.summary: The UK says Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

blocks.text: Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spending.
The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands.

It comes after The Daily Telegraph reported, external US defence officials were drawing up proposals to incentivise Nato allies to meet their spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among the possible options.
The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".
A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."
The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina.
The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.
The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine soldiers.
Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the Falkland Islands.
The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."
In April, an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters suggested the US was considering options to punish Nato allies it believed had failed to support its war in Iran.
The options reportedly included the prospect of the US reviewing its position on Britain's claim to the Falklands.

articles.title: Will Bangladesh join the Mecca defense alliance?
articles.summary: While Bangladesh is weighing the risks of signing the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, experts warn that such a move could complicate relations with neighboring India.

image.caption: The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan​, stipulates that an ​armed attack against any of the three would be regarded ​as an attack on allImage: Yasin Akgul/AFP

blocks.text: There has been widespread speculation about Bangladesh becoming part of a mutual defense deal struck last month by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. But the South Asian country says it has yet to receive an invitation.

The "Mecca Joint Defense Agreement," ​signed into force in early August, ​is intended to strengthen collective ​deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an ​armed attack against any of the three would be regarded ​as an attack on all.
Some analysts believe the pact has already changed the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East and South Asia.

"Although it is a collective defense understanding, from a strategic perspective it is primarily an initiative to maintain the regional balance of power and advance the respective interests of the participating states," ​Navine Murshid, professor in the Department of Political Science and Sociology at North South University in Dhaka, told DW.
South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere
Mecca pact and Bangladesh-India factor
Any move by Bangladesh to join, however, could complicate its foreign relations, particularly with neighboring India.
The two countries share a 4,096-kilometer-long (2,545 miles) land border, and have strong cultural and economic ties.
India, a fierce rival of Pakistan, sheltered many Bangladeshi refugees and provided military support to Bangladesh during its independence war against Islamabad in 1971.

However, ties between New Delhi and Dhaka have become increasingly contentious since a deadly student-led uprising in 2024 toppled then Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was considered a close ally of the Indian government.
Now living in exile in India, Hasina has since been convicted in absentia for crimes against humanity during the uprising. She denies the charges.
Bangladesh's current government, headed by the center-right Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), is in favor of the Mecca agreement.
"We view this pact positively," Bangladeshi Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman said in response to a question in parliament last week.
But he insisted that the question of Bangladesh joining the pact, or even considering membership, had not yet arisen, as that would depend on the intentions of its current members.
"If they express an intention to include Bangladesh in the pact, we will certainly consider it positively," he said.
In response to a question about such remarks by Bangladeshi officials remarks, India said the pact had implications for its national security and that it was closely monitoring the situation.

"We continue to follow all developments that have a bearing on India's security and take all necessary steps to safeguard it," Randhir Jaiswal, spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs, told reporters in New Delhi last week.
Can Pakistan still help end the US-Iran war?
Competing geopolitical interests
Analysts say Dhaka needs to consider its interests carefully before making any move to join the joint defense pact.

"The scope for direct conventional interstate war or military conflict in South Asia is limited. Therefore, the primary role of such an agreement is not confined to conducting border wars," Murshid said.
"In international relations, its significance lies mainly in strengthening bargaining power and maintaining one's position against the influence of other regional countries," the expert added.
Murshid underscored that Pakistan's interest in bringing Bangladesh closer through this agreement "is driven by geographical and political considerations."

"For India, the security of the Siliguri Corridor and its eastern frontier are important considerations. If Pakistan's defense-related influence in Bangladesh were to increase, New Delhi could view this as a development capable of affecting the regional balance of relationships."
Murshid believes that in such circumstances, Bangladesh needs to clearly define what it would and would not do by joining this alliance.

"In particular, a clear position would be necessary regarding Bangladesh's role if a military conflict were to arise between India and Pakistan. Taking Pakistan's side during such a conflict could create political and diplomatic pressures for Dhaka that may exceed Bangladesh's capacity to manage," she stressed.
Dhaka-based former diplomat M Humayun Kabir sees no reason for Bangladesh to join the pact. He thinks the country should maintain its position of not joining any such pact.
"Bangladesh has not joined any military alliance over the past 50 to 55 years. As far as I am concerned, I believe that position remains unchanged to this day," he told DW.

"They are talking about a regional security arrangement, but the region in question concerns Pakistan and the Middle East. We are not part of that region or geographical area. Bangladesh is located in the eastern part of South Asia. Therefore, there is no direct geographical rationale for Bangladesh to participate in such a military alliance," Kabir added.
Pakistan bets on fighter jet exports to boost its economy
Will Bangladesh benefit from joining the pact?
Murshid stressed that Bangladesh needs sustainable development of its own defense infrastructure and security systems.
She believes becoming part of an international security agreement could help modernize Dhaka's defense capabilities and facilitate access to military technology.

"The text of the agreement does not directly mention trade, labor markets, or economic relations. However, it is natural for economic elements to become linked with a security framework, a phenomenon known in international relations as issue linkage," she told DW.
However, Kabir, the former diplomat, fears joining the pact could limit his country's geopolitical options. He instead suggests pursuing a balancing approach.

"We contribute to peacekeeping missions around the world under the auspices of the United Nations, and that is important to us. Our economy is interconnected with many different countries in various ways, which is also important. Our workforce is present in countries across the world, and that, too, is an important consideration," he told DW.
"Therefore, before making any decision on this issue, we must take into account the many different dimensions and forms of our national interests."

blocks.text: Creamline routed Ho Chih Minh City, 25-18, 25-16, 25-6, to remain unscathed, while EST Cola swept Farm Fresh, 25-21, 25-16, 25-22, to barge into the win column in the PVL Invitational at the Smart Araneta Coliseumon Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The Cool Smashers exposed the Vietnamese’s lethargic plays, needing 61 minutes to dominate the guest team for their second straight win in as many outings.
Tots Carlos, Jema Galanza and Jaja Santiago-Minowa paced Creamline with 12 points apiece, including combined 21 kills from Carlos and Galanza, and three blocks from Santiago-Minowa.
So dominant were the Cool Smashers that they overpowered the Vietnamese spikers on attacks, 49-19; blocks, 11-4; and aces, 5-3.
None from Ho Chi Minh City scored in twin figures with skipper Dang Thi Kim Thanh and Le Thi My Xuyen pacing only eight and six points, respectively, as they absorbed their second straight loss.
Earlier, EST Cola made its title bid to improve its record to 1-1 behind the efforts of Papatchaya Phontham.
Phontham blasted 17 points built on 13 kills, three aces and one block to shackle Farm Fresh, which struggled despite the 15-point effort of Trisha Tubu.

articles.title: Yamsuan bent on helping CHEd once travel tax windfall stops
articles.summary: A solon who holds a key position in the House 2027 national budget process has vowed to help find alternative funding for the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd) should the measure abolishing the…

blocks.text: A solon who holds a key position in the House 2027 national budget process has vowed to help find alternative funding for the Commission on Higher Education (CHEd) should the measure abolishing the travel tax becomes a law this year.

Parañaque City 2nd district Rep. Brian Raymund Yamsuan has noted that CHEd, which regulates higher education and administers the government’s financial aid programs for tertiary-level students, gets part of its funding from 40 percent of the total gross collections from the travel tax.

Yamsuan, a member of the House Budget Amendments and Review Subcommittee (BARSc) pointed out that under Malacañang’s National Expenditure Program for Fiscal Year 2027, a portion of the allocation for the CHEd’s Higher Education Development Fund (HEDF) would still be sourced from the travel tax collections of the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA).

“Kami po ay magtatrabaho sa Kongreso para hanapan kayo ng alternative sources of funding once mangyari po ang pagsasabatas ng abolition ng travel tax,” Yamsuan told CHEd Chairperson Shirley Agrupis during the House Committee on Appropriations’ recent budget deliberations on the agency’s proposed 2027 budget.
(We will work in Congress to look for alternative sources of funding once the travel tax measure is enacted into law.)

Formed during last year's budget cycle as a pro-transparency measure, the BARSc effectively replaced the so-called "small committee", which incorporates individual ammendments to the General Appropriations Bill (GAB) or proposed national budget.

If the bill abolishing the travel tax is passed into law, Agrupis told the House Committee on Tourism last March that without a substitute funding source, the CHEd would lose 85.6 percent of the funding for the HEDF.
She calls this prospect “a structural loss that directly affects scholarships, research and institutional upgrading, and tourism education programs".

The House of Representatives approved on March 16 the measure seeking to abolish the travel tax. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian earlier said the Senate version of the measure is included in the chamber’s priority list of bills and will be passed this year.

“Kami bilang member ng BARSc, sisiguraduhin ko po na sa susunod na pagpupulong with (Committee on Appropriations) Chair Mika (Suansing) ay gagawa po kami ng paraan upang maibalik ang pondo para hindi maantala ang magagandang programa ng CHEd,” Yamsuan added.

(As member of the BARSc, I would make sure that in the next meeting with Committee on Appropriations Chairperson Mikaela Angela Suansing, we would find ways to restore CHEd’s funding so as not to delay the implementation of CHEd’s good programs)

During the hearing, the Parañaque solon also thanked the CHEd for its efficient implementation of the government’s higher education initiatives and financial assistance to tertiary-level students, particularly the Tulong Dunong Program (TDP).
The TDP provides a financial grant of up to P7,500 per semester or a total of P15,000 per school year to help cover the tuition and other daily expenses of qualified college students.
Yamsuan urged the CHEd to conduct more consultations with Local Universities and Colleges (LUC) to help them institute reforms that would allow them to take part in the TDP.
Out of 170 LUCs, only 116 are CHEd-recognized institutions qualified to accept TDP grants from its enrollees.

articles.title: ICC prosecution submits witness list, evidence vs Duterte
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution has submitted the list of witnesses and evidence in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution has submitted the list of witnesses and evidence in the crimes against humanity case of former President Rodrigo Duterte, the Office of the Prosecutor revealed on Tuesday.
In a three-page document, confidential files containing the prosecutors’ list of witnesses and evidence were submitted to Trial Chamber III, pursuant to the chamber’s order.
Under Regulation 23bis(1) of the Regulations of the Court, the files were filed confidentially because “both include sensitive witness information” relating to the witnesses.

Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity over the war on illegal drugs during his presidency, which killed at least 6,000 people based on government records, and more than 30,000, according to a human rights group’s records.
His trial will begin in November.
The prosecution previously disclosed that at least 6,909 pieces of evidence from Jan. 7 to July 31 were turned over to the defense. /mcm

articles.title: Norway's new King Haakon VIII takes oath in parliament
articles.summary: The new king swore to uphold the constitution in parliament in Oslo, the first major institutional step of his reign. Haakon VIII's wife Queen Mette-Marit had to skip the event in the aftermath of…

image.caption: King Haakon VIII swore to parliament to uphold the country's laws and constitution during his reignImage: Claudia Greco/REUTERS

blocks.text: New King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance to Norway's consititution in the parliament in Oslo on Tuesday, following him succeeding his father Harald V, who died last week.
This follows a day after Harald's coffin was taken to the chapel of the royal palace, where it will remain for the public to pay their last respects until a funeral on September 9.

blocks.caption: Nowrway's Storting parliament was packed for the cermonyImage: Claudia Greco/REUTERS

blocks.text: What happened in the parliamentary ceremony?
Haakon was driven the short distance from the royal palace to the Storting, or parliament in Oslo.
House speaker Masud Gharahkhani read the official announcement of Harald's death and Haakon's succession before the new constitutional monarch took the oath.
"I promise and swear that I will govern the Kingdom of Norway in according with its constitution and laws, so help me god, the almighty and omniscient," the 53-year-old said.

blocks.caption: Haakon's father Harald V died aged 89 last week, after a fairly protracted period of ailing healthImage: Claudia Greco/REUTERS

blocks.text: Queen Mette-Marit skips event amid complications following lung transplant
Ahead of he ceremony, the palace said that Haakon's wife Queen Mette-Marit would not be attending.
She had made her first public appearance since assuming the title on Monday in the coffin procession but is recovering after a lung transplant in June.

In a statement, the palace quoted Are Holm, a pumonologist at Oslo's University Hospital, as saying that complications following a transplant are not uncommon and that Mette-Marit had experienced them on several occasions, including Tuesday.
"As a result, the Queen must remain under observation throughout the day. Unfortunately, the Queen will therefore be unable to attend the swearing-in ceremony at the Storting today," he said.

blocks.caption: People flocked to the royal palace to lay flowers and other signs of respect over the weekendImage: Hanna Johre/NTB/picture alliance

blocks.text: What's the role of Norway's largely symbolic monarchy?
Norway's royal family can trace its roots bak to the ninth century.
When the country regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters supported the idea of reinstating a largely symbolic constitutional monarchy in a plebiscite.
Most political power lies with the elected government and parliament, but Norway's royals retain a predominantly soft power role in diplomacy and promoting the country around the world.

articles.title: 2 tankers carrying Saudi oil hit in Strait of Hormuz as war shows no signs of stopping
articles.summary: Two supertankers carrying Saudi oil were struck by unknown projectiles within ‌minutes of each other while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday, according to shipping…

image.caption: Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz are seen from Musandam, Oman, on Monday. (Reuters)

blocks.text: World

Two supertankers carrying Saudi oil were struck by unknown projectiles within ‌minutes of each other while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday, according to shipping intelligence and tracking firms Marisks and Kpler.
Tankers struck within minutes of each other off Oman
"The near-simultaneous incidents represent a further escalation in the threat environment ​within the Omani corridor," Marisks said.
The tankers each ​loaded two million barrels of Saudi crude at the Juaymah terminal last week, Kpler data showed.
Oil prices gained on Tuesday after ‌U.S. President Donald Trump threatened further strikes against Iran, following the first exchanges of fire since late July.

In the latest attacks on shipping, the Saudi Arabian-flagged very large crude carrier Sidr was struck by unknown projectiles about 31 kilometres northeast of Khasab, Oman, at around 3:52 p.m. ET, Marisks said.

Minutes later, the Liberian-flagged VLCC ⁠Senegal Prosperity was reportedly struck by three unknown projectiles approximately some 31 kilometres east ⁠of Khasab, Marisks said. All crew aboard were reported safe, it added.

The United ⁠Kingdom ⁠Maritime Trade Operations agency ​reported three projectiles striking a tanker in the same location as it sailed out of ​the Strait of Hormuz, ⁠in what appeared to be the same incident.
Can Iran really launch sea mines from rockets? | About That
Bahri, operator of Sidr, and Sinokor, operator of Senegal Prosperity, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Earlier on Tuesday, Iranian media reported that a Saudi oil tanker was stopped while transiting through the southern corridor ⁠of the Strait of ‌Hormuz.
Energy exports curbed
Iranian and U.S. blockades ⁠of the Strait ⁠of Hormuz have sharply curbed energy exports ‌from the Gulf as both sides tried to assert their authority over the waterway.

Efforts by mediators including Qatar and Oman to broker a deal to reopen the strait, which carried about a fifth of ⁠global oil supplies before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran more than six months ago, have so far proven inconclusive.

Iran said on Tuesday it would reciprocate if the U.S. honoured its commitments under a June interim deal on halting their conflict, but tensions remained high after Trump threatened Tehran with further strikes.

The six-month-old conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before a U.S. attack on Iran's Larak Island on Sunday, which Iran responded to by launching missiles overnight at two U.S. air bases ​in Jordan.

"We're going to hit them hard … There will be a response," a Fox News ​reporter quoted Trump as telling the channel on Monday, although the president separately told reporters that the renewed strikes did not signal a return to full-scale war.

items: Iran's Revolutionary Guard retaliates after U.S. bombs targets in Strait of Hormuz
Iran war hits 6-month milestone with Trump's attention largely elsewhere

blocks.text: A senior Iranian source told Reuters the exchanges of fire were a "limited and contained confrontation" but said Tehran would deliver a ​harsh response if attacked again.

While neither side appears to want a return to all-out war, their pledges to respond to further ⁠attacks highlight how quickly a conflict which has ⁠increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.
'Run and run'
Tehran has repeatedly said it will allow free navigation through the strait only if Washington implements the terms of the deal that was signed by both sides in June but quickly unravelled.
The agreement declared an end to fighting but deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period — which passed without further agreement.
But the heightened tensions this week have renewed fears of oil supply disruptions from the world's key crude-producing region.
"The tit-for-tat missile exchanges between the U.S. and Iran bring validation to those who believe that even if not a 'forever war,' this conflict will run and run," said PVM analyst John Evans.

Thousands ⁠have been killed in the conflict, mainly in Iran and Lebanon, since it began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28. Washington has increasingly relied ⁠on economic pressure to try to force Tehran to stop blockading the strait and end the war.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that countries doing business with ⁠Iran could ⁠face U.S. sanctions and said secondary sanctions are likely to be ​unveiled weekly in the effort to pressure Iran, with an initial focus on banks.
LISTEN | The state of the U.S.-Iran war:
Front Burner27:28Is Iran becoming a 'forever war'?
Iran's central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, said on Tuesday that Tehran had sufficient foreign currency reserves.
The central ​bank was ready to inject up to $2 ⁠billion US into the foreign exchange market to calm recent volatility, Hemmati was quoted as saying by the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
"I am telling the president of the United States: Iran has [foreign] currency and it has enough," he said.
His comments appeared partly aimed at reassuring markets after Iranian officials pointed to growing difficulties for Iran's economy.
