articles.title: NLEX operator MPTC steps up anti-flood measures; find out what
articles.summary: Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation (MPTC), owner and operator of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) said on Tuesday, Sept. 1 that it will continue to work with national and local agencies to speed up…

blocks.text: Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation (MPTC), owner and operator of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) said on Tuesday, Sept. 1 that it will continue to work with national and local agencies to speed up flood-prevention measures and restore reliable travel through the affected expressway corridor.
This, as MPTC told motorists that it recognized their difficulties as far as the recent episodes of floods were concerned.

In a statement, the company also said it is closely coordinating with the Department of Transportation (DOTr), Toll Regulatory Board (TRB) and other government agencies to assess immediate measures to support motorists affected by days of "Habagat" rains and rising water levels in the Pampanga River, while speeding up necessary flood-prevention measures.

As part of a permanent solution to recurring flooding in the San Simon segment of NLEX, MPTC said it will raise the northbound and southbound pavements in Tulaoc, San Simon, Pampanga once the Tulaoc Bridge elevation is completed.

Earlier, Pampanga Governor Lilia Pineda said the flooding reflects a broader drainage problem across the province, with water backing up because downstream areas like Macabebe and Masantol are already full and floodwater cannot readily discharge toward Manila Bay.
MPTC also shared observations by Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Vince Dizon that the sheer volume of water dumped by the southwest monsoon overwhelmed the system.
In a media interview, the DPWH chief acknowledged that pumping alone would not solve the problem as the water would simply flow back.
Heavy flooding disrupted traffic along NLEX, especially in San Simon, Pampanga, where water from the overflowing Pampanga River submerged lanes and caused hours-long gridlock.
Motorists faced diversions and road closures, while government agencies and NLEX management tried to mitigate the situation by deploying barriers, pumps, and emergency crews.

articles.title: Free NLEX toll amid flood? Palace says it's up to management
articles.summary: Waiving the toll fees for motorists affected by heavy traffic at the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) due to severe flooding is up to its management, Malacañang said. Palace Press Officer and…

blocks.text: Waiving the toll fees for motorists affected by heavy traffic at the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) due to severe flooding is up to its management, Malacañang said.
Palace Press Officer and Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro said the directive should come from the expressway's management.
President Marcos could only give a recommendation, but stressed that the management knows what actions should it take.

"Siguro, bago po magmungkahi ang Pangulo, alam naman po ng NLEX kung ano ang nangyari dito. At ano ang kanilang responsibilidad, dapat sa kanila manggaling ang kautusan na ito (Perhaps, before the President makes a recommendation, NLEX already knows what happened here and what their responsibilities are. The directive should have come from them in the first place)," Castro said in a Palace briefing on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
'Avoid NLEX'
The Palace official also advised motorists to avoid NLEX instead, arguing that waiving the toll fee would only further decongest the expressway.

"Iyong stranded doon? Libre? Bakit ka pa papasok kung trapik na. Huwag na muna kayong dumaan doon, kasi kung hindi naman siya makakalusot, so ano ang purpose ng libre (Those who are stranded there? Toll free? Why would you still enter if there is already heavy traffic? For now, avoid passing through that area, because if you won’t be able to get through anyway, then what’s the point of making it free)?" Castro questioned.

"Magandang adhikain iyong libre. Pero kung ililibre natin, ‘di ba mas maraming sasakyan ang papasok. So kapag maraming papasok na sasakyan, mas lalong magkakaroon ng trapik. So dapat nga iwasan na muna nila itong NLEX (Free toll is a good initiative. But if we make it free, won’t more vehicles enter? And when more vehicles enter, it will only make the traffic worse. So, for now, they should really avoid using NLEX)," she stressed.
'Imposing sanction, not a priority'

Asked whether the President would instruct the Toll Regulatory Board to impose sanctions on the management of North Luzon Expressway for hours-long traffic caused by floods, Castro said it is not the President's priority at present.

"Kahapon ay napag-usapan ang problemang iyan, pero hindi napag-usapan kung anumang sanction. Ang nasa proposal po ng Pangulo ay paano po matutulungan iyong mga naipit nating mga kababayan sa NLEX (Yesterday, that problem was discussed, but no sanctions were discussed. The President’s proposal focuses on how we can help our fellow citizens who are stranded on NLEX)," Castro said.

"Most probably, kapag nakausap ko ang Pangulo ay itatanong ko po iyan, dahil hindi po sa ngayon ang pag-sanction ang inuuna ng Pangulo, kung hindi ang kaginhawaan ng ating mga motorista (Most probably, when I speak with the President, I will ask him about that. For now, the President’s priority is not imposing sanctions, but ensuring the convenience and welfare of our motorists)," Castro added.

articles.title: Putin-Modi meeting at SCO: Can Russia-India ties hold?
articles.summary: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to meet in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, Bishkek, on Monday on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization…

blocks.text: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to meet in Kyrgyzstan’s capital, Bishkek, on Monday on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit — a bloc often seen as a counterweight to US influence.
The meeting comes against the backdrop of the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted global energy markets, and Russia’s war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
India has remained engaged with the SCO while resisting efforts to turn it into an anti-Western bloc. Its position reflects a broader effort to maintain relationships with competing powers.

That approach is under greater pressure. Russia remains under Western sanctions over the war in Ukraine. Meanwhile, India has faced US pressure over its purchases of Russian oil, alongside wider trade tensions.
A former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, told DW that India’s relationship with Russia should not be seen as directed against the US.
“India has a long-standing strategic relationship with Russia. This is not directed against any country but intended to help India meet its national goals,” said Shankar.
Energy ties deepen between India, Russia
Energy has become the most visible change in the India-Russia relationship.

Before 2022, when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it supplied only a small share of India’s crude imports. Discounted Russian oil rapidly changed that, making Moscow one of India’s biggest suppliers.

It has also become the most contentious part of India’s relationship with the US, which has pressed New Delhi to reduce its purchases from Russia. India maintains that securing affordable and reliable energy is a national interest.

The disruption to traditional energy supplies has made that calculation more complicated. This year’s US-Israel war on Iran and disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz have affected India’s purchases from the Gulf and pushed up prices.
Shankar said India is responding by diversifying its sources of supply, including both Russia and the US.
“In the long run, a transition to a non-fossil fuel economy would strengthen India’s energy independence. But this will not happen overnight,” she added.
Until then, Shankar said, India will take steps it considers necessary to stabilize supplies and protect its people.
Future of India-Russia defense cooperation
Defense remains the other major pillar, but here the direction of travel is clearer: India’s dependence on Russian equipment has been declining.
The Ukraine war has raised questions over Russia’s production capacity, delivery schedules and ability to supply spare parts after decades as a major supplier of India’s military hardware.

“India remains one of Russia’s oldest and largest arms buyers, and perhaps the last major one,” Aravind Yelery, an associate professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University in the Indian capital, New Delhi, told DW.

“New Delhi is increasingly reluctant to commit to Russia’s fifth-generation fighter program and has little appetite for new Russian hardware unless it can be incorporated into India’s indigenous production plans,” he added.
While India has diversified its purchases, that does not mean the defense relationship is disappearing.
However, the terms are changing, with India looking for a relationship that contributes to its own defense production, so that it can move away from simply buying finished systems.
The China question
Russia’s growing dependence on China has also become an unavoidable part of the India-Russia equation.

Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in early 2022, China has become indispensable to Russia as a market, supplier and economic partner. That has reduced Moscow’s ability to serve as a counterweight to Beijing.
Yelery sees an important distinction in the two relationships.
“Strategically, Russia’s relationship with China remains structurally transactional, a dependence it can ill afford to compromise, whereas its relationship with India rests on partnership,” he said.
India still has reasons to keep Moscow close: energy, defense, access to the Russian market and a longstanding political relationship across Eurasia. But the strategic calculation has changed.
India’s ‘America plus’ strategy
Strategic affairs expert C Raja Mohan said that Russia’s growing dependence on China has changed its strategic value for India.
“Russia is no longer in a position to help India balance China,” Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University, told DW.
This changes India’s expectations from the relationship with Russia.

The emphasis is increasingly on specific interests — energy security, defense supplies, trade and access to technology — while India’s larger strategic weight increasingly rests on relationships with the US and its allies.
India has expanded defense and technology cooperation with Washington, while deepening ties with partners such as France and Israel.
Mohan describes this approach as an “America plus” strategy, whereby India maintains its partnership with the US while widening its engagement with other major powers.
“India is trying to reduce its exposure to American volatility, but it still recognizes that Washington is its most important partner,” he said.
What do Modi and Putin want?
Rajan Kumar, a professor of Russian studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said Putin wants reassurance that India will remain engaged with Moscow despite pressure from Washington.
“President Putin needs an assurance from Prime Minister Modi that India will not ditch Russia when the latter is facing the worst possible crisis after the 1990s,” Kumar told DW.
He expects continuity rather than a dramatic reset. “I think it is more about continuation of existing ties amid US pressure,” he added.

Energy trade and payment mechanisms, ways to increase Indian exports to Russia, defense cooperation and the two countries’ assessments of the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran are likely to remain important.
The bigger test will come in Delhi in September, when Putin is expected to return for the BRICS summit.
The Bishkek meeting can keep the political relationship on track, but the Delhi talks will show whether that political continuity can produce progress on trade, energy, defense and technology.

The relationship is no longer what it was before the Ukraine war. Energy has become far more important, India’s defense dependence is being recalibrated, and Russia’s closeness to China has altered the strategic equation.

“The relationship has a value that goes beyond individual deals. Putin appears well aware that India carries an independent strategic weight that China’s structural leverage cannot substitute,” said Yelery. /dl

articles.title: The floods keep coming. Nepal keeps starting over
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — When the flash flood tore through the Bhotekoshi corridor on August 26, it hit a road that had already been taken once. The stretch connecting Syaphrubesi to the Rasuwagadhi border…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — When the flash flood tore through the Bhotekoshi corridor on August 26, it hit a road that had already been taken once. The stretch connecting Syaphrubesi to the Rasuwagadhi border crossing was rebuilt and reopened about a month after the July 2025 flood that destroyed the “friendship bridge” linking Nepal to China and killed at least eight people. That repair was the fast part. The rest of the valley’s reconstruction was still unfinished 13 months later when the water came back, this time carrying ice and debris from a collapse high on Langtang Lirung.

“People were starting to forget the pain of last year’s flood,” Kaisang Nurpu Tamang, chairperson of Gosaikunda Rural Municipality, told the Kathmandu Post. “Everything was becoming normal.” Tamang’s own municipal building, thirteen kilometres up the valley in Timure, is gone now too, swept away along with the rest.

The 2026 flood has killed more than 900 people in Nepal, with over 4,200 still missing. Forty-one bridges and 42 kilometres of road were gone in a single morning. Swarnim Wagle, the country’s finance minister, told Reuters the preliminary estimate to rebuild could be anywhere between $4 billion and $5 billion. Binod Chaudhary, Nepal’s only billionaire, told Bloomberg Television days earlier that rebuilding could cost $5 billion.

Both estimates are less than what the 2015 earthquake reconstruction took. It is a fair comparison, except that Nepal was still working through pieces of that earthquake recovery when the floods of 2024 arrived, killing 300 more people across the eastern lowlands. Then came Rasuwagadhi in 2025. Last week’s was the latest.

For anyone paying attention — which most Nepalis are — three consecutive years of disaster have been described in strikingly similar language. Officials called last week’s Bhotekoshi flood unprecedented. The 2025 flood was described the same way. The 2024 floods were the worst rainfall the region had recorded since 1970. At some point, one has to ask: when the same word is used every year for the same kind of event, does it still describe the event, or has it started describing our relationship to it?

I asked Nepal’s foreign minister, Shishir Khanal, whether the government sees a pattern here or is still treating each flood as its own emergency. “We should anticipate such disasters are likely to be more frequent occurrences than in the past, and be prepared for them,” he said.

blocks.caption: The 2026 flood has killed more than 900 people in Nepal, with close to 4,250 still missing.  Angad Dhakal/TKP

blocks.text: There is a useful contrast next door. Bangladesh used to be cyclone country the way Nepal is flood country now — a place where a single storm could kill on a scale that defied comprehension. The 1970 Bhola cyclone is estimated to have killed between 300,000 and 500,000 people, among the deadliest disasters of the twentieth century. Bangladesh did not stop having cyclones after that. It has been hit by dozens since, but Bangladeshis now have a system that works. They have built a national network of concrete shelters, trained tens of thousands of volunteer evacuators village by village, and tied a warning system so tightly to that structure that a storm of comparable strength now kills in the dozens.

There’s a caveat in the comparison, of course. A cyclone is a meteorological event that announces itself days out, and the people at risk live in a flat, densely settled area where they can be moved to a shelter. A glacial collapse, like the one last week, forms in a high-altitude terrain, sometimes across an international border, and arrives down a narrow valley in minutes.

Nepal’s own mountain research body has been saying something similar about the ground itself. Five months before last week’s flood, the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) published findings that ice loss across the Hindu Kush Himalaya had doubled since 2000. Of 38 glaciers it monitors, only seven meet global monitoring standards; large parts of the range, it said, remain unmonitored altogether.

“We are trying to navigate a rapidly changing future with an incomplete map,” Mohd Farooq Azam, a cryosphere specialist at ICIMOD, said at the time. “Accelerated changes in water flows and cryosphere risks could remain undetected until the impacts are severe.” ICIMOD’s director general put it even more matter-of-factly. “These aren’t blind spots becoming surprises anymore,” he said. “They are our new reality.”

Nepal’s pattern over the last three years runs the other way from Bangladesh’s. Each flood over the past few years has been met with an improvised response built largely from scratch: army units are mobilised after the fact and drone surveys are ordered once the water level has receded.

“Our primary challenge is that our initial hydrological station was swept away on the first day,” Dharmaraj Upreti, chief executive of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told the Post on Sunday. Replacing it, he said, requires the consent of both Nepal and China — a diplomatic step now unfolding in the middle of a disaster.

blocks.caption: Each flood over the past few years has been met with an improvised response built largely from scratch: army units are mobilised after the fact, and drone surveys are ordered once the water level has receded. Photo: Courtesy of Nepali Army

blocks.text: Prime Minister Balendra Shah, five months into office, said the state has been mobilised at full capacity. He visited Nuwakot to assess the damage, which is what his predecessor did after the 2025 flood, standing in front of a different stretch of the same river. Part of what makes the pattern hard to see, let alone address, in a country like Nepal is that each flood resets the political clock. Every natural disaster is an act of geology or weather that no government could have prevented, so the response gets judged only on the speed and visibility of relief.

When the Post asked the head of NDRRMA what it had learned, Upreti had this to say: “We are reviewing helicopter deployment logistics, helipad placements, body management procedures, and the availability of body bags. We have many lessons to implement from this experience.” But these are machinery for responding faster next time, not for catching the next flood before it happens.

Tamang, the Gosaikunda chair whose rural municipality has yet to receive federal coordination since the flood, described the same sequencing problem locally. A geologist needs to survey the area to determine what ground is safe, he said, before any long-term plan can be made. “Right now, we haven’t even been able to think that far,” he said.

Minister Khanal told me that two months before the flood, he had been pressing Chinese counterparts for a bilateral framework on hydrological and meteorological data-sharing across the border. The two sides, he said on Monday, were actively exchanging communications toward a framework agreement. It was not in place as of last week.

“I was told by some scientists who know the region very well that the glacial collapse didn’t even have a name in Nepali,” Khanal said, which probably means that Nepal either didn’t know it existed or didn’t consider it an imminent threat. Since the disaster, he said, Chinese authorities have been sharing real-time information on the new lake that formed upstream — the cooperation the framework was meant to formalize before there was a lake to worry about.

That new lake, high in the mountains in Tibet and formed by the same landslide, is being labelled “extremely concerning” by global scientists. Tamang, cut off from his own municipal building, said he and his community have no idea what’s happening above them. “There’s no electricity here, the telephone network still has no signal,” he said. “So we’re quite confused about what’s happening further up.” /dl

articles.title: Thai resort city Pattaya readies for US carrier’s 5,000 sailors
articles.summary: THAILAND — A US aircraft carrier at the center of a political row over conditions on board was set to arrive in Thailand on Tuesday, the first port call for its 5,000 crew since November. The…

blocks.text: THAILAND — A US aircraft carrier at the center of a political row over conditions on board was set to arrive in Thailand on Tuesday, the first port call for its 5,000 crew since November.

The resort city of Pattaya, a rest-and-recreation destination for US troops since the Vietnam War, has stepped up security as it prepares to welcome the sailors and Marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln.
“About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” provincial Governor Narit Niramaiwong told AFP.
The nuclear-powered ship left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.

Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on board — including attempted suicides — have made headlines in the United States, provoking criticism of President Donald Trump’s war against Iran.
Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said the massive carrier would dock just after midnight (around 1701 GMT on Tuesday) at Laem Chabang port.
Around 40 buses have been laid on to transport the sailors to Pattaya and back in staggered groups until the carrier departs on Sunday.
“They come to relax because it’s been almost 280 days since anyone came ashore,” Poramase said in a Facebook post.

blocks.caption: An aerial photo shows the main beach in Pattaya on June 1, 2020. FILE PHOTO/Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: “Our preparations will focus on safety and ensuring fair pricing, so we don’t take advantage of them.”
No jet skis or cannabis
Once a sleepy fishing village, Pattaya was transformed by the Vietnam War in the 1960s, when US soldiers on leave began coming for rest and recreation (R&R).
The city has since become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.
Poramase told AFP there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied it was linked to the US arrivals.
In his Facebook post, the mayor said he was hoping the soldiers could bring in up to 100 million Thai baht ($3 million) during their stay — a boon to the city during low season.

They have been banned from water sports such as jet skis, and from taking advantage of Thailand’s lax cannabis laws, he added, encouraging them to take part in the city’s many other attractions, from malls to religious sites.

“We’re happy to get business from anybody,” Nicko, the French owner of a go-go bar in Pattaya, told AFP. “We’ll have to be careful because as we know, things can get out of hand with alcohol involved.” /dl

articles.title: Used bookstores navigate 'suspicious' bulk orders amid AI book-shredding fears
articles.summary: Used booksellers in Canada are navigating how to handle mysterious bulk orders, as suspicions grow that companies are buying up their old books so they can be scanned for AI training — and then…

image.caption: Canadian bookstore owners say they've been getting unusual requests for bulk orders, which they suspect are being sent to AI companies to train large language models. (Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Used booksellers in Canada are navigating how to handle mysterious bulk orders, as suspicions grow that companies are buying up their old books so they can be scanned for AI training — and then trashed.

Their concern stems from a U.S. copyright lawsuit brought against AI giant Anthropic, which revealed the company was spending millions on physical books, chopping off the spines to quickly scan the pages to train its large language model Claude, and discarding the remains.

A 404 Media investigation revealed two weeks ago that large orders of books are also going to an Amazon facility in Las Vegas to undergo "destructive scanning" for LLM training, offering further evidence that the practice may be widespread. Similar concerns are being raised by bookstore owners in Australia and elsewhere.

Physical books, particularly those published before OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022, are in demand for AI companies. That's partly because some experts say the language models degrade when repeatedly trained on their own output, so they need to be fed with content that is guaranteed to be free of AI-generated text.
Some AI companies have also encountered legal issues using copyrighted digital content.
'There's something not right here'

Peter Sellers, proprietor at Sellers & Newel bookstore in Toronto, says bulk book requests in the past have come from designers staging homes or film sets, and typically are accompanied by colour and size requirements.
But around June, he started getting "very suspicious" calls for bulk orders for seemingly random lists of books, he told CBC News in an interview.
"It's kind of tempting, because I can unload a lot of stuff that may otherwise be unsaleable," he said. "And then you start thinking about it — no, no no, there's something not right here."
The facts about AI companies destroying books

On June 10, he received a message on LinkedIn from someone claiming to represent data engineering company Innodata, saying they were "currently looking to purchase large volumes of secondhand books" and "exploring potential sourcing partners."

Sellers said he ignored the request and thought little of the message until he later read an article about AI book scanning. Suddenly, he said, all those "odd" requests seemed to make a lot more sense.
"My whole staff is now attuned to this," he said.

items: Twitch users: Amazon could use your content for AI training. Here's what you should know
Meta launches new AI model as Zuckerberg lays out vision for open-weight AI

blocks.text: "If somebody wants stuff in bulk, the answer's no — unless you're a designer that we know or someone we've dealt with, or you've got some kind of legitimate credentials and you want these books for a legitimate reason," he said.

Innodata, based in Ridgefield, N.J., offers "data and domain expertise" for AI projects, according to its website, which says it works with "seven of the world’s largest tech companies." Innodata recently posted a senior book buyer job on LinkedIn.
CBC News has requested comment from Innodata but has not heard back.
B.C. company named as suspected supplier

Other booksellers told CBC News they have received similar requests in recent months, often for obscure educational books that sat unsold for years. Some say it's hard to turn down those requests, especially in an industry that's not exactly booming.
The names of the companies making these requests seem to change quickly, sellers say, and none of the buyers have publicly admitted to supplying AI companies.

Zoom Books, a company based in Pitt Meadows, B.C., that says it resells and recycles secondhand books, has been frequently mentioned in online bookseller forums and on Reddit for making large numbers of perplexing bulk orders.

Booksellers in Spain, Germany, Australia, New Zealand and elsewhere have raised suspicions that Zoom's orders are intended to be resold for AI scanning, though none have shown proof that this is the case.
AI-written books divide publishing world
Patrick Hempelmann, the owner of a BMV Books in Toronto, told CBC News that Zoom started buying hundreds of books from him about six months ago.

The orders were primarily for specialized technical books with small print runs, typically selling for between $5 and $30, he said. Some were old medical texts or graduate student-level math and physics books that had sat on shelves for a decade.
"We couldn't really figure out what their motivation was or what their specialty was, because they were kind of buying things all over the place. There seemed to be no real rhyme or reason," he said.
Hempelmann said Zoom Books made the purchases online through AbeBooks, a third-party seller, and BMV fulfilled the orders.
The orders were shipped to Wood Dale, Ill., care of PrepFort, a third-party logistics and fulfilment centre that works with major companies including Amazon, Walmart and Shopify.
Hempelmann says he was unaware of the AI book scanning controversy until CBC News contacted him, but after reading about it, he says it's "just sad."
"I mean, we are booksellers. Books shouldn't be destroyed," he said.
Another Canadian bookseller who did not want to be quoted in this article told CBC News they received similar orders from Zoom Books several weeks ago.

Until mid-March, Zoom Books' chief growth officer, Reed Pannell, was a business development director at U.K.-based World of Books, according to his LinkedIn account. Court documents reported on by The Washington Post named World of Books one of the companies that Anthropic purchased from for its secretive destructive scanning project.

In an email to CBC News, Pannell said that Zoom does not sell to Anthropic, but he did not directly confirm that the company hasn't dealt with any other AI companies or shipped books to companies that may have scanned and destroyed them.
Pannell would not disclose Zoom's customers, citing confidentiality.

items: With a decline in reading is our capacity to think eroding?
Canada's data centre boom, and backlash

blocks.text: He said Zoom collects and processes more than three million books each month and that its mission is to keep books in circulation.
"We acquire secondhand books and resell them intact. We do not digitize books," Pannell said. "Our priority is always reuse, and when a book can no longer be rehomed, it is responsibly recycled."
PrepFort co-founder Sufyaan Kalota said in an email to CBC News that the company "cannot share any details regarding our customer agreements due to our confidentiality commitments."
Buyers may be 'cat's paw': store owner

Chris Brayshaw, owner of Pulpfiction Books in Vancouver, says he saw a two-week "sales bump" several weeks ago where he was making about a dozen sales a day of primarily non-fiction books that he considered "dated" and had been sitting for years.
The books were purchased at prices between $10 and $80 US each and shipped to various locations across North America and Europe, he told CBC News.

Brayshaw would not provide the names of the buyers, but says he suspects they were "limited liability companies created specifically for this purpose, maybe as kind of a cat's paw to disguise the ultimate source of where the items were going."
He says he has refused sales of valuable books in the past when the purchasers had destructive or esthetic reasons for buying.
Although Brayshaw has strong negative feelings about AI, the books purchased by the mysterious bulk buyers were ones he was generally "delighted" to finally move.
"I don't think it was a great loss to civilization," he said.

blocks.text: Morning opening: 12 killed in latest round of Russian attacks on Ukraine

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
At least 12 people, including an Indian citizen, were killed in overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine with “dozens” more injured, the country’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

blocks.caption: A woman looks out of a window of her apartment damaged by a Russian missile strike in the town of Boryspil, amid Russia’s attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv region, Ukraine. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

blocks.text: Zelenskyy said the Russian strikes also left “thousands” of families without electricity in the Odesa region, and a border crossing with Romania “deliberately damaged.”

Over the last few days, Ukraine suffered a series of prolonged Russian attacks, including daytime bombing, in the latest attempt to “wear down” the war-torn country. Kyiv has now been targeted for six consecutive days.

The issue of Russian threat will no doubt also come up during an informal meeting of EU defence ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, with some suggestions that Germany could be close to attributing last month’s Leipzig incidents to Russia.

A number of other countries also saw incidents believed to be linked with Russia, including a suspected arson of a drone factory in Poland on Sunday night. Both Estonia and Latvia briefly activated their air alert systems on Tuesday amid reports of drones near their airspace.
I will bring you all the latest here.
In other news, over in Norway, King Hakoon VIII will take his oath in the Norwegian parliament following the death of his father, King Harald. I will keep an eye on that, too.
It’s Tuesday, 1 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 13m agoGermany to formally blame Russia for attempted Leipzig drone attack today - reports
38m agoMorning opening: 12 killed in latest round of Russian attacks on Ukraine

blocks.text: Germany to formally blame Russia for attempted Leipzig drone attack today - reports
Separately, we are picking up reports in the German press that Germany is set to formally blame Russia for last month’s failed drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig.

Bild newspaper says the German interior and foreign ministers are set to announce the results of their investigation into the incident later today. This is yet to be formally confirmed by any of the ministries involved.
Over the weekend, German chancellor Friedrich Merz sort of suggested that a formal response from the government was coming soon, but did not go into the details.
I will keep an eye on this.

On behalf of the Irish presidency in the EU Council, Ireland’s defence minister Helen McEntee said the talks in Wicklow come “at a moment of profound challenge for all of us in terms of defence and security,” with closer cooperation needed “more than ever.”
Ukraine, maritime security, and resilience against hybrid and cyber threats will be top of the agenda today, she says.

Opening the meeting, EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said today’s talks in Ireland will primarily focus on the EU’s support for Ukraine, with further discussions on other current affairs, including maritime security and Lebanon.

She said that Nato remained “the cornerstone of our security,” but with the US urging its European partners to “assume greater responsibility for their own defence,” there is more scope for internal discussions.
She urged ministers to “challenge the conventional thinking to look beyond simply doing more of the same,” and look for ways in which Europe can innovate and offer new capabilities.

Curiously, Kallas also said she would be forming “a high-level group of former political and military leaders from several EU countries, but also the UK and Ukraine, to have a fresh look at how to respond to current and increasing, very real, military threats.”
Will look out for names.

articles.title: Nxled thumps PLDT, bounces back from loss
articles.summary: Nxled came out sizzling dumped defending champion PLDT, 25-19, 25-22, 25-20, to barge into the winning column of the PVL Invitational 2026 at the Smart Araneta Coliseum on Tuesday, Sept.1. Still…

blocks.text: Nxled came out sizzling dumped defending champion PLDT, 25-19, 25-22, 25-20, to barge into the winning column of the PVL Invitational 2026 at the Smart Araneta Coliseum on Tuesday, Sept.1.

Still licking their wounds from their four-set loss to the Creamline Cool Smashers less than 24 hours ago, the Chameleons took out their frustrations on the High Speed Hitters to even their win-loss record at 1-1.
MJ Phillips spearheaded the Nxled assault by pumping in eight kills and four aces to finish with 13 points, while skipper Myla Pablo took charge defensively with three blocks to chip in 12 points.
Nxled coach Ettore Guidetti said his stalwarts responded well with the defeat by playing better.
“(Today) simply confirmed we played pretty good volleyball. We’re getting better. Our defense especially worked better compared to (yesterday) and we also served much, much better today,” he said.
So impressive were the Chameleons that they only gave up 12 points on errors throughout the one hour, 30-minute match compared to the High Speed Hitters, who stumbled into 21 unforced errors.

Though PLDT held the edge in attacks, 44-41, Nxled made the most of its net defense with seven blocks. The Chameleons also capitalized on the High Speed Hitters’ shaky first ball, firing six aces to keep PLDT on the back foot.
Lyann De Guzman also paced Nxled by pouring all her 10 points on attacks, while Gel Cayuna distributed the ball well with 15 excellent sets.

Savi Davison was the lone bright spot for PLDT after erupting for 20 points, but couldn’t get the needed support as none from her teammates scored in double figures. Mika Reyes was limited to eight points, while Kianna Dy and Majoy Baron were held to just four and three points, respectively.
The High Speed Hitters fell to a 1-1card, failing to follow up their four-set win over EST Cola on Monday, Aug. 31.

articles.title: Foreign debt service burden climbs to $6.21 billion at end-May on higher principal payments
articles.summary: The Philippines ’ external debt service burden (DSB) increased by 4.8 percent to $6.21 billion in the first five months of 2026 from $5.93 billion in the same period in 2025 on the back of scheduled…

blocks.text: The Philippines ’ external debt service burden (DSB) increased by 4.8 percent to $6.21 billion in the first five months of 2026 from $5.93 billion in the same period in 2025 on the back of scheduled repayments. The latest Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) data showed that the increase in the country’s servicing of its foreign debt was fueled by a rise in principal payments, which offset a marginal decline in interest payments (IPs). An increasing external DSB indicates that a larger portion of the country’s financial resources is being used to pay off foreign obligations. Amortization, or principal payments, rose by 13.6 percent to $3.01 billion during the five-month period from $2.65 billion last year. Meanwhile, IPs edged down by 2.3 percent to $3.2 billion from $3.28 billion a year ago. SM Investment Corp. (SMIC) group economist Robert Dan Roces said the rising debt service largely reflects “scheduled repayments, not financial stress.” “More debt matured during the period, pushing principal payments higher, while IPs declined. With ample reserves and steady foreign currency inflows, the country remains well-positioned to meet its external obligations,” Roces said. As of end-March, the Philippines’ total external debt stood at $147.35 billion, a slight increase from $146.74 billion a year ago. Government debt accounted for approximately $95.66 billion, or nearly two-thirds of total, while the private sector accounted for $51.7 billion. Foreign borrowings were equivalent to 26.1 percent of the country’s annualized gross national income (GNI) as of end-March, down from 27.8 percent a year ago. Meanwhile, the ratio fell to 30 percent of annualized gross domestic product (GDP) as of end-March, compared with 31.5 percent as of end-March 2025. GNI measures the total income generated by a country’s residents, both domestically and abroad, while GDP accounts for local output. As of end-May, the DSB-to-export shipments ratio eased to 21.6 percent from 22.4 percent in the same period of 2025, while the DSB-to-current account receipts ratio remained unchanged at 8.9 percent. Furthermore, gross international reserves (GIR) stood at $103.99 billion by end-May, down from $105.18 billion a year ago. Despite the lower reserves, the annualized GIR-to-DSB ratio rose to 773.6 percent from 616.2 percent a year ago, reflecting a strengthened liquidity buffer relative to the DSB. According to the BSP, the foreign DSB represents principal and IPs. This covers payments on fixed medium- and long-term (MLT) credits, including those from the Washington-based multilateral lender International Monetary Fund (IMF) and new money facilities. It also includes IPs on fixed and revolving short-term liabilities of banks and nonbanks. However, it excludes prepayments on future maturities of foreign loans and principal payments on short-term obligations.

articles.title: 11 Pangasinan towns placed on alert ahead of opening of two San Roque Dam gates
articles.summary: SAN MANUEL, Pangasinan — Residents in San Manuel, San Nicolas, Asingan, Tayug, Sta. Maria, Rosales, Villasis, Sto. Tomas, Alcala, Bautista and Bayambang are being urged to remain alert as the San…

blocks.text: Pangasinan Provincial Mobile Force Company personnel inspect San Roque Dam and monitor water levels as part of disaster preparedness and critical infrastructure security efforts on Tuesday. (Photo courtesy of PMFC via Liezle Inigo)

SAN MANUEL, Pangasinan — Residents in San Manuel, San Nicolas, Asingan, Tayug, Sta. Maria, Rosales, Villasis, Sto. Tomas, Alcala, Bautista and Bayambang are being urged to remain alert as the San Roque Dam prepares to open two gates beginning 8 a.m. on Sept. 2, 2026.
The National Power Corporation (NPC) said the planned gate-opening will release water at a rate of about 300 cubic meters per second (cms), equivalent to a two-meter gate opening.
As of 12 noon on Sept. 1, the dam’s water level was recorded at 283.68 meters above sea level (MASL).
The NPC said the discharge is a precautionary measure to manage the continuing rise in the dam’s water level.
Residents living near riverbanks and downstream areas are advised to closely monitor official advisories from local disaster risk reduction and management offices.

articles.title: Canada’s ruling Liberals sweep special elections in boost to Mark Carney
articles.summary:
Three projected victories are ‘a message’ to US that Carney ‘has the support of the Canadian people’, says one lawmaker

Canada’s ruling Liberal party has swept three special elections in a…

blocks.text: Canada’s ruling Liberal party has swept three special elections in a result that showed voters backing the prime minister, Mark Carney, after his face-off with the US president, Donald Trump.
The Canadian Press, Canada’s national news agency, projected Liberal victories in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord in Quebec, Beaches-East York in Toronto and North Vancouver-Capilano in British Columbia.

Carney said the results of Monday’s votes amounted to an endorsement of his government’s approach. “At this consequential time for Canada, voters have placed their trust in our government’s plan,” he said in a statement.

The Quebec result was the most dramatic shift. The Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil was projected to win big in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, a district held by the opposition Conservatives since 2018. The region is home to aluminium producers, dairy farms and other industries caught in the escalating trade war.
“This victory means we can maintain Canadian unity all across the country,” Gobeil said.
The other two seats were previously held by Liberals. In British Columbia, Carney’s former deputy chief of staff Braeden Caley won North Vancouver-Capilano.
The Liberal lawmaker Hedy Fry told the Canadian Broadcasting Corp: “The United States is getting a message tonight. Our leader has the support of the Canadian people.”

US-Canada trade talks collapsed on 21 August after the two sides failed to reach a deal, and Trump imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20bn of Canadian goods. Canada responded with plans for tariffs on US products.

Trump has escalated his attacks on Canada since the talks failed. He signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America,” and the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said on Monday that Canada had limited leverage in the dispute because the US economy was roughly 13 times larger. Trump has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st state.
Meanwhile, Carney has accelerated efforts to deepen economic ties with Europe and other partners.
The Liberal sweep would bring Carney’s party to 173 seats in the 343-seat House of Commons, further strengthening its position in parliament.
The special elections were called after the lawmakers who previously held the three seats resigned from parliament earlier this year.

Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University, said the sweep showed Carney retaining strong support across regions, but called the Quebec result the most significant. He said the easy win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord likely reflected, in part, the popularity in Quebec of Carney’s decision “to pull the plug on trade negotiations with the White House”.

He said the Conservative collapse there was also bad news for the party’s leader, Pierre Poilievre. The party had about 41% of the vote in last year’s federal elections, but fell to about 13% and third place on Monday. “These numbers do look bad,” Béland said.
Carney won Canada’s election last year, fuelled by public anger over Trump’s annexation threats, and he has vowed to reduce Canada’s reliance on the US.
